abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.

title: Bayesian Nonparametric Survival Regression with Time-Varying Covariates and Random Effects
abstract: In longitudinal survival studies, biomarkers and treatments change across visits, their associations with event risk may be nonlinear and change over time, and subjects with identical measurements may differ in risk. Existing tree-ensemble survival models address these features separately: discrete-time formulations accommodate covariate updates without subject-specific random effects, and hazard-based ensembles with frailty take covariates as fixed at baseline. We propose Time-Varying Survival Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (TVSurvBART), a continuous-time hazard model combining a flexible baseline, a log-linear tree ensemble, and subject-specific random intercepts and slopes; covariates enter as predictable step processes, and interval-start time among the tree inputs lets effects change across visits. Integrated exposure offsets absorb the within-interval variation of the baseline and random slopes, so the tree leaves retain conjugate updates. Re-centering moves along likelihood-invariant directions and alternating centered and non-centered covariance updates address the resulting posterior dependence. In two simulation families, TVSurvBART's landmark predictions from held-out subjects' histories up to the landmark time have higher time-dependent AUC than the Cox, frailty Cox, and forest benchmarks in every setting and lower Brier scores in all but one comparison, although population-summary gains are not uniform. In the CARRA juvenile idiopathic arthritis registry, discrimination for recorded flares is similar to Cox regression, while a secondary interval-probability score favors TVSurvBART.

title: GridAnchor: Specialized Multi-Agent AI for Safeguarding Autonomous Energy Systems Against Cyber-Physical Hallucinations
abstract: Autonomous energy systems increasingly chain specialized learned agents, such as a forecaster, a state estimator and a dispatcher that may be a language model. These agents can emit confident outputs that contradict physics, and downstream agents may act on them. We define such cyber-physical hallucinations and their cascades, organize them in eight types, and build CPH-Bench, a generator of labeled episodes on SimBench feeders. We propose GridAnchor, a verification layer whose Physics-Residual Graph Transformer scores every claim from residuals between the claims, the measurements and a linearized grid model. Mondrian conformal p-values with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure turn the scores into decisions, a root head attributes cascades, and a quadratic program repairs unsafe actions with a voltage margin calibrated at repaired steps. On a simulated rural medium-voltage feeder, GridAnchor reaches a message-level area under the precision-recall curve of 0.846, against 0.837 for the strongest of six baselines, a difference within the confidence interval. It leads on estimates and actions, whereas a self-consistency check that knows the label tolerances reaches 0.874 by leading on forecasts. The false-alarm rate stays within 0.17 percentage points of the nominal level on steps without injected hallucinations. In closed loop, GridAnchor leaves no bus outside the voltage band on the test days, against 0.0700% of the bus-steps without protection, and simpler detectors with the same mitigation come close. Stale but coherent messages and single-bus forecast errors remain mostly undetected.

title: An AI-Powered Multiverse Analysis of Empirical Finance Research: Evidence from Reused Natural Experiments
abstract: Empirical finance research often reuses natural experiments to study other outcomes, raising concerns about multiple testing and publication bias. We use AI agents to run a multiverse analysis of 324 papers that reuse 13 natural experiments. The agents rebuild the data, reproduce each paper's main estimate and re-estimate it across grids totaling 62,409 estimated defensible specifications. Based on the reproductions and the specification grids, we develop measures of empirical robustness. We reproduce 42% of the main estimates of claims with a signed effect under the papers' own specifications. Across all defensible specifications, on average 25% keep the published sign and have $p < 0.10$. Across experiments, claims based on regression discontinuity are more robust than difference-in-differences claims. Within experiments, claims about first-order effects, claims with larger published $t$-statistics, claims whose authors' data or code we find, claims in top journals, and claims with fewer earlier papers on the same experiment are more robust. Claims on experiments that more papers reuse are not less robust on average. Our findings quantify how much published claims depend on analysis choices, thereby showing that large-scale multiverse analysis becomes feasible with agentic coding.

title: From Self-Play RL to Constrained Control: Distilling DiffMPC Students with DAgger
abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.

title: When AI Analysts Disagree: Agentic Multiverse Analysis and the Robustness of Empirical Research
abstract: Every empirical analysis on observational data rests on dozens of defensible analytical choices ("forks") that its readers cannot see. We develop an agentic multiverse analysis (AMA) framework that makes a conclusion's sensitivity to those choices visible at scale, and we position it as a decision-support instrument for human experts. A pilot study first deploys 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset and one set of research questions and finds that they disagree through the same defensible methodological choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range. AI peer review leaves their dispersion almost unchanged. Exposure to top-rated exemplar reports then collapses it, largely through imitation rather than analysis. Built on those lessons, AMA has agents enumerate a published paper's possible fork space, score every fork against a validity rubric, execute the validated specification grid, and cross-examine one another's work under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), the framework reproduces every paper's original estimates, and shows that some conclusions hold across every specification the assessment validates, while others are sensitive to individual analytical choices that the published texts do not discuss. The case studies suggest our AMA-based measures can serve as robustness proxies for empirical findings. AI makes multiverse analysis practical, where it once required resources few research teams can afford: our exercises take hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper. We discuss the implications for replication policy and for AI-assisted peer review in information systems.

title: From FAIR to AWARE: Data Readiness for Agentic AI in the Earth Sciences
abstract: Artificial intelligence in the Earth sciences is beginning to act: prototype agents already search archives, run simulations and draft analyses. Scientific data were curated for researchers who bring expert judgement; an autonomous agent cannot be assumed to supply it. Data can satisfy the FAIR principles and still mislead a machine acting alone. We propose that Earth-science data become AWARE (Actionable, Well-described, Auditable, Recipe-equipped, Epistemically labelled), an agent-specific requirements layer that extends FAIR, within a three-part agenda: AWARE data, bounded tools, layered validation. The ingredients exist across community infrastructure. We outline a staged, measurable path to adoption, intended to reduce silent error.

title: The American Medical Directory Panel: Comparing AI-Assisted and LLM Transcription with Manual Data Entry at Scale
abstract: How closely does machine transcription agree with manual double-entry data? We digitize the 1912 and 1921 editions of the American Medical Directory, a national register of US physicians with roughly 140,000 and 150,000 entries in the two volumes, and compare five machine-extraction workflows with a full-count double-entered manual transcription. Like many historical directories, the AMD is semi-structured rather than tabular, so errors arise from misreading the layout as well as the text. A script that parses commercial OCR text using rules written by coding agents recovers about 97 percent of manually transcribed records with similar precision, more than a multimodal language model workflow (gemini-2.0.flash) that reads the page images and the OCR text. When the two methods fail, they fail on partly overlapping sets of records, so reconciling their outputs raises both recall and precision to about 98 percent. An open-weight LLM pipeline run on a local GPU server falls between the parser and the multimodal workflow in recall, and replacing the commercial OCR model with an open-source alternative lowers its recall by only about 2 percentage points. As the manual transcription's own error rate is unknown, these rates measure agreement rather than accuracy. Direct processing charges for the commercial OCR and multimodal workflow were about 0.03 euro per page, compared with 14.70 euro per page for manual transcription.

title: Reject and Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks for Generative Image Models
abstract: Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10^{-6} FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.

title: LSP-RAG: Latent Scoring Perspectives for Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in open-domain question answering, but often struggle with factual accuracy and multi-hop reasoning due to the incompleteness of the training corpora. A promising solution is Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG), which supplements LLMs with structured knowledge retrieved from external knowledge graphs (KGs). However, existing KG-RAG methods either rely on large-scale language models (e.g., ChatGPT) to guide the retrieval process, which leads to high computational costs, or suffer from limited retrieval quality when using lightweight language models, particularly under multi-hop scenarios. We propose LSP-RAG (Latent Scoring Perspectives for Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Knowledge Graphs), a novel KG-RAG framework that enhances hop-wise KG knowledge retrieval through multi-perspective prompted scoring. Each latent scoring perspective is guided by a combination of two types of soft prompts: a perspective-specific soft prompt induces a distinct prompt-conditioned scoring function over candidate triplets, while a contextual soft prompt evolves with each reasoning hop by encoding the query and previously explored KG triplets, enabling the model to preserve consistency and relevance across multi-hop retrieval. Rather than assuming manually defined semantic roles, these latent perspectives are adaptively aggregated to capture heterogeneous relevance signals during retrieval. This design allows LSP-RAG to perform accurate and robust retrieval using lightweight language models. LSP-RAG achieves superior performance across multiple KG-based Question Answering benchmarks compared to existing retrieval systems, including those that rely on much larger language models, demonstrating its effectiveness under limited computational budgets.

title: ScaleDiag: Diagnosing the Limits of Test-Time Scaling in GUI Grounding
abstract: GUI grounding maps a screenshot and a natural language instruction to the coordinates of the intended interface element. Existing approaches improve grounding through visual scaling, instruction scaling, and sampling scaling, yet it remains unclear which grounding bottlenecks these strategies address and where their gains saturate. To address this gap, we introduce ScaleDiag, a controlled diagnostic framework that isolates the effects of visual input, instruction information, and prediction sampling on GUI grounding by independently varying target scale and surrounding context, target-specific information and auxiliary descriptions, and candidate coverage and selection, respectively. We evaluate ScaleDiag across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models and find that each scaling strategy operates within a much narrower regime than commonly assumed. (1) Visual scaling is governed by target occupancy rather than a fixed crop ratio, with full-screen errors typically rescued once the target occupies only 0.32% of the cropped view, while further zooming eventually becomes harmful. (2) Instruction scaling is driven by information that identifies the target rather than description richness itself, as even ground-truth-derived attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful, while appearance and spatial descriptions account for over 90% of the achievable gain. (3) Repeated sampling exposes a different limitation, as correct coordinates are frequently generated but remain difficult to select, leaving 5.1--11.0 points of oracle headroom while geometric consensus provides almost no improvement. Together, these results show that test-time scaling is constrained by distinct operating regimes rather than benefiting monotonically from more visual focus, richer instructions, or additional samples. Our code is available at https://github.com/YenanLiu/ScaleDiag.

title: Proof Checking Continuous Reachability
abstract: This paper introduces a proof format and proof checker for certifying reachability computations of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with polynomial vector fields. Establishing a proof checking framework for certifying ODE reachability is similar to the checking of UNSAT proofs for propositional satisfiability solving, but it is even more important due to the challenges inherent in dealing with ODEs, and even more challenging due to the numerical nature of ODE reachability algorithms. The proofs are expressed in differential dynamic logic (dL), and can be independently verified with symbolic theorem provers for dL (e.g. KeYmaeraX). Such proofs are naturally generated by reachability algorithms based on Taylor models, a popular technique to obtain rigorous bounds on approximations of ODEs. This paper proves the completeness of such proofs - if an approximation was correctly computed by some (possibly untrusted) reachability algorithm via Taylor models, then a corresponding proof in dL can be automatically generated and checked to be correct in dL's proof calculus. A dedicated proof checker is implemented in Lean4 for improved performance, which is capable of formally verifying benchmarks in the ARCH competition.

title: Conditional-Hierarchical Open-Set Deep Learning for Robust Radio Signals Intelligence
abstract: This paper proposes an open-set radio-frequency (RF) deep learning (DL) framework that jointly performs conditionally hierarchical multi-level radio signal classification and out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. To exploit image-based classification models, the raw radio samples are transformed into time-frequency representations using the short time Fourier transform (STFT) to pre-process the radio signals. A lightweight novel architecture using neural network (CNN), that applies con- ditional hierarchical multi-task classification heads, is introduced, and compared to two baselines including: (1) The conventional convolutional neural network (CNN) and (2) Swin-T model with multitask classification heads, where the model accuracy and complexity perspectives are considered for the comparison. Moreover, to address open-set scenarios, we introduce the fusion of two OOD detectors each of which is fitted to a Gaussian mixture model by using the learned feature space (e.g. the feature embeddings and logits) from the multi-head classifica- tion network. The overall training process is achieved on two stages following a post-hoc design: the in-set classification neural network is trained first, then the learnable parameters are frozen in the evaluation mode to process the training dataset again to aggregate the embeddings and logits used to fit the GMMs for OOD detection. Moreover, a proof of concept using experimental setup is implemented to validate the operation of the introduced models and algorithms in practical scenarios. The simulation- based trained model is fine-tuned using experimentally measured radio signals. For the experimental setup, a USRP-B210 acting as a transmitter, and an edge Deepwave Air-T software-defined radio, which is equipped with the fine-tuned neural networks is used as a detector or receiver.

title: Synthesizing hyperspectral Data using generative Models to train spectral Unmixing Methods for low-cost Crop Residue Cover Mapping
abstract: The spectral range of the Field Imaging Nanosatellite for Crop residue Hyperspectral Mapping (FINCH), developed by the University of Toronto Aerospace Team's Space System Division, poses significant challenges for hyperspectral unmixing to determine crop residue cover fractional abundances. The severe lack of standard indices necessitates the use of complex, data-driven unmixing models. Complex unmixing models require dense, well-distributed manifolds, whereas ground-truth datasets are sparse and expensive. To better leverage the information content in existing ground-truth datasets, this study presents a framework that decouples interpolation and abundance-mapping estimation via an intermediary conditional data generator, contrasting with traditional single-model unmixing pipelines. This decoupling enables the inclusion of physical prior knowledge about spectra, which is not natively accessible to unmixing models, thereby artificially expanding the dataset to serve as a Monte Carlo approximation of the population risk. To test this hypothesis, we have proposed two generator models: a 1D Conditional U-Net with Conformer Layers (GD-Streamline) and a Dual-Path Transformer Conditional Variational AutoEncoder (TCVAE), and two unmixing models: Multi-Layered Perceptrons (MLP) and Fourier Neural Operators (FNO). The results of the study indicate a need for rigorous integration and introduction of spectral priors within the scope of the proposed decoupling framework to prevent domain and mode collapse and hallucination by the generator models; otherwise, this leads to falsely approximated data manifolds, ultimately resulting in unsatisfactory and out-of-distribution unmixing performance.

title: When "brain outsourcing" becomes habit: governmentality dilemmas and learning alienation in agentic workflows
abstract: The spread of generative AI has made "brain outsourcing"—delegating cognitive tasks to AI—a common phenomenon in higher education, especially in low-tier private undergraduate colleges. Existing studies explain it mainly at the individual level, neglecting the institutional consequences of the technologies used to govern it. Drawing on design-based research principles, this study conducted a three-group quasi-experiment in a Data Structures course at such a college: an adversarial workflow (Group A, n = 36), a negotiative workflow (Group B, n = 40), and a traditional control group (n = 44), triangulated across five chains of evidence. Results show that Group A's direct-dumping rate fell to 11.1% (vs. 57.5% and 75.0%), yet concealed forms—cosmetic modification and division-of-labor outsourcing—rose compensatorily, leaving the composite outsourcing index unchanged across groups (p = 0.864). Process engagement rose sharply while output authenticity stayed low (comment–code matching 3.62/5; only 27.8% of difficulty tags authentic), indicating "performative engagement". Only 1 of 120 students adopted a self-regulated strategy. In Group A, perceived control rose (+2.17) and negotiation space fell (−0.91) without meaningful growth in autonomy; the 18.3-point advantage over the control group in comprehension depth shrank to 6.8 points in transfer application. The "non-outsourceable" workflow thus changed outsourcing's form, not its deep structure, alienating learning into an adversarial game of evading detection—a new hidden curriculum. Agent design should shift from adversarial surveillance to dialogic support.
journal: Journal of Education and Educational Policy Studies

title: Geospatial Mapping and Classification of Soil Fertility Status of Chochi Irrigation Farmlands for Effective Crop Production in Yola South LGA, Adamawa State
abstract: This research work saddled to study the geospatial mapping and classification of soil fertility statuses of Chochi irrigation farmlands for effective crop production in Yola South LGA, Adamawa state. Forty (40) samples were collected in the area at the depth of 0-20 cm and 20-40 cm making 80 soil samples respectively. Three standard (3) profile pits were dug where soil samples were collected from the identified horizons of each pit. The collected soil samples were analyzed in the laboratory and used I for mapping and classification of the soil and its fertility statuses using Fertility Capability Classification (FCC) System. The spatial mapping results shows that the southern part of the study area has dominated with slightly acidic moderate to high OM, TN, AvP and K content while the northern part was neutral with low to moderate values respectively. The FCCC classified the soil with the following symbols; LCdsn - km at pit 1, SCdsn - km at pit 2 and pit 3 classified as SLdsn - km. it is therefore recommended that to realize effective irrigation practices integrated nutrient management should be adopted.

title: Comparative Review of AI Self-Aided Assistant Applications
abstract: There has been an increasing excitement in the development of Conversational Agents (CA) commonly known as “Chatbot”, “Chatterbot”, “Talkagent”, “Smart Agent” and many other similar terms. From its inception in the 1950 with the ELIZA, computing giants such as Apple, Amazon, IBM have developed different CAs such as Siri, Alexa, and Watson Assistant. These selfaided AI powered applications has influenced human-computer interaction, and the demand is on the rise, and so is the technology. The large availability of these applications makes it difficult for prospective users to decide which is most appropriate considering their objectives. The research reviewed selected chatbot applications with the capability of creating customized and customer oriented chatbot. Using the explorative methodology, the research systematically identified the features, strengths, weaknesses, and made recommendation.
journal: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF PURE SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY

title: Climate-smart Agriculture and Youth Agribusiness Participation in Kaduna State: the Mediating Role of Digital Financial Inclusion Among Small Holder Farmers
abstract: This study examined the effect of Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) and Digital Financial Inclusion (DFI) on Youth Agribusiness Participation (YAP) in Kaduna state, Nigeria. The increasing concern over low youth involvement in agribusiness necessitated an empirical investigation into factors that influence youth engagement in the agricultural sector. The study adopted a cross-sectional survey research design. A sample of 384 respondents was selected from a population of 1.3 million farming households using the Krejcie and Morgan sampling technique. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) through SmartPLS software. The results revealed that Climate-Smart Agriculture has a strong and significant positive effect on Youth Agribusiness Participation (β = 0.812, t = 71.526, p < 0.05). Digital Financial Inclusion also shows a positive and statistically significant but weak effect on Youth Agribusiness Participation (β = 0.058, t = 1.974, p < 0.05). The model further indicates a substantial explanatory power with an R² value of 0.683, suggesting that CSA and DFI jointly explain 68.3% of the variation in youth agribusiness participation. The study was anchored on Systems Theory, which explains how Climate-Smart Agriculture, Digital Financial Inclusion and Youth Agribusiness Participation are viewed as interconnected elements whose interactions influence youth engagement in agribusiness. The study concludes that while both CSA and DFI are important determinants of youth agribusiness participation, Climate-Smart Agriculture plays a more dominant role.

title: Decoding Cold-Induced Ca$^{2+}$ Signals: the CaM/CML-CBP Sensor Network in Plant Cold Tolerance and Its Functional Dissection by CRISPR-Cas9/Cas12a Genome Editing
abstract: Cold stress limits the geographical distribution and the yield of crops, and climate variability is raising the frequency of chilling and freezing events. Within seconds of cold perception, plant cells generate cytosolic Ca$^{2+}$ transients, the so-called Ca$^{2+}$ signatures, whose information content is read by Ca$^{2+}$ sensor proteins. This review synthesises current knowledge of the sensor network formed by calmodulins (CaMs), calmodulin-like proteins (CMLs) and their downstream calmodulin-binding proteins (CBPs), with a focus on cold stress. Because the literature mixes genetically validated interactions with plausible but untested ones, every reported interaction is graded here as validated [V], inferred [I] or hypothetical [H]. We argue that cold-associated Ca$^{2+}$ decoding is better described as a distributed network than as a linear CaM-CML-CBP cascade. The strongest genetic support exists for the CAMTA-CBF module that lies downstream of Ca$^{2+}$/CaM; by contrast, placing CRLK proteins upstream of the MEKK1-MKK2-MPK4 pathway, and linking that branch to ICE1 turnover, remains a working model assembled from separate studies. Evidence for CBL-CIPK and CML-dependent branches is thinner and context dependent. We then discuss how CRISPR-Cas9, Cas12a and transcriptional-regulation tools can be used to test these gaps, bearing in mind that editing outcomes, pleiotropy and regeneration capacity differ between species and target loci.

title: Foundation Models for Medical Image Segmentation Across Centers
abstract: Foundation models provide reusable representations, promptable interfaces and volumetric priors for medical image segmentation. Translating these capabilities into reliable performance at a new hospital requires attention to imaging variation, task definitions and the information available for adaptation. This critical narrative review focuses on organ and lesion segmentation in computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. It examines three connected questions: how transferable segmentation capabilities are formed, how adaptation mechanisms address differences between centers, and which external results support practical model selection. Pretraining objectives, dense prediction interfaces, support examples and spatial modeling are compared as complementary sources of capability. Transfer strategies are then organized by access to target images, training and validation labels, and case-specific interaction, with separate consideration of parameter, representation and input optimization at test time. Evidence from center-held-out studies, external disease cohorts and human annotation experiments shows that appropriate initialization, task adaptation and interaction can yield useful gains. Their interpretation depends on the comparator, the information supplied and the unit of evaluation. Accuracy, difficult cases, prompting requirements and the cost of the complete workflow therefore need to be considered together. An information-conditional framework links changes between centers to capability requirements, available resources, adaptation mechanisms and external benefit. This framework supports study design, model comparison and annotation resource allocation for deployment at new centers.

title: Explaining Institutional Resilience through Educational Governance: A Latent Mediation Model of Strategic Management
abstract: This study examines how Educational governance is associated with institutional resilience among Chinese university students, with strategic management proposed as an explanatory mechanism. Drawing on self-determination and self-regulated learning perspectives, a conditional process model was specified and evaluated using a synthetic dataset of 486 cases. The simulated measurement model demonstrated acceptable reliability (composite reliability = 0.88) and fit (CFI = 0.93, TLI = 0.92, RMSEA = 0.051, SRMR = 0.038). Structural estimates suggested that Educational governance was positively associated with strategic management (β = 0.41, p .002) and with institutional resilience (β = 0.31, p .002). The standardized indirect effect through strategic management was 0.18, with a synthetic 95% bootstrap interval excluding zero. Together, the modeled predictors explained 48% of the variance in institutional resilience. The paper contributes a concise mechanism-based account of adaptive learning and demonstrates an empirical structure aligned with the Journal of Adaptive Learning and Psychological Growth. Because all results are simulated, the findings are illustrative and require validation with ethically collected data.
journal: The Journal of Interactive Social Sciences

title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children
abstract: Background Misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis of children in pediatric emergency departments lead to complications, and are particularly problematic in settings with limited pediatric expertise. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in diagnostic reasoning for adult emergency department patients, but utility for pediatric cases is largely untested. Methods Retrospective study of patients seen in the emergency department of a major urban pediatric academic medical center and subsequently admitted to the operating room or inpatient service. Records from 100 patients were randomly selected, stratified by age. We compared the accuracy of differential diagnoses (up to five, ranked by likelihood) generated by an LLM agent, Dr CaBot (one configuration with literature search, the other without), with those of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians (diagnosticians), all masked to outcome. Encounters were presented to diagnosticians stepwise across four touchpoints: triage, the initial physician evaluation (the a priori primary touchpoint), the full emergency department encounter, and the admission. Ground truth diagnosis was determined by two independent, board-certified pediatric emergency physicians (reviewers) based on the entire clinical encounter. The reviewers, masked to source, then assigned each differential a Bond score (0 to 5; 4 or above was high-scoring). Findings The median patient age was 4 years and 41% had a complex chronic condition. Bond score agreement between the two reviewers had a weighted kappa of 0.64. For the primary comparison at the initial physician evaluation touchpoint, the LLM agent and the diagnosticians both achieved high-scoring differentials in 95% of cases (difference 0%, 95%CI: -5.8, 5.8%). No differences were detected at the other touchpoints. Interpretation Dr CaBot and attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians showed similar performance in generating differential diagnoses from clinical documentation, suggesting potential as a diagnostic aid. Whether this performance improves care, particularly outside pediatric specialty centers, requires prospective evaluation.

title: Psi-programmes of the Human Psyche: Key Aspects
abstract: The aim of the study was to provide a theoretical substantiation and conceptualisation of the notion of a “psi-programme” in order to explain the mechanisms by which stimuli are transformed into controllable mental processes. The methodology combined theoretical modelling based on fundamental psychological works with a secondary analysis of contemporary statistical reports on the state of mental health in the United States, Germany and Ukraine. The main result was the definition of a psi-programme as a dynamic informational-energetic structure that operates through four successive stages: the catalysis of a fixed set, the search for a strategy, the formation of an algorithm, and implementation. Comparative analysis revealed unique national patterns of dominant psi-programmes. In the United States, where 23.4% of adults have a diagnosed mental disorder, programmes of personal success and social anxiety were identified. In Germany, where only 25% of the population is in a state of psychological flourishing, programmes of stability and perfectionism are characteristic. In Ukraine, where 83% of the population experiences a high level of stress due to the war and overall satisfaction with psychological well-being has fallen to 36%, programmes of collective resilience and individual trauma were identified. Three levels for the practical modification of maladaptive psi-programmes were also defined: individual (psychotherapy), educational-media (high-quality content), and socio-institutional (supportive policies). The conclusions indicate that the psi-programme model is a valid tool for analysing mental activity. It was established that the sociocultural context is a key factor in the formation of dominant mental patterns that determine the psychological state of both the individual and society. The practical significance lies in the possibility of developing comprehensive, multi-level strategies for correcting maladaptive programmes and strengthening mental health.

title: Design and Implementation of an IoT Based Smart Home System for Motion Triggered Object Detection and Automated Ventilation Control
abstract: Internet of Things (IoT)-based smart homes enable the automation of home devices to improve comfort and security. This study designs and develops a smart home system in which passive infrared (PIR) sensors are used only to detect motion, while an ESP32-CAM and YOLOv3 are used for camera-based object detection and class labeling. A human-presence indication is therefore generated only when a PIR-triggered camera frame contains a person detected by YOLOv3; PIR motion alone is not interpreted as occupancy. The system also features MQ-2 sensor-based gas leak detection and automatic ventilation control using a servo motor as a safety response. Data and alerts are transmitted through Telegram, while Blynk is used for integrated monitoring. System development followed requirements analysis, design, implementation, functional testing, and corrective refinement. The dedicated YOLOv3 object test documented 11 confidence values ranging from 53% to 99% (descriptive mean 86.2%; median 94%); these values are detector confidence scores and not classification accuracy because no annotated ground-truth benchmark was used. In an additional 11-trial illuminance-oriented functional test, object detection succeeded in all six trials conducted at 624–950 lux and failed in all five trials conducted at 0–147 lux. The contribution of this work is an event-driven IoT architecture that coordinates motion sensing, visual verification, remote notification, and closed-loop gas mitigation, together with field-oriented evaluation of lighting effects on low-cost camera-based detection.

title: Developing a Framework for Innovative Engineering Practice Competence in Electrical Engineering Education in the Context of New Quality Productive Forces
abstract: To address gaps in the continuity of competence development, sustained mentoring, the integration of industry needs, and assessment in electrical engineering practical education, this study proposes a five-level framework for developing innovative engineering practice competence. The framework considers the requirements associated with new quality productive forces and the educational objectives of electrical engineering programs at regional agricultural universities. It encompasses five interconnected levels: understanding and applying engineering knowledge, designing and developing solutions, investigating complex engineering problems, integrated engineering application, and community engagement and application of project outcomes. Course-based experiments, practical training, course design projects, and extracurricular innovation activities are coordinated to align competence objectives, practical tasks, and assessment evidence. Stage-specific mentoring and university–industry collaboration driven by authentic projects are incorporated to translate digitalization, intelligent technologies, and green development requirements into task specifications and engineering constraints. A multidimensional assessment approach combines process performance with the quality of project outcomes, while assessment feedback informs subsequent teaching arrangements. The resulting framework integrates practical learning content, instructional support, and assessment-informed improvement. Its applicability and educational effectiveness remain to be evaluated through subsequent implementation.

title: Algorithmic Sustainability Bias: How AI-Driven Recommendation Systems Influence Consumer Choices Toward Sustainable Products in Developing Economies
abstract: With the growing influence of e-commerce infrastructure in determining consumers’ choices, a novel and insufficiently studied type of bias has cropped up that is jeopardizing the sustainability agenda in the emergent digital economies. Recent sources indicated that online platforms are considerably changing the consumption patterns (WEF, 2022). But the exact effect of algorithmic sorting on green products has not yet been studied. The policy discourses in India have also highlighted the problem regarding the necessity of responsible and transparent AI systems to reduce unintended effects on society (NITI Aayog, 2021). This study formally defines Algorithmic Sustainability Bias as a structural penalty where algorithms prioritize short-term engagement over environmental externalities (Kitchin, 2017). This threatens responsible consumption efforts in the Global South, defined here as developing digital economies with high price sensitivity and unverified eco-labels (Deloitte, 2024). In order to examine this, paper takes the mixed-method approach to study the connection between digital marketplace architecture and consumer preference. The research approach analyses the outcomes obtained at the major e-commerce sites that are currently functioning in the Global South, that is, product ratings, search visibility, and metadata of the platform. It is complemented by the testing of simulated user profiles in order to track the placement of sustainability-labeled goods relative to the general inventory in the algorithms. This architecture provides a fair evaluation of algorithmic impact not based on proprietary information of a platform. The study seeks to prove a relationship between profit maximization parameters in terms of click through rates- and invisibility of sustainable products. This study will be useful in the area of AI ethics and sustainable consumption as it defines and empirically tests the Algorithmic Sustainability Bias. Last but not least, it provides a policy analysis model that policymakers and designers can use to restructure recommendation systems to allow and not restrict sustainable consumer decision-making.
journal: Jharkhand Journal of Development and Management Studies

title: Breeding Heat-resilient Crops in Synergy with Agronomic Management: Genotype × Management Interactions
abstract: Rising temperatures and more frequent heat extremes increasingly coincide with the most temperature-sensitive developmental windows of the major food crops, and both plant breeding and agronomic management are promoted as adaptation pathways. These pathways are usually studied in isolation, although the benefit realised in farmers' fields depends on how a cultivar performs under the management in which it is grown. This critical narrative review examines whether, when and why breeding for heat resilience and agronomic management act synergistically, additively or antagonistically. Peer-reviewed literature published from 2000 onwards was identified through structured searches of multidisciplinary and life-science indexes, supplemented by citation tracking, and was appraised for design, temperature measurement, field relevance and consistency. The strongest evidence concerns phenology: aligning flowering and grain filling with cooler periods through combined changes in cultivar development rate and sowing date consistently reduces exposure, and model-assisted co-design of slower-developing cultivars with earlier sowing has been validated in the field. Evidence that irrigation lowers canopy temperature and thereby alters the apparent heat tolerance of genotypes is also robust. Interactions involving nutrient supply, foliar protectants and conservation agriculture are inconsistent, frequently derived from pot or enclosure studies, and occasionally antagonistic, as when greater nitrogen supply magnified heat losses or when shifted sowing dates failed to avoid heat around silking. Traits conferring transpirational cooling may conflict with water-conserving traits favoured under drought, so the value of a trait depends on the water regime created by management. Persistent weaknesses include reliance on air rather than tissue temperature, few factorial field trials crossing genotypes with management, geographical concentration and limited attention to delays in varietal delivery. Heat resilience is better treated as a property of genotype–management packages tested across target environments than as a fixed varietal attribute, and progress depends on factorial field experimentation, tissue-temperature reporting and faster varietal turnover.

title: Market Vulnerability and Smallholder Agriculture: A Review of Price Risk, Market Access and Livelihood Adaptation
abstract: Smallholder agriculture contributes substantially to global food supplies but remains exposed to unstable output and input prices, restricted market access and climate-related disruptions. This critical narrative review examines the interactions among price risk, market institutions, household sensitivity and livelihood adaptation using an integrated framework informed by agricultural household theory, vulnerability analysis, asset-based poverty traps and sustainable livelihoods. Evidence indicates that price changes have different welfare consequences for net food sellers and buyers, while seasonal price gaps and input costs can intensify existing constraints. Market participation depends on transaction costs, production scale, information, finance and institutional conditions rather than physical distance alone. Digital information services, cooperatives, contract farming and index insurance offer potential benefits, but outcomes vary according to household assets, liquidity, trust and the wider market environment. Households also respond to shocks through diversification, changes in production choices and the use of assets to maintain consumption. Such strategies may reduce immediate exposure yet constrain longer-term asset accumulation. The reviewed evidence is limited by differences in research designs, geographic concentration and inadequate observation of repeated or combined shocks. The findings favour differentiated interventions that account for net market position and resource endowments, strengthen inclusive market institutions and improve access to appropriate risk-management options. Longer-term research is needed to clarify how these mechanisms interact to influence smallholder resilience and livelihood trajectories.
journal: Asian Journal of Agricultural Extension, Economics & Sociology

title: Remote Sensing, Artificial Intelligence, and the Internet of Things in Precision Agriculture: A Critical Review of Opportunities, Challenges, and Pathways to Sustainable Intensification
abstract: Sustainable intensification requires more output from existing farmland with lower environmental costs, and digital precision agriculture is widely promoted as one of its principal instruments. Remote sensing, artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) now generate crop, soil and microclimate data at unprecedented resolution, yet the extent to which these capabilities translate into verified agronomic, environmental and social gains remains contested. This critical narrative review examines the evidence linking the three technology families to sustainable intensification outcomes in crop production. Peer-reviewed literature published from January 2010 to September 2026 was identified through multidisciplinary, life-science, open-access and regional scholarly indexes, supplemented by citation tracking and institutional reports, and was appraised for design, validation practice, external validity and outcome relevance. The synthesis shows a persistent asymmetry between technical performance and demonstrated impact. Satellite and unmanned aerial observation reliably captures within-field and between-field variability, but its value is constrained by cloud cover, spectral saturation, scale mismatch with small fields and scarce ground truth. AI models frequently report near-perfect accuracy on curated datasets, whereas independent tests under field conditions, on new locations or in unseen seasons show marked degradation, a pattern amplified by non-spatial validation. IoT deployments are technically feasible but depend on sensor calibration, connectivity, energy supply, interoperability and cybersecurity that are seldom evaluated over multiple seasons. Field evidence for input savings is strongest for sensor-guided nitrogen management and spot spraying of herbicides, yet economic returns are variable, benefits are smaller and less stable on small farms, and efficiency gains in irrigation can be offset by expanded water use. Adoption remains skewed towards large commercial farms, while connectivity gaps, data-governance asymmetries and corporate lock-in shape who benefits. The review concludes that digital precision agriculture can contribute to sustainable intensification only conditionally, when sensing, inference and actuation are validated together against explicit sustainability metrics, embedded in on-farm experimentation and accompanied by institutional arrangements for inclusion and data stewardship.
journal: International Journal of Environment and Climate Change

title: A Study on the Economic Aspects of Market Price, Crop Arrivals and Minimum Support Price for Wheat in Madhya Pradesh
abstract: Wheat marketing in Madhya Pradesh is characterised by concentrated seasonal arrivals and the coexistence of administered minimum support prices (MSPs) and wholesale market price observations. This descriptive study examines a compiled monthly wheat-market series for 2015–2024, with official MSPs matched to the relevant rabi marketing seasons. The analysis covers market arrivals, a source-reported indicator of arrivals classified below MSP, a monthly price series associated with that classification and percentage deviations of reported prices from the applicable MSP. Annual arrivals ranged from 7,006 thousand tonnes in 2021 to 10,835 thousand tonnes in 2022; 62.97% of total recorded arrivals occurred during March–May. Arrival-weighting the monthly classified shares yields an overall reported below-MSP indicator of 21.62%, with annual estimates from 11.60% in 2019 to 37.78% in 2016. The arithmetic mean of monthly reported prices increased from ₹1,379 per quintal in 2015 to ₹2,130 in 2024. However, seven monthly price entries exceed their contemporaneous official MSPs, demonstrating that the reported classification and aggregate price series cannot be interpreted as verified transaction-level below-MSP sales. The results document substantial seasonality and variation in reported market indicators but do not establish causal effects of MSP policy or farmers’ individual price realisations.
journal: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports

title: The Digital Eye in Plant Disease Surveillance: A Critical Synthesis of Imaging, Artificial Intelligence and Smart Diagnosis
abstract: Plant disease surveillance is moving from episodic visual inspection towards image-supported observation across leaves, crop canopies and landscapes. Digital cameras, spectral and thermal sensors, uncrewed aerial vehicles and artificial intelligence have expanded the measurable manifestations of plant stress, yet the ability to recognise a pattern is not equivalent to identifying its cause or improving disease management. This critical narrative review examines the evidence linking imaging modalities, computational models and diagnostic workflows to operational surveillance. Peer-reviewed studies and methodological reviews published from 2010 to 10 September 2026 were considered, with earlier concepts addressed where necessary. The synthesis evaluates sensor-specific biological signals, experimental design, dataset provenance, cross-domain generalisation, object detection and severity estimation, aerial and satellite monitoring, and the role of human and laboratory verification. Controlled-image classification has demonstrated substantial technical feasibility, but independent field evaluations frequently reveal reductions in recall and weak transportability across sites, cultivars, seasons and acquisition devices. Spectral and thermal measurements can detect altered physiology before obvious visual injury in selected experiments; nevertheless, such responses are seldom pathogen-specific and may be confounded by abiotic stress or crop development. Multi-scale mapping can locate suspected disease foci, although spatial resolution, timing, sampling design and ground-truth uncertainty constrain interpretation. Recent advances in domain adaptation, multimodal learning, anomaly detection and explainability are promising but have not consistently established prospective diagnostic or management value. The review proposes a surveillance-oriented framework that separates detection, aetiological diagnosis, severity estimation, forecasting and intervention. Progress depends less on marginal improvements in benchmark accuracy than on independent prospective evaluation, calibrated uncertainty, representative datasets, expert-mediated confirmation and measurements of decisions and outcomes. Digital imaging is best understood as an additional evidential layer within plant health surveillance rather than a stand-alone substitute for plant pathology.
journal: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports

title: Break‐even reference dependence in crop insurance decisions: Theory and evidence
abstract: We study farmers' crop insurance choices using a behavioral framework in which break‐even status serves as a salient, economically grounded, and empirically observable reference point. The framework nests the standard expected‐utility model as a special case and incorporates three forces: risk reduction, aversion to falling below break‐even status, and disutility from paying premiums. It yields sharp predictions about coverage choices, including bunching at the break‐even coverage level (BECL), defined as the coverage level where the insurance guarantee just covers total cost. We test these predictions using a survey of corn producers in Iowa and Kansas that elicits farmers' perceived BECLs, attitudes toward break‐even protection and premium costs, and their actual Federal Crop Insurance Program coverage choices. Coverage decisions display pronounced and asymmetric bunching around the BECL, with a sharp decline in frequency just below it and a smoother distribution above. Proxy measures of behavioral attitudes are also associated with observed choices in the predicted directions: farmers reporting stronger aversion to not breaking even are more likely to insure exactly at the BECL but not above it, while those reporting stronger premium aversion are more likely to insure below it. Using illustrative simulations, we further examine how subsidy changes interact with these behavioral forces and find that aversion to not breaking even may play an anchoring role that dampens the effects of premium subsidy cuts on coverage choices.

title: How Do Standard Time Series Forecasting Benchmarks Translate to Finance? A Broad Study of Risk Adjusted Performance
abstract: Forecasting financial asset returns is challenging due to low signal‐to‐noise ratios, nonstationarity and heavy‐tailed distributions. We benchmark 16 deep learning architectures for time series forecasting, including Transformers, State Space Models (SSMs), xLSTMs, and recurrent hybrids, on a 15‐year daily futures dataset using an end‐to‐end volatility‐targeted Sharpe ratio optimization task. Our results challenge prevailing assumptions in the literature. Several widely used “state‐of‐the‐art” architectures, including generic Transformers and SSMs, underperformed a simple AR(1) benchmark in a realistic financial forecasting task. The strongest results came from comparatively simple hybrid approaches using recurrent structures: a Variable Selection Network combined with an LSTM achieved the highest Sharpe ratio, while xLSTM showed the greatest robustness to transaction costs. These findings suggest that success on standard time‐series benchmarks does not reliably transfer to finance, and that architectures tailored to the unique properties of asset returns may remain more effective than generic attention‐based approaches for financial forecasting.

title: Ethical Risks of Medical AI Agents and a Governance Framework: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Policy Responses.
abstract: This systematic review identified ethical risks associated with medical AI agents and developed a governance framework adapted to China's healthcare context. PubMed, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang Data were searched for records published or publicly released between January 1, 2020 and 30 June 2025. Of 1239 records identified, 837 underwent title and abstract screening, 68 were assessed in full, and 58 were included in the synthesis. The evidence base comprised 12 core agentic sources, 24 agent-focused boundary sources, and 22 governance, policy, legal, or normative sources. Eight non-exclusive ethical-risk themes were identified, led by safety, reliability, and hallucination; accountability and liability; bias and fairness; and privacy and security. Core agentic evidence indicated that multi-step execution, external tool use, persistent memory, and multi-agent coordination may amplify error propagation, provenance, privacy, and responsibility-allocation risks. Six representative cases and governance events were analyzed separately using the Four Principles of Biomedical Ethics to examine how similar risks arise across different technologies, jurisdictions, and institutional settings. The synthesis informed a four-component governance framework linking ethical and legal challenges, biomedical ethical principles, operational governance mechanisms, and expected outcomes. The proposed mechanisms include lifecycle risk monitoring, human oversight and escalation, responsibility allocation, privacy and data governance, documentation and auditability, fairness and equitable-access safeguards, and multistakeholder ethics review. The framework is intended as a policy-oriented and institutionally adaptable proposal rather than a validated intervention and requires prospective evaluation in specific cases of healthcare organizations and governance events.

title: The Stanford Multifaceted Dissociation Questionnaire: A 9-Item Measure of Trait and State Dissociation.
abstract: Dissociation is a common and increasingly studied phenomenon with substantial relevance for mental health. To date, researchers have often relied upon broad conceptualizations and retrospective measures, making it difficult to identify a consistent subset of experiences for dissociation, explore their links to related phenomena, and differentiate habitual from momentary dissociation. To address these issues, we introduce the Stanford Multifaceted Dissociation Questionnaire (SMDQ), a 9-item measure that assesses three facets of dissociation and can be employed to assess either trait or state dissociation. In Study 1, we evaluated the content validity of the initial SMDQ item pool using feedback from individuals with lived experience of dissociation (N = 73) and content experts (N = 14), detailing our focus on detachment-type experiences that may help the dissociation construct to be more cleanly distinguished from other clinical phenomena. In Study 2 (N = 400), we described the item selection process and examined the factor structure, internal consistency, and convergent/discriminant validity of both the trait and state versions of the SMDQ. In Study 3 (N = 500), we further investigated the psychometric properties of both versions, including their factor structure, measurement invariance, internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and convergent/discriminant validity. Across the studies, scores on the trait and state versions of the SMDQ showed strong content validity and a theoretically congruent factor structure, comprised of alteration in the perception of one's mind, body, and world (suggesting a tripartite model of dissociation). This structure was largely invariant across demographic groups and time. We also demonstrate good convergent and discriminant validity, internal consistency (ω > 0.80), and temporal stability over 1 week (r > 0.70 for the trait version). Overall, we conclude that the trait and state versions of the SMDQ are promising measurement tools that can enhance our understanding of dissociation's structure, antecedents, and consequences.

title: Plantamajoside Alleviates Osteoporosis by Suppressing Nrf2 Ubiquitination to Mitigate Oxidative Stress and Mitochondrial Damage.
abstract: As a prevalent skeletal disorder, osteoporosis is characterized by reduced bone mass, disrupted bone microarchitecture, and increased bone fragility. Excessive oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are key contributors to the pathogenesis of osteoporosis. While plantamajoside exhibits anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-apoptotic bioactivities, the mechanism underlying its preventive effect against osteoporosis remains unclear. This study aimed to explore whether plantamajoside produces protective effects against oxidative stress-mediated osteoporosis. An ovariectomized rat model of osteoporosis was constructed, and bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells were stimulated with hydrogen peroxide. Oxidative stress-related indicators and signaling pathways were assessed, together with bone phenotyping, cellular staining, Western blot analysis, and Nrf2 ubiquitination assays. Plantamajoside ameliorated ovariectomy-induced bone loss, recovered trabecular microarchitecture, suppressed excessive reactive oxygen species production and mitochondrial damage, and restored osteogenic differentiation capacity. It facilitated Nrf2 nuclear translocation by inhibiting Nrf2 ubiquitination. Plantamajoside alleviates osteoporosis by stabilizing the Nrf2 signaling pathway through reducing Nrf2 ubiquitination. These findings offer mechanistic evidence supporting the application of plantamajoside for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis.
