title: Machine learning insights into environmental and biological triggers of fumonisin outbreaks in Texas corn
abstract: Contamination of corn with fumonisin mycotoxins (FUM) caused by the fungus Fusarium verticillioides is a recurrent issue in Texas corn production that results in significant economic losses for corn producers. Both prediction and management of FUM outbreaks are challenging due to a lack of information regarding region-specific environmental and biological drivers of contamination. We analyzed 683 historical FUM contamination events for 12 years that were categorized as low (<5 mg kg −1 ; <5 ppm) or high (≥5 mg kg −1 ; ≥5 ppm) and evaluated geo-spatial, environmental and biological drivers of outbreaks using a machine learning approach. We applied Ratkowsky-based growth and toxin production models for five genetically diverse F. verticillioides strains and found strain-specific predicted growth and Fumonisin Risk Index (FRI) profiles. Using FRI (strain-specific) or weather-only feature sets, each combined with soil biogeochemistry properties, we developed Random Forest (RF) and Neural Network (NNET) models. Historical balanced accuracy averaged ~74% for RF and ~70% for NNET models. Feature importance revealed that RF models consistently ranked barometric pressure and latitude among top predictors, while NNET models emphasized soil moisture and FRI. Among the overlapping drivers between RF and NNET were FRIs at the beginning of February and mid-October. Critical influential weeks for soil moisture (May–August), barometric pressure (July–October), and FRI (August–November) overlapped with corn developmental stages susceptible to F. verticillioides infection and FUM accumulation in a region-dependent manner due to differences in planting dates across the state. Soil biogeochemical properties such as organic matter, electrical conductivity, and clay content were also influential in models’ predictions indicating region-specific relationships with historical outbreaks. This study highlights the combined roles of weather patterns, fungal strain diversity, soil properties, and crop phenology in shaping FUM outbreak risk across Texas and underscores the importance of integrating strain-specific biological responses and regionally relevant environmental factors into predictive modeling frameworks for improved mycotoxin risk assessment. In addition, results suggest that region specific management of soil physico-chemical properties could reduce FUM risk, offering insights into new mitigation strategies for on-farm prevention of mycotoxin contamination and the potential to develop a novel early-warning system as well as mitigation tools for FUM outbreaks in Texas.

title: Real-time mulberry fruit ripeness recognition for selective harvesting using edge-deployable object detection: a single-orchard case study
abstract: Mulberry is a seasonal cash crop with a short ripening window, where delayed harvesting readily leads to fruit deterioration and economic losses. Real-time ripeness recognition is therefore important for selective harvesting. Existing detection models face challenges including excessive model parameters, low discriminability between immature fruits and background foliage, and severe occlusion caused by clustered fruits. We present Mulberry-Net, a lightweight three-class mulberry ripeness detector that adapts and systematically evaluates three established components: Partial Convolution integrated into the C2f bottleneck to form the Cross-Stage Feature Compression and Cooperation (CSFCC) module; Mixed Local Channel Attention (MLCA) placed after multi-scale feature concatenation in the neck; and an occlusion-aware training strategy based on Focal-DIoU loss. The components target computational cost, fruit-background discrimination, and localisation under occlusion, respectively. Mulberry-Net achieves an mAP@0.5 of 97.80% with 2.41M parameters, improving on the YOLOv8n baseline by 5.10 percentage points while reducing parameters by 19.9%. The largest class-specific gain occurs for green fruits (+8.60 percentage points). Five-fold tree-level cross-validation yields 96.02 +/- 0.74% mAP@0.5. Three-class ripeness accuracy on correctly localised fruits reaches 96.83%, with residual grading errors concentrated at the color-turning/mature boundary and missed detections concentrated in the green stage. A controlled comparison against four alternative lightweight convolution designs at the same bottleneck position shows that the adopted configuration attains the highest accuracy at comparable computational cost. The results support the feasibility of lightweight three-class mulberry ripeness detection for selective harvesting under the conditions studied. Because all data originate from a single orchard, cultivar, and acquisition device, the reported figures should be interpreted as single-site feasibility evidence rather than established generalisation across cultivars and growing regions.

title: Flower-DETR: relation-aware DETR with position priors for king and lateral flower detection in apple blossom thinning
abstract: Apple blossom thinning is a critical crop load management practice for improving fruit quality, and automated thinning shows strong potential to replace manual labor. However, a key challenge for the vision module of robotic systems is to effectively distinguish between king and lateral flowers during apple blossom detection. To address this challenge, an efficient relation-aware DETR model, termed Flower-DETR, is proposed for detecting king and lateral flowers in apple inflorescences. To capture spatial correlations among individual flower instances, a relation-assisted decoder with position relation embeddings is developed. Position relations are incorporated as attention bias into the DETR decoder to establish instance-level relation priors among flowers. Through progressive attention refinement, the model learns discriminative geometric features of flower spatial positions, which helps it distinguish between king and lateral flowers during detection. The proposed Flower-DETR achieves AP 50 scores of 0.970, 0.873 and 0.928 for inflorescences, king flowers, and lateral flowers, respectively. The overall mAP 50 and mAP 50:95 across the three categories are 0.924 and 0.770, respectively. Comparative experiments show that Flower-DETR achieves the highest mAP 50 and mAP 50:95 among all compared methods while maintaining competitive computational efficiency, with 9.664 M parameters, 26.0 GFLOPs, a model size of 156.4 MB, and an inference speed of 30 FPS. The model provides a favorable balance between detection precision and computational efficiency for multi-class flower detection in apple inflorescences. This work offers a useful reference for efficient detection of king and lateral flowers in automated blossom thinning applications.

title: Screening and evaluation of three biological control bacterial strains against Meloidogyne incognita
abstract: Root-knot nematodes represent one of the most severe soil-borne pathogens, causing extensive damage to plant root systems, reducing crop yields, and resulting in substantial economic losses. Owing to the environmentally sustainable and highly effective properties, biological control methods have emerged as the primary strategy for managing root-knot nematodes. Current research on the biological control of root-knot nematodes mainly emphasizes the use of biocontrol agents such as bacteria, fungi, actinomycetes. This study isolated three new strains with high nematocidal efficacy against Meloidogyne incognita. To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive report on the biocontrol efficacy of Staphylococcus warneri (GZ5), Priestia megaterium (H14), and Bacillus zanthoxyli (L16) against root-knot nematodes. These strains displayed significant nematocidal activity against several plant-parasitic nematodes, including Meloidogyne incognita , Heterodera glycines , Bursaphelenchus xylophilus , Aphelenchoides besseyi as well as the free-living model nematode Caenorhabditis elegans . Among the three strains, GZ5 exhibited the highest control efficacy, achieving 89.27% corrected mortality against M. incognita J2 within 48 hours and significantly reducing root-knot index in greenhouse trials. These findings suggest that S. warneri GZ5 is a promising biocontrol agent for the sustainable management of root-knot nematodes and warrants further investigation under field conditions.

title: Retrospective prediction of registration-derived pesticide mixture restriction associations: evaluating knowledge graph and graph-free models
abstract: Pesticide tank mixing is widely used to improve the efficiency and flexibility of crop protection. However, mixture performance depends not only on the molecular structures and physicochemical properties of the constituent pesticides but also on practical application contexts, including formulation types, target crops, target organisms, application methods, and technical requirements. These context-dependent factors make potentially incompatible or antagonistic combinations difficult to identify from molecular structures and physicochemical properties alone; in registration texts the corresponding constraints appear as documentary mixture-restriction evidence rather than as experimentally measured outcomes. Although pesticide registration documents contain authoritative information on practical use conditions, most of this information remains embedded in unstructured text and is rarely incorporated into computational analysis of registration-derived mixture restrictions. This study addresses binary prediction of registration-derived restriction associations for pesticide pairs. Positive labels are derived from mixture-restriction evidence recorded in pesticide registration texts, which primarily reflect antagonistic interactions. The model outputs a relative association score for registration-derived restriction evidence and is not intended to represent other risk types such as physical incompatibility, chemical instability, or phytotoxicity, nor does it provide experimentally verified incompatibility conclusions. This study developed FMPIP as a computational framework for predicting pesticide-pair associations with restriction evidence derived from pesticide registration information. The current study was designed as a retrospective computational evaluation rather than a prospective validation of physical, chemical, or biological mixture incompatibility. To address this limitation, we propose a structured knowledge-driven framework integrating registration-text structuring, multi-source knowledge graph construction, and graph-based registration-derived restriction association prediction. First, a previously validated single-stage entity–relation extraction method is adapted as the knowledge-generation component to transform pesticide registration descriptions into structured usage-context knowledge. Direct statements indicating mixture restrictions are excluded from predictive inputs and are used only to generate registration-evidence-derived supervision labels, thereby separating label-generating evidence from model features. Second, non-label registration-derived contexts are integrated with molecular information and physicochemical attributes to construct a multi-source pesticide knowledge graph. Third, FMPIP is developed to estimate relative restriction-association scores for registration-derived restriction evidence by combining graph-based random neighborhood sampling with attention-based aggregation. FMPIP provides a relative association score for registration-derived restriction evidence. Within the retrospective benchmark, the score ranks pesticide pairs by their association with registration-derived restriction evidence; however, ranking-oriented metrics and practical baselines are not evaluated in this study, so practical prioritization capability is not demonstrated. The model output should not be interpreted as a direct prediction of physical, chemical, or biological mixture compatibility under specific application conditions. The knowledge-generation module achieved an F1-score of 96.6% on the pesticide registration dataset. For the downstream restriction-association prediction task, FMPIP achieved an AUC of 90.4%, an AUPR of 84.8%, and an F1-score of 84.4% on PID, outperforming all graph-based baselines re-evaluated under the same deduplicated, pair-disjoint protocol (AUC 85.5-85.9%, AUPR 72.3-75.3%, F1-score 71.9-76.3%). Ablation analysis showed that, after deduplication, removing any single information source did not reduce performance, suggesting that the contribution of registration context observed in the earlier, non-deduplicated evaluation. An order-invariant evaluation, in which pair scores do not depend on the storage orientation of a pair and the classification threshold is selected on validation data, obtained an AUC of 90.8% (SD 0.5), an AUPR of 82.5% (SD 1.0), and an F1-score of 85.0% (SD 0.5) on PID, confirming that this comparison is not an artifact of pair storage. The resulting scores should be interpreted as retrospective recovery of held-out restriction labels within the benchmark rather than as evidence of experimentally verified incompatibility or of practical prioritization capability. Independent regulatory or experimental validation is required before these predictions can be interpreted as evidence supporting prospective practical mixture decisions. These findings illustrate how regulatory pesticide-use text can be converted into structured contextual knowledge for retrospective mixture-restriction analysis.

title: Research on base detection method for an intra-row weeding robot in goji berry plantations
abstract: Goji berry is an important specialty crop in Ningxia, China, where large-scale cultivation has increased the demand for efficient orchard management. However, the intelligence level of weeding equipment in goji orchards remains limited, particularly in the basal region of the plant, where improper operation may cause root damage and incomplete weed removal. To address this problem, this study developed a DeepLabV3+-based perception framework for goji berry basal-region recognition in orchard environments. An autonomous mobile testing platform was established according to the planting pattern of the Bairuiyuan plantation in the Helan Mountains, and a binocular camera was used for image acquisition. Based on the collected orchard images, a semantic segmentation model was constructed to identify the basal regions of goji berry plants. The proposed framework was evaluated under different weed conditions through static image-based testing and continuous row-level field testing. In static image-based testing, the group-level missed detection rate and false detection rate were 12.5% ± 7.6% and 2.2% ± 1.9%, respectively. In continuous row-level field testing with the mobile platform, the corresponding rates were 2.0% ± 2.0% and 2.7% ± 2.7%, respectively. The results indicate that the proposed framework can provide stable basal-region perception during continuous field operation, despite variations in weed conditions. This study provides practical support for the development of intelligent intra-row weeding systems in goji orchards.

title: Soil quality index as a predictor of wetting-front dynamics under surface drip irrigation
abstract: Efficient soil water movement is essential for improving crop water-use efficiency under drip irrigation, yet the role of Soil Quality Index (SQI) in predicting wetting-front under surface drip irrigation has not been comprehensively studied. This study investigated five land-use systems—bare fallowing for 2 years (BF2), bare fallowing for 3 years (BF3), monocropping (MOC), crop rotation (CR), and fallowing with vegetation (FV)—on soil quality and wetting-front development under surface drip irrigation. Soil hydro-physical and chemical properties at 0–30 cm depth were assessed, including bulk density (BD), water-holding capacity (WHC), pH, effective cation exchange capacity (ECEC), available phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), organic carbon (OC), total nitrogen (N), and base saturation (Bsat). Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to derive the Soil Quality Index (SQI), while wetting width and depth were measured after 15, 30, and 60 min of irrigation. Land-use management significantly (P 0.70 and reaching 0.984 between SQI and wetting depth at 60 min. The principal component regression model explained 92.75% of SQI variability. These findings demonstrate that vegetation-based fallowing and crop rotation enhance soil quality and water movement, supporting sustainable irrigation water management.

title: Influence of the rural digital economy on rural innovation and entrepreneurship: evidence from counties in China
abstract: The rural digital economy (RDE) has the potential to support innovation and entrepreneurship in rural areas. On the basis of county-level panel data for China, this study systematically examines the effects of the RDE on county-level rural innovation and entrepreneurship (RIE), as well as the underlying mechanism, by employing a two-way fixed effects model, a mediating effect model, a threshold effect model, and a spatial Durbin model. The results of this study reveal that (1) the RDE is positively and significantly associated with RIE at the county level, an association that survives robustness testing and is consistent with the instrumental-variable estimate, although the exclusion restriction of the instrument cannot be tested directly and part of the association is mechanical because the two indices share an indicator; (2) the relation between the RDE and RIE is nonlinear and is better characterized by a threshold than by a quadratic specification; (3) the estimates are consistent with three mechanisms, namely the development of nonagricultural industries (DNI), higher economic density (ED), and the alleviation of financing constraints (FC), which we interpret as evidence on potential channels rather than as identified causal mediation; (4) a heterogeneity analysis suggests that the positive association between the RDE and RIE is stronger in areas that feature lower levels of modern agriculture, relatively weak information infrastructure, and smaller government size; and (5) the estimates indicate positive spatial spillovers from the RDE to RIE, and the estimated spillover across the truncated weight matrices rises to a maximum and then declines, a pattern consistent with attenuation but conditional on the specified weight matrix. This study provides empirical evidence regarding the intrinsic connection between the RDE and RIE in counties and has important reference value for efforts to promote policy practice and theoretical research in related fields.

title: Predicting Fruit-Drop Severity in ‘Rojo Brillante’ Persimmon: An Ordinal Classification Approach with Implications for Irrigation Scheduling
abstract: Physiological fruit drop is a major determinant of crop load and yield in ‘Rojo Brillante’ persimmon and is closely linked to irrigation management, yet its severity has not been addressed as an ordinal prediction problem. This study evaluated whether fortnightly fruit-drop severity, recorded in 2015–2019 in trees grafted onto Diospyros lotus and Diospyros virginiana under different irrigation treatments, could be predicted one fortnight in advance with four ordinal classification algorithms (cumulative link model, LogitBoost, random forest and support vector machine). Nested and reduced predictor sets were evaluated with leave-one-year-out cross-validation against a persistence and a seasonal baseline, with Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) as the pre-specified primary metric. LogitBoost with the complete predictor set achieved the highest agreement (QWK = 0.718), outperforming the persistence baseline (QWK = 0.510) in all five years and the seasonal baseline (QWK = 0.591) in four. Reduced models with cumulative growing degree-days and rootstock reached similar agreement, indicating that predictive ability arises mainly from seasonal phase. In contrast, the previous fruit-drop count and additional agroclimatic predictors improved the discrimination of low and moderate drop. Because irrigation enters the models through the cumulative hydric balance, the approach could support the evaluation of irrigation scenarios, once validated in other orchards.

title: Evaluation of Drought Monitoring and Prediction Methods for Dryland Croplands in Northeast China
abstract: Against the backdrop of intensifying climate change, the increasing risk of droughts, floods, and other climate-related hazards affecting crop production poses a growing threat to regional agricultural production and ecological environments. Northeast China is an important grain-producing region in China. Accurately assessing meteorological drought conditions in dryland croplands and improving short-term prediction capabilities are of great significance for agricultural risk management and food security. This study focuses on dryland croplands in Northeast China and investigates SPEI reconstruction and one-month-ahead prediction driven by environmental variables. The performance of different machine learning and deep learning methods is compared, and the effect of incorporating root-zone soil moisture on model prediction performance is further evaluated. Considering multiple environmental factors, precipitation, soil temperature, land surface temperature, potential evapotranspiration, and soil moisture at different soil depths are selected as model input variables. The Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) at accumulation timescales of 1, 3, and 6 months (SPEI-1, SPEI-3, and SPEI-6) is used to characterize meteorological drought conditions at different timescales and serves as the target variable for the drought monitoring and prediction models. Model performance is evaluated using the coefficient of determination (R2), root mean square error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE). The results show that, for meteorological drought monitoring, the SPEI reconstruction model based on the Convolutional Neural Network–Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) performs best, with R2 values of 0.82, 0.81, and 0.81 for SPEI-1, SPEI-3, and SPEI-6, respectively. Drought frequency in dryland croplands in Northeast China decreases with increasing drought severity, with high-frequency drought areas mainly concentrated in the central, central–western, and western parts of the Songnen Plain. For one-month-ahead prediction, the LSTM model achieves relatively good performance. Although incorporating root-zone soil moisture improves prediction accuracy to some extent, the overall improvement is relatively limited. Prediction performance varies across drought severity categories, and prediction errors generally increase with increasing drought severity, indicating that the model’s ability to predict extreme drought conditions requires further improvement. This study provides a methodological reference for meteorological drought monitoring and short-term prediction in dryland croplands in Northeast China.

title: Key Technology Research and Applications of Agricultural Inspection Robots Based on Machine Vision and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The rise in agricultural digitalization is progressively reshaping the conventional extended management model through the profound integration of intelligent sensing technology and artificial intelligence [...]

title: The Effect of Straw Returning on Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration in Arid Farmland Under Future Climate Change Scenario: A Comparison Based on Major Crops
abstract: Soil organic carbon (SOC) vulnerability is particularly acute in arid agricultural regions. However, existing studies have yet to systematically examine the SOC sequestration effects of varying levels of crop residue return under diverse future climate scenarios, despite the well-established efficacy of crop residue incorporation in enhancing SOC stocks in croplands. To address this critical knowledge gap, the present study investigates this issue. Overall, by integrating an optimized RothC soil carbon model with multi-source high-resolution datasets, we quantified the SOC sequestration potential of cotton, maize, and wheat croplands under four straw return rates across the three future climate scenarios SSP1–1.9-, SSP2–4.5, and SSP5–8.5 at the regional scale from 2020 to 2100. Cropland carbon inputs were calculated based on detailed yield data for cotton, maize and wheat. These were then extrapolated to the pixel scale using a weighting method to serve as model inputs, effectively enhancing the accuracy and credibility of simulation results. Model simulations show that under the SSP1–1.9 scenario during 2020–2100, cotton croplands had the lowest absolute SOC sequestration potential (relative to the 2020 baseline) across the four straw return treatments (0%, 5%, 10%, and 20%), with mean annual sequestration rates of 0.37, 0.42, 0.46, and 0.54 Mg C/ha/yr, respectively. The corresponding rates for maize croplands were 0.50, 0.56, 0.63, and 0.75 Mg C/ha/yr, whereas wheat croplands attained mean annual rates of 1.36, 1.45, 1.54, and 1.75 Mg C/ha/yr under the identical straw return gradients. Under the SSP2–4.5 scenario, SOC sequestration potential decreased across all three crop types. Further declines were observed under the SSP5–8.5 scenario, during which cotton and maize croplands exhibited negative SOC sequestration rates—a trend that could not be reversed even with 20% straw return. In terms of relative SOC sequestration potential (relative to the no-straw-return treatment during the same period), increasing straw return rates elevated the relative SOC sequestration potential for all three crops. Wheat exhibited the largest growth magnitude when straw return was raised from 10% to 20% under the SSP1–1.9 scenario. The three major crops are widely distributed across the entire study area, and their SOC sequestration potential exhibits substantial spatial heterogeneity. Overall, the potential follows a spatial pattern of higher values in the south and lower values in the north. Interestingly, SOC sequestration potential showed pronounced spatial heterogeneity as the straw return rate increased. Additionally, we found that even under the maximum straw return ratio assumed in this study, the spatial proportion of net SOC sequestration areas for cotton and maize croplands did not exceed 50% under the SSP5–8.5 scenario. To mitigate SOC losses in cotton and maize croplands under the SSP5–8.5 scenario, we performed inverse calculations to determine the equilibrium straw return thresholds required to achieve net SOC sequestration. The results showed that a straw return rate of 34.7 ± 0.7% was needed for cotton fields, while 25.8 ± 0.5% was required for maize fields. This study adopts the RothC soil carbon turnover model to comprehensively explore SOC sequestration potential of arid croplands from 2020 to 2100 under joint influences of three climate scenarios and varied straw incorporation measures. The results deliver referential insights for targeted agricultural regulation that helps arid farmlands adapt to future climate change.

title: Comparative GGE Biplots Derived from BLUP and SVD-Based Imputation for Mega-Environment Delineation and Genotype Selection in Unbalanced Multi-Environment Maize Trials
abstract: Crop multi-environment trials (METs) commonly produce highly unbalanced datasets. This mainly arises from annual turnover of test genotypes and occasional changes in trial locations across years. The GGE biplot method is widely applied to interpret genotype-by-environment interactions (GEI) and carry out mega-environment (ME) classification for variety-testing datasets. Two practical approaches are available for handling missing entries in MET two-way matrices: iterative imputation built upon singular value decomposition (SVD), and best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) derived from linear mixed models (LMM). We used two five-year (2021–2025) regional maize trial datasets from Henan Province, comprising 160 genotypes tested at 13 locations. The two datasets shared the same locations and field management, but contained largely different genotypes. Variance partitioning, ME investigation, and the selection of broadly adapted versus ME-specific genotypes at 10% and 20% selection intensities were compared. The SVD-completed matrices retained a markedly larger share of GEI variance than the LMM-BLUP matrices. A full variance component analysis revealed that variation arising from year-by-location interactions dominated total phenotypic variance, representing 54.3–65.3% of the total. By comparison, variance from the year-by-genotype interaction made up at most 2%. Part of the observed difference in GEI variance between the two analytical workflows stems from their intrinsic algorithm behavior. SVD-based imputation only estimates values for missing matrix cells and preserves all originally observed data points. In contrast, LMM-BLUP imposes shrinkage across every matrix entry. This shrinkage is a well-recognized statistical feature, which can enhance prediction performance when dealing with unbalanced field trial datasets. The SVD-based which-won-where view of the GGE biplot separated the trial locations into two MEs whose rankings were nearly uncorrelated or negatively correlated, and the resulting boundary lay at about 34°30′ N, broadly coinciding with the existing agroecological zoning of the province; this correspondence is reported as an empirical observation that still requires independent corroboration with environmental covariates. In a 100-run bootstrap resampling cross-validation based on field replicates, the two workflows differed little in prediction accuracy for the present datasets, with small differences favoring SVD imputation in some metrics. This outcome is specific to these data and to this resampling scheme; it does not establish the general superiority of either method, and prediction accuracy is not equivalent to the recovery of GEI patterns. Genotype selection outcomes differed between the workflows: more ME-specific and fewer broadly adapted genotypes were retained under SVD imputation, whereas BLUP-GGE biplots retained more broadly adapted genotypes and fewer region-specific elite materials. These findings indicate that, for unbalanced MET data, the choice of missing-data workflow can substantially change ME delineation and genotype selection. Analysts applying GGE biplots to unbalanced datasets should therefore evaluate the sensitivity of their conclusions to the treatment of missing data. Establishing the relative reliability of the two workflows will require independent validation across additional environments and datasets.

title: Perceptions and Biosecurity Practices Regarding Bovine Viral Diarrhea: A Qualitative Study with Dairy Farmers in Western Thailand
abstract: Bovine Viral Diarrhea (BVD) inflicts economic losses on global dairy production. In Thailand, BVD remains outside national control priorities, shifting the burden of disease management entirely to local biosecurity choices. Using a qualitative approach, this study investigated dairy farmers’ perceptions and biosecurity practices within Thailand’s certified Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) sector. Semi-structured, face-to-face in-depth interviews and field observations were conducted with smallholders in western Thailand, and the transcripts were analyzed using thematic analysis. The results revealed a profound “biosecurity paradox” driven by salience bias: while farmers showed universal awareness and strictly enforced emergency protocols for highly visible epidemics like Foot-and-Mouth Disease and Lumpy Skin Disease, they exhibited an acute awareness deficit regarding subclinical pathogens like BVD. Crucially, visual animal selection and structural trust routinely led to introducing persistently infected replacement heifers without screening. Furthermore, unstandardized management of reproductive waste was widespread, with most participants discarding infectious tissues into open fields. Rigid top-down GAP rules induced intense regulatory fatigue among financially stressed smallholders. Farmers explicitly rejected conventional extension group workshops due to acute labor constraints, preferring decentralized digital micro-learning (mobile short videos and on-farm posters) and clinical interactions with visiting practitioners. This study provides an empirical blueprint for livestock policy to shift from passive, farmer-dependent reporting to government-led active surveillance to protect national dairy herd health.

title: Hierarchy-Aware Adaptive Forgetting with Differentiable Cognitive Stratification for Robust and Interpretable Knowledge Tracing
abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) is a core task for intelligent tutoring systems, which aims to model learners’ knowledge states and predict learning performance. To address the drawbacks of homogeneous forgetting decay and single-granularity cognitive modeling in existing KT models, this paper proposes the Hierarchy-Aware Adaptive Forgetting Knowledge Tracing (HAAF-KT) framework. Compared with existing models, the core innovation of this framework lies in the deep coupling of three-level cognitive hierarchy and adaptive forgetting mechanism for the first time. It adopts learnable hierarchical weighting to replace conventional hard discrete stratification, and introduces mask consistency regularization at the input level to boost noise robustness, achieving end-to-end joint optimization of cognitive stratification, personalized forgetting and anti-noise regularization. Extensive experiments on three public benchmark datasets including Algebra2005, ASSISTments2017 and ASSISTments2009 demonstrate that the proposed HAAF-KT achieves competitive prediction performance on all datasets. For Algebra2005, the AUC is 0.8728 and the ACC is 0.8154. For ASSISTments2017, the AUC is 0.8372 and the ACC is 0.7704. For ASSISTments2009, the AUC is 0.9314 and the ACC is 0.8536. All results are reported as the average of five independent repeated runs with standard deviations less than 0.001, which verifies the superior stability of the model. Meanwhile, the distribution entropy of the learned KCH hierarchy drops to 0.79, which is considerably lower than the entropy of uniform distribution (1.79). Validated by the levels-of-processing theory in cognitive psychology, the model can effectively mine discriminative cognitive hierarchical structures and support fine-grained and personalized knowledge tracing, and the learned cognitive representations carry explicit educational interpretability.

title: Temporal-Aware Hybrid Machine Learning for Nutrient Prediction in Precision Tomato Cultivation
abstract: Precise nutrient management strategies should consider the variability in crop growth and cultivation periods in precision agriculture. This paper proposes a temporal-aware hybrid machine learning approach based on Ridge Regression and Least-Squares Regression (LSR) for predicting soil nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) in precision tomato cultivation. The dataset comprises 180 observations collected over three cultivation periods, including soil, climate, and plant attributes. The proposed approach was evaluated using a standard random 80:20 train–test split and an unseen-period validation strategy to assess temporal generalization. The hybrid model produced an average R2 of 0.94 and 0.90 in the conventional and unseen-period validation, respectively. Results show that the proposed approach still had substantial predictive capability when applied to a new cultivation period. These results illustrate the potential of temporal-aware hybrid machine learning to achieve season-aware nutrient prediction and decision support in precision tomato cultivation.

title: Artificial Neural Network Prediction of Daily Upper Respiratory Tract Infection Burden from Meteorological and Air Pollution Data: An Out-of-Time Test
abstract: Background/Objectives: Upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) create seasonal emergency department demand. We assessed whether temporal representations of meteorological and air pollution variables improve artificial neural network (ANN) prediction of daily URTI presentations and generalize to a later period. Methods: Daily presentations at a tertiary hospital in Istanbul (October 2022–September 2025) were modelled using 30 combinations of three environmental domains and ten temporal representations. Expanding-window validation on 682 development days selected nine ANN finalists, evaluated on 365 subsequent out-of-time days. Prespecified permutation importance was evaluated; reference-model comparisons, uncertainty estimation, calibration and sensitivity analyses were post hoc. Results: The lowest ANN test mean absolute errors (MAEs) were 38.53 (Combined_D02), 38.78 (Weather_D01), and 39.75 (Pollution_S0) presentations/day; differences between leading models were small and imprecise. Test R2 ranged from 0.039 to 0.168, with negative bias in every model. On 45 high-demand days above the development-derived 90th percentile, all models underpredicted (observed mean 229.0; predicted means 95.6–111.6). A seven-day trailing mean (MAE 34.03), seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (33.51), and autoregressive baseline (33.52) outperformed all ANNs; paired intervals for the two fitted baselines excluded zero. A calendar-only ANN achieved MAE 38.83, outperforming seven environmental models. Seasonally balanced splitting yielded lower MAEs (26.5–29.1), without consistent deterioration after training-size matching. Conclusions: No temporal representation consistently dominated. Environmental ANN models generalized poorly, underestimated peak demand and did not demonstrate gains over calendar predictors; simple outcome-history benchmarks were more accurate. They should not be used as stand-alone forecasting tools.

title: Forecast-Error-Aware Dual-Time-Scale Hierarchical Energy Management for Sustainable Operation of PV Microgrids with Battery–Supercapacitor Hybrid Energy Storage
abstract: The increasing penetration of photovoltaic (PV) generation introduces substantial uncertainties into microgrid energy management due to deviations between forecasted and actual generation and load demand. Conventional single-time-scale scheduling may impose additional regulation demands on batteries, increasing energy throughput, power fluctuations, and associated degradation costs. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a forecast-error-aware dual-time-scale hierarchical energy management strategy for a grid-connected PV microgrid equipped with a battery–supercapacitor hybrid energy storage system. The upper layer performs hourly economic scheduling by considering grid electricity transactions and battery degradation costs, while the lower layer conducts corrective optimization at 5 min intervals using updated source-load forecasts. Through receding-horizon optimization, reference tracking, and battery power-variation regulation, corrective power is coordinated among the battery, supercapacitor, and utility grid while respecting their operating constraints. A 48 h benchmark with three comparative strategies is conducted under a 10% normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), with all cases terminating at 10% battery SOC. Compared with conventional battery-based hourly scheduling, the proposed strategy reduces the total operating cost, battery energy throughput, and the battery power fluctuation index by 4.34%, 16.69%, and 38.40%, respectively. An additional 96 h evaluation, with battery SOC restored to 50% at successive period boundaries, retains a 9.96% reduction in the power fluctuation index but yields a higher operating cost and battery throughput. Sensitivity analysis under 5–20% NRMSE further shows relatively stable battery power fluctuations and increased supercapacitor utilization with forecasting uncertainty. These findings demonstrate the potential benefits of forecast-aware hierarchical coordination while indicating that economic and battery utilization outcomes depend on the operating scenario, evaluation horizon, and terminal-energy policy.

title: Identification and Categorisation of Factors Used to Evaluate Systems That Combine Photovoltaic Panels and Cultivated Land
abstract: Agrivoltaics (AVs) are systems that integrate photovoltaics with crop cultivation or livestock farming. Considering (1) the rapid pace of AV evolution and (2) the fact that there is a lack of a recent classification of factors influencing AV performance, the main goal of this study is to identify/classify factors used to evaluate AVs, focusing on open-field crop-based systems. The methodology used is based on a search across databases to retrieve publications. Using inclusion criteria, various categories of factors have been organised into a multi-dimensional framework and classified into seven categories (technical and socio-economic factors, among others), providing a taxonomy and identifying areas where further research is required. Moreover, this classification highlights critical challenges. For instance, stilt-mounted systems offer space for machinery and human activity, but they increase costs and impacts. In this case, advances such as bifacial and semi-transparent photovoltaics could offer benefits compared to traditional photovoltaic modules (monofacial; opaque; silicon-based). On the other hand, the analysis of 101 studies demonstrates that factors related to design, agronomy, microclimate, the physical environment and performance/outputs represent the dominant focus of the literature on AVs, comprising around 90–95% of the analysed publications.

title: Artificial Intelligence News and Digital-Financial Connectedness: Cluster Identification and Common Equity Exposures
abstract: This paper examines whether apparent dependence among artificial intelligence (AI) newspaper coverage, cryptocurrencies, financial-market stress, and technology-related equity portfolios reflects distinct intersectoral transmission or common asset-pricing exposures. We analyze 2016 aligned daily changes from January 2018 to April 2026 using generalized and clustered vector-autoregressive forecast-error variance decompositions, common equity-factor conditioning, alternative partitions, rolling estimation, and paired moving-block inference. Baseline clustered connectedness is 18.731% (16.011 percentage points within clusters and 2.719 across clusters), versus 20.685% under generalized identification. Residualizing fintech, cybersecurity, and clean-energy equity returns on SPY and QQQ reduces clustered connectedness to 6.741%. The reduction persists with VAR(2) and VAR(3), alternative forecast horizons, Monday exclusion, and economically plausible cluster structures. With 2000 paired bootstrap draws, the 95% intervals for adjusted-minus-unadjusted total connectedness are [−13.676, −10.207], [−13.777, −10.220], and [−13.815, −10.107] percentage points for VAR(1)–VAR(3). Cross-cluster attribution remains partition-dependent; one data-driven grouping yields essentially no reduction in its small cross-cluster component. HAC-robust tests across alternative AI transformations and lag orders show no incremental AI-news predictability after adjustment for multiple testing. The results favor an identification-aware, factor-conditioned account of digital-financial connectedness rather than a structural claim about technology shocks or economic contagion.

title: Effects of Southern Green Stink Bug Damage Severity on Soybean Yield and Seed Fatty Acid Composition
abstract: Soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merr.) is a key animal feed crop, in which seed oil fatty acid composition is a critical determinant of energy value, oxidative stability, and overall feed quality. Feeding damage caused by the southern green stink bug Nezara viridula (L., 1758) is known to impair the quality of soybean seeds. However, the relative contributions of sampling position, isolation, and visible damage severity to fatty acid compositional changes remain poorly resolved. In this study, thousand-seed weight, estimated yield, and fatty acid composition were analyzed in relation to sampling position, isolation status, and graded categories of visible seed damage. Thousand-seed weight and estimated yield declined markedly with increasing infestation intensity, with the greatest reductions observed under controlled infestation. Fatty acid composition varied moderately among treatments and between isolation groups, with no significant differences by sampling position. In contrast, stratification by visible damage severity revealed a strong, graded response in fatty acid composition, characterized by increasing saturated fatty acid proportions, decreasing oleic acid, increasing α-linolenic acid, and a pronounced reduction in the n-6:n-3 ratio with increasing damage severity. Visible seed damage severity was associated with the most extensive pattern of differences in fatty acid parameters among the classifications examined. However, these comparisons do not establish an independent contribution relative to infestation treatment, isolation, or sampling position. Although increasing damage category was associated with a lower n-6:n-3 ratio, this should not be interpreted as a nutritional advantage given the concurrent reductions in seed mass and yield, which probably reduce metabolizable energy availability. The compositional changes may also compromise the oxidative stability of soybean-based feeds. The results emphasize the importance of effective stink bug management for ensuring both the quantity and nutritional quality of soybean feed materials.

title: Urban Expansion and Its Impacts on Agricultural Land and Climatic Variables in Multan, Pakistan: A Remote Sensing and Trend Analysis Approach
abstract: Urban sprawl in developing countries may cause loss of agricultural lands and modifications in the climatic profile of the region. In this context, this research explores three decades’ worth of changes in land use/land cover (LULC) in Multan City of Punjab Province in Pakistan and analyzes their effects on the climatic profile in terms of temperature and rainfall. Landsat Thematic Mapper images of 1988 and 1999 and Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager images of 2020 were classified by applying a per-pixel supervised classification method with the Maximum Likelihood Classification algorithm to urban, river, fishpond, orchard, and field crop land classes. Accuracy assessment of the classification was done via an error matrix and kappa statistic. Monthly and yearly climatic data (temperature and rainfall) from 2000 to 2020 were analyzed using the non-parametric Mann-Kendall trend test. Innovative Trend Analysis (ITA) was used independently to analyze trends in the low, medium, and high datasets. Urban land increased from 14.6% to 34.1%, i.e., a 125% increase in LULC, whereas orchard land decreased from 42.6% to 8.5%. There was an increase in field crop land from 42.4% to 56.2%. Classification accuracy ranged between 84.5 and 87.6% (κ = 0.79–0.83). Seasonal trends in temperature and rainfall were found significant, whereas trends in annual temperature and rainfall were non-significant.

title: Crop-Specific Microbial Responses and Soil Quality Improvement Under a Bio-Based SBT-Crop System in Saline Desert Soils
abstract: Saline desert soils limit microbial activity and crop establishment. This study evaluated microbial and soil-quality responses to a soil bioactivation technology (SBT)-crop system in Sandy Desert and Gobi Desert soils of northwestern China planted with maize, cotton, or alfalfa. Here, SBT refers to a soil amendment composed mainly of marine active chitosan, plant fermentation liquid, natural oils, cellulose, and lignin, applied to the topsoil at 3000 kg ha−1 before sowing. Soil properties, bacterial and fungal marker-gene abundances, microbial richness, and the activities of five soil enzymes—sucrase (SC), cellulase (CL), urease (UE), alkaline phosphatase (AKP), and alkaline protease (ALPT)—were assessed. A minimum data set (MDS) approach was used to calculate the soil quality index (SQI), a composite indicator integrating multiple soil properties to assess overall soil quality, and partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) was used to examine its statistical associations with soil physicochemical and biological indicators. Compared with the corresponding SBT-only controls, maize cultivation significantly increased maximum water-holding capacity from 175 g kg−1 to 213 g kg−1 in Sandy Desert soil (21.7%) and from 195 g kg−1 to 225 g kg−1 in Gobi Desert soil (15.4%). In Gobi Desert soil, total salt content under maize decreased from 12.31 g kg−1 to 5.56 g kg−1, a reduction of 54.8%. In Sandy Desert soil, bacterial and fungal marker-gene abundances under maize were 61.63 and 85.81 times those in the control, respectively, while bacterial abundance under alfalfa in Gobi Desert soil was 77.93 times that in its control. In Gobi Desert soil, Chao1 and observed species richness were significantly higher under maize and alfalfa than in the SBT-only control (p < 0.05). The soil quality index calculated using a linear scoring function and minimum data set (SQI-L-MDS) increased from 0.29 to 0.40 under maize in Sandy Desert soil (37.9%) and from 0.34 to 0.62 under maize in Gobi Desert soil (82.4%); the value under maize in Gobi Desert soil was significantly higher than that under the other treatments. PLS-PM identified nutrient availability as the strongest positive correlate of soil quality, whereas total salt content and pH showed negative path coefficients. These findings demonstrate that soil-quality and microbial responses to SBT-amended crop management depend on both soil type and crop species. The results provide quantitative evidence to guide crop selection and soil-improvement strategies for saline desert agricultural systems, while longer-term field validation is needed to establish the persistence of these benefits.

title: Molecular Regulatory Networks of Plant Male Sterility: Nuclear Regulation of Stamen Development and Mitochondrial–Nuclear Crosstalk
abstract: Male sterility is the cornerstone of heterosis utilization and hybrid crop breeding. This review provides a comprehensive update on the molecular frameworks of genic male sterility (GMS) and cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS). We highlight how structural sterility is dictated by the ABCDE floral organ identity model, with class B, C, and E genes defining stamen fate. We further detail the SPL/NZZ-triggered DYT1-TDF1-AMS-MYB80-MS1 regulatory cascade that orchestrates sporogenous development encompassing microsporogenesis, tapetum function, programmed cell death (PCD), and pollen wall formation. Additionally, we explore functional sterility, which arises from impaired anther dehiscence and pollen release governed by regulators such as ARF6/8, NST1/2, TCP5, and ICE1. For CMS, we discuss how chimeric mitochondrial ORFs drive sterility via cytotoxicity, energy collapse, aberrant tapetal PCD, and retrograde regulation. The restoration of fertility, primarily achieved through Rf-encoded pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, is examined alongside emerging non-PPR restorers acting at DNA, translational, and metabolic levels. The dynamic coevolution of mitochondrial–nuclear interactions is reflected in the rapid expansion of Rf-like gene clusters. We conclude by outlining future perspectives emphasizing single-cell transcriptomics, CRISPR-based precision breeding of sterile lines, and the expanded deployment of male sterility in agriculture.

title: Climate Transition and Digital Asset Information in Forecasting European Sector Volatility: Signal Versus Noise
abstract: Investors and supervisors increasingly monitor oil, carbon, green asset and cryptocurrency markets as sources of equity risk. This study tests whether these markets improve forecasts of the realised volatility of ten STOXX Europe 600 sectors beyond a heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) benchmark that already includes market volatility and the VIX. Using weekly data from 2020 to 2026 and 181 out-of-sample weeks, it compares HAR models augmented with fossil energy, carbon, green and digital asset predictors, forecast combinations, penalised regressions and tree ensembles. The external predictors are jointly significant in sample for five sectors, but out of sample, the fossil, carbon and green blocks do not improve one-week forecasts on average. The digital asset block yields small gains (mean out-of-sample R2 of 0.33%) that survive false discovery rate control for five sectors but for only one when weeks end on Friday. Penalised regressions gain 2.0–2.6%, yet versions restricted to the benchmark predictors achieve 1.3–2.1%, so most of the gain comes from regularisation. With retransformation-corrected variance forecasts, model confidence sets retain almost all models, and volatility timing strategies underperform buy and hold after feasible execution. Robust incremental gains from climate transition information are not established; digital asset information offers small, fragile, sector-specific gains.

title: Class-Conditioned Evidence Recovery in Frozen Vision Transformers for Remote Sensing Object Detection
abstract: Aerial object detectors must resolve small, closely spaced objects while retaining enough context to recognize large structures. RS-Adapter uses an image-level class prior to update intermediate features in a frozen vision transformer. The prior combines a learned classifier, fixed class prototypes, and class-conditional descriptor statistics. Cross-attention links the prior to local features, which are fused across scales and gated before being added to the transformer. The adapted features guide a denoiser that generates box prompts for the detection decoder. On VisDrone, RS-Adapter achieved 39.2% average precision (AP) and 28.4% small-object AP, 3.1 percentage points above DEIM-D-FINE-L on the latter metric. AP50 was 78.3% on DIOR, 84.5% on NWPU VHR-10, and 87.7% on RSOD. RS-Adapter trained 16.8 million of its 103.2 million parameters and used less peak training memory than full tuning in the VisDrone comparison.

title: Beyond Construction: The Platform Effect of Environmental Infrastructure in Carbon Capture and Storage
abstract: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) remains one of the most capital-intensive clean energy investments in the United States. Despite its importance, regional science and environmental economics have paid limited attention to its economic effects. This study presents a comprehensive, replicable, multi-scalar framework based on IMPLAN to analyze the economic effects of a proposed CCS facility in a U.S. Gulf Coast county with a deep-water port. The framework examines four components: sequestration field construction, pipeline system development, annual operations, and on-site carbon capture installations. It assesses the impacts at the local, regional, and state levels using five metrics: jobs, earnings, value added, revenues, and taxes. The analysis shows how infrastructure-driven downstream investment can support economic growth. The framework combines the Leontief input–output model with a social accounting matrix (SAM) to measure infrastructure investment in complex regional economies. Customer-platform effects generate substantial local activity, supporting more than 30,000 jobs and $8 billion in revenue. These figures exceed the comparable impacts of the hub’s $337.8 million construction program by more than 14 times. Input–output models measure gross activity rather than net welfare, and analysts cannot observe counterfactually how much investment customers would capture. Therefore, these figures represent the scale of activity associated with a fully subscribed hub, not impacts attributable to the hub alone. Annualizing a capture cost of $1 billion per million metric tons, the upper end of the published range of roughly $350 to $1500 per annual ton of capacity, across a 20-year asset life and at an 8 percent cost of capital, yields approximately $102 per metric ton. This figure exceeds the $85-per-metric-ton Section 45Q credit, which helps explain why most of the announced U.S. capture capacity has not yet reached a final investment decision. At benchmark central costs of $450 to $700 per annual ton, the capital charge alone ranges from $46 to $71 per metric ton. However, peer-reviewed estimates of the cost of CO2 avoided include energy costs and span the value of the credit. Under these conditions, the customer effect falls to roughly 6 to 10 times the hub’s construction impact. The study frames the platform effect as a conditional upper bound that depends on viable capture economics, rather than as a forecast. It provides a replicable, multi-scalar methodology for regional science and introduces the CCS Platform Effect as a tool to assess infrastructure-enabled industrial investment.

title: NITE-TIME: Exploring the Economic Potential of Weather-Informed Fertiliser Application Timing
abstract: Optimising fertiliser application timing represents an underutilised opportunity to improve nitrogen use efficiency and reduce economic losses in agricultural systems. This study introduces NITE-TIME (Nitrogen Impact of Timing on Emissions), a simplified predictive framework developed to investigate whether weather-informed fertiliser timing can identify economically favourable application windows. Rather than attempting to represent the full nitrogen cycle, the model uses a simplified process-based approach to simulate short-term nitrogen losses through ammonia volatilisation and rainfall-driven runoff over a 7-day period using ERA5 meteorological data. Application timing was systematically varied within crop-specific windows for winter wheat, barley, and oilseed rape. Results indicated that nitrogen losses are controlled primarily by the interaction between rainfall events and subsequent meteorological conditions, producing optimal application windows rather than discrete optimal times. High-input systems such as winter wheat exhibited narrow application windows (~1 h) and large potential savings (>£3000 per field), whereas oilseed rape exhibited broader windows (~3.5 days) and lower economic sensitivity. Monte Carlo and multi-year analyses indicated that economically favourable application windows emerged consistently across a wide range of parameterisations and meteorological conditions. Although NITE-TIME is intended as a proof-of-concept rather than a validated decision-support tool, the results suggest that weather-informed fertiliser optimisation warrants further investigation, particularly in the context of precision and autonomous agricultural systems.

title: Modeling the Term Structure of Interest Rates in Bangladesh: Evidence from a Dynamic Nelson–Siegel Macro-VAR Approach
abstract: This paper examines the term structure of interest rates in Bangladesh from April 2015 to January 2026 using the dynamic Nelson-Siegel (DNS) model, incorporating macroeconomic variables. The DNS model breaks down the yield curve into three latent variables: Level, Slope, and Curvature, and models the evolution of these latent factors within a Vector Autoregression (VAR) framework, including the policy rate and inflation. The DNS specification provides an excellent cross-sectional fit to Bangladesh government bond yields, with an average (𝑅2) of 0.991 and a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 24.7 basis points. Both the estimated Level and Slope factors show a high degree of persistence (0.905 and 0.956, respectively), whereas the estimated Curvature factor shows significantly less persistence. Impulse-response and forecast-error variance decomposition analyses suggest that monetary policy shocks have a small but growing impact on yield-curve dynamics at longer horizons. DNS-Macro-VAR yield curve forecasts remain upward-sloping and gradually converge toward a stable long–run configuration. These results show that the DNS framework is useful for modelling and forecasting the yield curve in the Bangladesh government bond market, offering valuable insights for monetary policy design, bond market development, and risk management.
journal: The American Journal of Interdisciplinary Innovations and Research

title: StrawNet-Lite: A Lightweight Attention-Based Deep Neural Network for Strawberry Leaf Disease Detection in Smart Agriculture
abstract: Accurate strawberry disease classification remains challenging due to visual similarities among disease categories, variations in symptom appearance, and class imbalance. Conventional whole-image classifiers may overlook localized disease-associated information that could complement global visual representations. This study proposes StrawNet-ROI, an annotation-guided dual-view deep learning framework integrating a multi-scale EfficientNet-B0 global classifier, a polygon-supervised region-of-interest (ROI) prediction network, and a separately fine-tuned local classifier. A connected-component-based procedure generates spatially constrained crops from predicted ROI maps, while confidence-adaptive probability fusion combines global and local predictions without requiring ground-truth annotations during inference. Experiments were conducted on an audited seven-class strawberry disease dataset comprising 2,457 images, partitioned into 1,426 training, 294 validation, and 737 testing samples. Across five random seeds, StrawNet-ROI achieved a mean test accuracy of 98.78 ± 0.25%, macro-precision of 98.26 ± 0.60%, macro-recall of 97.40 ± 0.43%, and macro-F1 of 97.79 ± 0.47%. Compared with the global-only classifier, the framework achieved a numerical macro-F1 improvement of 0.59 percentage points; however, the paired difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.1268). Additional cropping controls did not establish statistically significant superiority of ROI-guided selection. The complete framework contains 12.58 million parameters and achieved a mean end-to-end inference latency of 18.80 ms on a server-class GPU. These findings suggest that global–local representation fusion may provide complementary information for strawberry disease classification, although the additional computational cost and limited statistical evidence warrant caution. Because the evaluation relied on a historically examined internal test partition, independent field generalization and resource-constrained deployment remain unverified.
journal: Journal of Applied Science and Technology Trends

title: Model-Driven Stellar Spectroscopy with the Total Differential Spectral Model (TDSM): Framework and Its Application to 11 Million LAMOST Low-Resolution Spectra
abstract: Deriving stellar astrophysical parameters from large-scale spectroscopic surveys requires accurate modeling of spectra across a wide wavelength coverage and a broad range of stellar parameter space, which remains a great challenge. In this work, we present \texttt{TDSM}, a physically motivated neural network architecture that self-consistently emulates both the flux and its first-order derivative of the ab initio stellar spectra. The method enables accurate and precise emulation of Kurucz synthetic spectra with severely blended features at $R \simeq 2000$ in a high-dimensional parameter space, achieving a typical pixel-wise flux precision of 0.05\% in the wavelength range $3700<λ<9000$Å over the parameter range of $3000 < T_{\rm eff} < 45,000$~K, $-1 < \log g < 5$, and $-4.0 < \mathrm{[Fe/H]} < 0.5$. The model is applied to LAMOST DR10 to derive stellar parameters for 11 million spectra spanning the full model parameter range. We conduct detailed refinement and calibration efforts to mitigate systematic errors, which are revealed to be significant and complex due to imperfections in the ab initio model atmosphere. The resultant catalog provides eight stellar labels -- $T_{\rm eff}$, $\log g$, $v_{\rm mic}$, [Fe/H], [$α$/Fe], [C/Fe], [N/Fe], and [Mg/Fe] -- for 8 million unique stars (11 million spectra including repeat observations) across the full parameter space. This adds a valuable dataset for studies of Galactic structure and archaeology, stellar populations, and related areas of astrophysics.

title: Formally verified harness for Shor's order finding algorithm with $O(n^{2+\epsilon})$ gate cost
abstract: It is commonly understood that factoring a general $n$-bit biprime via Shor's order finding algorithm requires $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ gates by leveraging schoolbook integer arithmetics for addition and multiplication. Recent developments in quantum arithmetic circuits leveraging recursive Toom-Cook schemes have improved the cost scaling to $O(n^{2+\epsilon})$. Here $\epsilon>0$ depends on algorithm implementation details of the recursive multiplication steps, which allow for a vast number of design choices. The challenge in navigating such design space also presents an opportunity for demonstrating innovative practices in quantum software engineering in the era of open agentic science. We present a formally verified harness that ingests a design specification (namely a"policy"that describes a recursive circuit design scheme) from an external source, which may be an AI agent, and produces a set of formalized proofs covering mathematical correctness of the algorithm implementation, asymptotic scaling of the end-to-end gate cost, as well as the correctness of translating the verified algorithm to a detailed circuit implementation with an intermediate representation. The harness is published as an open challenge where human researchers and AI agents can search for more efficient factoring circuits while retaining machine-checked guarantees of correctness and end-to-end asymptotic complexity.

title: Adaptive Koopman Predictive Control without Persistent Excitation via Matrix Normal Invariant Priors
abstract: Finite-dimensional Koopman models are increasingly used in predictive control, but their accuracy remains limited by truncation errors and offline identification data. Adaptive Koopman predictive control promises to address this limitation, but typically requires closed-loop persistent excitation (PE). Since this is difficult to achieve in practice, in this paper we develop an adaptive generalized Koopman (GeKo) predictive controller that does not require PE. To this end, we formulate a recursive matrix regression in fixed lifted coordinates that extends the Kalman filter with back-to-the-prior forgetting to matrix-valued operators and uses a matrix normal invariant prior, centered at the operator identified offline. For any regressor sequence, and thus under any feedback law, we prove that the covariance remains between two multiples of the prior covariance and that the estimation error is input-to-state stable. On an academic example, a differential-drive robot and a power system with plant changes and little excitation, the invariant-prior estimator yields the lowest overall tracking error among the compared estimators and prevents covariance windup.

title: The Optimal Interface Method: A Modelling Paradigm for Two-Body Contact Problems via Optimal Control and $\Gamma$-convergence
abstract: This paper is concerned with the derivation of a model governing the equilibrium configuration of two linearly elastic bodies that may come into contact with each other. The contact zone, or coincidence set, is an \emph{a priori} unknown of the model, and the equilibrium configuration is governed by variational inequalities. We introduce a new modelling paradigm in which the contact interface between the two linearly elastic bodies under consideration is now regarded as the \emph{primary variable} of an optimal control problem whose states are the unique solutions of two \emph{independent} unilateral contact problems for which this very contact interface represents the obstacle itself. As a result, the free boundary emerges as the solution of a low-dimensional optimisation problem rather than as the active set of coupled variational inequalities. We establish the existence and uniqueness of optimal controls minimising the reduced cost functional arising from the modelling paradigm introduced beforehand, and we show that the family of marginal energy functionals associated with such model $\Gamma$-converges to the energy functional associated with the original variational inequalities as the positive \emph{cost parameter} $\beta$ in the reduced cost functional tends to zero. This $\Gamma$-convergence argument also yields a characterisation of the coincidence set of the limit problem in terms of the optimal interfaces. We further show that, after a suitable regularisation, the reduced cost functional is G\^{a}teaux differentiable, and that its G\^{a}teaux derivative can be explicitly computed \emph{without solving any adjoint system}. Finally, we corroborate the $\Gamma$-convergence result obtained beforehand with numerical experiments on a simplified and exactly solvable configuration.

title: Straight to the Product: What Online Retailers Miss When Shoppers Ask AI First
abstract: When people ask an AI assistant what to buy, what happens next at the store? We link the same people's assistant conversations to their later browsing at twenty large online retailers. People go to the product the assistant named: among shoppers who had not visited the store in the past week, visits to the named product within a day rise from 0.02 to 2.07 per 100 answers (+2.0 points [1.7, 2.4]), and on days with a product-page visit at the store, 44% show a product from their own answer, against 1.5% for a matched answer given to someone else. The result replicates in a separate five-month period. Few arrive through the assistant's link: 89% of visits carry no sign of it, and 54% follow a web search, the same share as their usual visits. When a search comes just before the first visit, it names the answer's product 28% of the time (1% in earlier weeks), as if the search box were an address bar. The chat names the product; the store logs a search. Once there, shoppers keep browsing. We propose product follow-through, the share of answers followed by a visit to the product they named, as a way to evaluate shopping assistants and agents by what people do next: it needs no referral data or provider logs and can be computed for each assistant.

title: Signs of Wear: Evaluating Intelligent Speed Assistance Under Synthetic Adverse Conditions
abstract: Intelligent Speed Assistance (ISA) systems rely on cameras to recognize speed-limit signs, yet existing benchmarks underrepresent the weathered, dirty, and overgrown signs commonly encountered on rural roads. We use generative image editing to introduce different forms of wear into real street-level images of speed-limit signs. The resulting ISA-Wear dataset contains paired original and edited images. Guided by text instructions, a multimodal image-editing model adds snow, rust, vegetation, faded paint, or mud to the speed-limit sign in a street-level frame at three severity levels. Where appropriate, the surrounding scene is adapted as well, and the viewpoint is kept. Every edited frame has an unedited counterpart, and we only evaluate frames whose original is recognized correctly, so any failure can be attributed to the wear. Since the model alters the sign's geometry in 21\% of the edits, all edits are filtered by a geometric check and a manual review. Severity is measured as the LPIPS distance between the original and the edited sign plate. On 716 worn frames, we find that in detect-then-read pipelines, wear breaks detection before it breaks reading. The detector finds only 62\% of the worn signs, even though it finds every one of them in the original frames. Missed detections account for 78--87\% of failed reads, a pattern that a zero-shot detector shares. Given the annotated sign box, as in the crop-based benchmarks, a classifier still reads 78\% of the worn signs, but only 56\% when it has to rely on the detector

title: Lean-Verified No-Go Theorems for $R$-Symmetries and Modular Symmetries in 4D GUTs
abstract: $R$-symmetries are instrumental in supersymmetric model building. However, a no-go theorem restricts us from using them in a large class of four-dimensional (4D) grand unified theories (GUTs). Specifically, it has been shown that a supersymmetric 4D GUT based on SU(5), with finitely many chiral multiplets, cannot be broken spontaneously to the exact minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) while preserving a discrete $\mathbb{Z}_M^R$, with $M \geq 3$, or continuous U(1) $R$-symmetry. We use Lean 4 to formalize this proof. In the process, we identify and close a gap in the general case of the published argument. Further, we discuss the implications for GUT models with modular symmetries. We point out that modular symmetries are inevitably $R$-symmetries in a supersymmetric framework that also describes gravity. At certain critical points in moduli space, discrete $R$-symmetries are linearly realized. In the context of 4D GUTs, the no-go theorem then implies that exotic states become massless at these points, provided the GUT-breaking vacuum preserves these symmetries. In the vicinity of these critical points, these exotics are parametrically light, which may spoil gauge coupling unification.

title: Where the Evidence Lives: Measuring Privacy and Diagnosability of Exported AI-Agent Traces
abstract: Execution traces help diagnose AI-agent failures, but sharing them can expose customer identities. For example, detecting that an agent handled the wrong customer's records requires knowing whether the records belong to the requested customer, but not necessarily knowing who that customer is. Our executable benchmark measures what a trace export reveals and whether a proposed repair restores the correct output in synthetic multi-tenant workflows. Conventional redaction can remove evidence needed for repair while leaving encoded identifiers recoverable. Two exports preserve ownership comparisons by reporting the match as a comparison fact or by using pseudonyms consistent within each execution. Both preserve the original diagnostic program's repairs. The tested identifier matchers identify no requested customer from either export. An independently written program produces correct outputs on 39 of 42 faulty cases with comparison facts and on all 42 with execution-scoped pseudonyms. Row counts still expose identities. With prior knowledge of customers' row counts, an attacker uniquely identifies the requested customer in 97 of 240 executions under each of the 15 export policies. Removing selected counters from the comparison-fact export stops this attack and preserves the original program's repairs. The benchmark lets engineers test what their diagnostic program can repair and what an attacker can still infer from the same export.

title: Deploying a Control-Logic LLM Assistant in Air-Gapped Power Plants: Lessons in Source Authority and Bounded Retrieval
abstract: Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in industrial operational technology environments poses constraints largely absent from cloud applications: site policies restrict engineering and operational data from leaving the plant, on-premises compute is limited, and incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response. We report lessons from deploying a control-logic evidence layer that underpins a broader on-premises operator assistance system at two gas power plants. Two prototypes revealed where generative models added avoidable uncertainty and cost. The first used a Vision Language Model (VLM) to reconstruct control topology from PDF printouts routinely exchanged by engineers. Across the full 6,979-page document, extraction reached 0.51 connection precision and required 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs; consultation with controls engineers then revealed a native structured export from the authoring system. The second used an LLM tool-calling agent to plan repeatedly over eight predefined graph operations. In a controlled benchmark of 40 template-generated questions, replacing this agent with explicit execution plans reduced mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x, with identical retrieved node sets across repeated runs. The deployed design ingests the authoritative export into a versioned knowledge graph, executes bounded graph operations in fixed software, and confines the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation. At one site, the graph contains 221K nodes across seven controllers. Our experience suggests a practical division of labor for high-consequence AI: LLMs interpret natural-language requests and explain results, while deterministic software constructs and retrieves technical evidence grounded in authoritative sources. Abstention, entity disambiguation, graph versioning, and read-only integration provide additional safeguards.

title: Implicit-Reasoning-Enabled Elastic Semantic Communications for AI-Agent Networks
abstract: AI-agent networks introduce new communication demands driven by proactive interactions and autonomous task execution. Existing adaptive semantic communication schemes primarily adjust semantic representations and resource configurations within predefined processing scales and capability sets, which may be insufficient for evolving task requirements. To address this gap, we introduce elastic semantic communications (ESC), a task-driven framework that extends semantic adaptation to the runtime execution and participation of task-supporting capabilities. ESC comprises two complementary dimensions: vertical elasticity adjusts the execution intensity of existing capabilities, while horizontal elasticity reconfigures the participating capability set. The framework connects these dimensions through the expected marginal value of additional information and computation. To realize ESC, we propose an implicit-reasoning-enabled device--edge mechanism that supports variable-depth local inference through shared-parameter state updates and edge-side continuation through wireless transfer of intermediate reasoning states. Experiments on Sudoku-Extreme demonstrate that the benefits of additional inference depend on wireless conditions, while task-aware edge invocation can preserve task accuracy with substantially lower state-transfer overhead.

title: Augmenting Pretrained Language Models with N-gram Embeddings through Incremental Training
abstract: As a new scaling technique for large language models, the n-gram embedding improves the base ability of a model while adding almost no inference cost. Mainstream research realizes it through joint training of the n-gram embedding with the backbone, which severely restricts the settings in which an n-gram embedding can be used. We therefore propose training an n-gram embedding onto an existing model through incremental training, to extend where the technique can deliver value. Specifically, we explore several settings of the n-gram embedding under incremental training---the learning rate of the embedding, the vocabulary size, and the injection position---and train an n-gram embedding onto the existing model under the best configuration.
