abstract: Quantitative electron microscopy includes imaging, diffraction, spectroscopy, and tomography measurements, and the analysis of these measurements increasingly requires solving inverse problems with physical forward models. Open-source software has made many of these analyses widely available, but most packages are organized around a single modality, so that multimodal analyses require moving data between packages, and new methods cannot easily reuse the physical models and optimizers of existing ones. Here we present quantEM, an open-source Python package for quantitative electron microscopy that uses PyTorch tensors for computation and automatic differentiation, and Zarr for storage. We implement each analysis method by writing a differentiable forward model and choosing a representation, loss function, constraints, and optimizer from a library of components, so that every method runs on CPUs and GPUs, can be saved and resumed, and uses the same calibrated data structures and visualization tools. We describe the current modules, including orientation and strain mapping, direct and iterative ptychography, tomography with neural representations, and X-ray and electron energy-loss spectroscopy, and show how we assemble combined methods such as ptychographic tomography from existing components. quantEM is available under the MIT license, together with documentation, tutorials, and curated example datasets.

title: Wrong Input, Wrong Threshold: Re-evaluating Adversarial Facial Privacy
abstract: Published face-privacy methods report protection above 90% against black-box recognition models. That number comes from an evaluation protocol with two independent defects, reported in a measure that cannot size either one. The input is wrong: methods published since 2022 feed the network the whole photograph, or a detector's box, where deployed systems detect, align to a landmark template and crop. Re-scoring the same files through a realistic front end costs a standard transfer attack 56% of its dodging protection and a budget-allocating attack 7%, with no image regenerated. The measure is wrong: that loss is a difference of success rates, so it saturates, moving by 8.2x over a budget sweep while the effect beneath it moves by 1.34x. We therefore report the paired cosine shift, in which both thresholds cancel algebraically, so the input defect holds without committing to a calibration. Measured that way it is 2.2x and 10.7x larger on three unseen recognizers, and at matched budget it reverses the L-infinity transfer ranking: the one surveyed method that aligns at evaluation gains 0.18 where MI-FGSM loses 0.05. The cause is a resampling mismatch, not perturbation lost outside the crop; optimising through a differentiable alignment operator largely removes it, adding +24 to +58 points on unseen recognizers and a commercial system, with a residual on one of them. The thresholds are wrong: the four constants inherited since 2021 hold the false-accept rate near its nominal 1% on aligned crops but admit 2.3-5.4% on whole images, with an opposite-signed bias across dodging and impersonation, the two tasks reported side by side. Differentiable alignment and gallery scoring are not new: the first generation of this literature used both, and we show what dropping them cost.

title: Physics-informed neural networks for spacecraft trajectory optimization with exact boundary conditions
abstract: We use neural networks to optimize trajectories by modeling the position as a function of time and minimizing the thrust with respect to the network parameters. This corresponds to an unsupervised training procedure in which physical laws are incorporated directly into the optimization objective. In standard physics-informed neural networks, initial and terminal states are enforced through additional weighted loss terms, resulting in a multi-objective optimization problem that is highly sensitive to the choice of loss weights and can lead to poor convergence and reduced accuracy. To address this challenge, we construct a simple transformation, exploiting the mathematical structure of trajectory optimization problems, to enforce boundary conditions exactly a-priori. This transformation can be interpreted as a reparameterization of the solution space that embeds the boundary conditions directly into the function. This converts the original constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one over admissible trajectories. I.e. the transformation eliminates the boundary condition penalty terms and reduces the problem to a single-objective optimization. Crucially, trajectory optimization comes with a low-dimensional boundary, which allows particularly simple and stable constructions of distance functions compared to general domains in partial differential equations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach meaningfully improves convergence behavior and solution accuracy.

title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.

title: DiscoveryAgent: A Framework for Scientist-centric Agentic AI
abstract: AI agents can assist scientific research, but balancing autonomous investigation with scientists' ability to inspect and redirect ongoing work remains a central design challenge. We present DiscoveryAgent, a domain-agnostic, scientist-centric system that combines autonomous investigation with scientist-directed hypothesis steering. Scientists select, refine, or replace hypotheses between research rounds, while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims, reproduce analyses, and inform subsequent decisions. Across two predictive modeling tasks, DiscoveryAgent produced the best variable-star classifier among evaluated baselines and, with scientist steering, a protein variant-effect predictor surpassed by only one of 106 ProteinGym baselines. We develop a rigorous checkpointing system that enables highly capable audit agents, a scalable form of oversight for agentic research. Audit agents autonomously identify errors at higher rates than previous AI scientist agents, and scientists collaborating with audit agents identify 14x more valid errors versus scientists performing manual review. In three case studies led by domain experts across physical science, social science, and life science, we developed a multimodal photometric-redshift estimator that resolves complementary failures of images and photometry, achieving 0.971 AUROC for low-redshift classification; documented an 83% rise in Florida homeowners-insurance premiums from 2013 to 2023, with a growing, regressive burden; and identified CD4+ T-cell relay genes, which both receive and exert broad transcriptional regulation, enriched for autoimmune disease associations. Together, these results show how autonomous research can expand scientists' empirical reach while centering their authority over research direction and their ability to understand and challenge the evidence.

title: SCAN: Site-Aware Collaborative Privacy-Preserving Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Neurological Disease Classification
abstract: Worldwide neuroimaging data could strengthen diagnostic foundation models, but privacy rules often prevent centralizing brain MRI scans. We present SCAN, a site-aware collaborative adaptation framework for Neurological Disease Classification that lets new sites adapt a 3D medical vision-language model (VLM) without retraining or sharing patient scans. Each site keeps exact class prototypes for local prediction and can share privacy-protected class summaries: norm-bounded sums and counts perturbed once with calibrated noise. Using 7,641 scans from 67 sites across 12 countries, covering Alzheimer's disease (AD), stroke, epilepsy and controls, we assess local adaptation, cross-site benefits, and effects on existing sites. At seven unseen sites, the frozen VLM's zero-shot AUCs were 0.833-0.945 for AD and stroke. Training-free local prototypes improved epilepsy AUC at three sites from 0.598/0.625/0.508 to 0.684/0.729/0.762 and AD AUC at one site from 0.833 to 0.863, nearly matching a classifier trained at each site (mean AUC 0.757 vs. 0.759). With differential privacy ($ε$ = 4), new sites contributed without materially reducing accuracy at existing sites (AUC change $\leq$0.2%), although gains from sharing were limited, and membership attacks performed near chance. SCAN offers hospitals a worldwide framework to adapt and share brain MRI VLMs without exchanging scans or retraining.

title: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
abstract: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.

title: Solver to System: LLM Reasoning Across Representations and Execution in Scientific Simulation
abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.

title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
abstract: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.

title: From Apology to Action: Apologies, Compensation, and Cooperation in LLM Agents
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can make decisions that affect other agents, but what happens after a harmful or unsuccessful interaction remains poorly understood. We investigate whether apologies by LLM agents are associated with subsequent cooperative behaviour, using controlled Prisoner's Dilemma experiments with four commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Mistral Large 3). Across payoff conditions, we examine when agents apologise, the reasons they provide, and the actions that follow. We also examine how access to one round of interaction history affects behaviour and, in a second experiment, whether and how agents offer compensation alongside their apologies. Apology behaviour differed substantially across models and preceding interaction outcomes, and verbal expressions of cooperation did not always align with subsequent actions. Notably, Claude Opus 4.8 apologised even after mutual cooperation, while Mistral Large 3 apologised after being exploited but continued to defect even when its opponent cooperated. After unilateral defection, positively compensated apologies from GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro were followed by mutual cooperation, unlike those from Claude and Mistral. Our findings suggest that apologies, compensation, and strategic behaviour are distinct: conciliatory messages may precede continued defection, while costly apologies may go unanswered. This has important implications for the study of machine behaviour and human-AI interactions, as verbal signals alone may not reliably reflect an AI system's subsequent actions.

title: Supporting Researcher Control in AI-Assisted Social Media Analysis: A Mixed-Methods Study of AI4OSN
abstract: High-quality annotated datasets are critical for advancing computational social science (CSS) research, yet collecting, curating, and analyzing large-scale data from dynamic sources such as online social networks (OSNs) remains a persistent bottleneck. Researchers must also translate substantive questions into queries, relevance criteria, and defensible interpretations. Large language models (LLMs) can assist, but they can also obscure the judgments, potentially reducing researcher oversight and critical evaluation. We present AI4OSN, a mixed-initiative platform that keeps researchers in control of data collection, relevance labeling, and sensemaking while making AI assistance available as an inspectable advisory resource. In a systematic user study (N=18) using X/Twitter data, participants reported above-benchmark perceived usability (mean SUS score of 79.7), increased confidence in LLM-assisted annotation and analysis tasks, and low cognitive workload during AI-supported sensemaking. Notably, novice participants showed descriptively greater alignment and higher reported agreement with AI output than experienced participants, underscoring the need to support differentiated verification practices across expertise levels. Overall, this work contributes both a human-centered system for social data analysis and empirical insights into how AI-assisted interfaces shape researcher behavior, trust, and decision-making. Our findings highlight design opportunities and tensions in building accessible, transparent, and agentic AI systems for social media and web research.

title: Training for sustainable scientific software in the AI era: from code production to scientific stewardship
abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are changing how researchers interact with scientific software. Their effects on productivity vary across tasks and users, but they can weaken the connection between producing a successful computational artifact and retaining scientific command over the consequential choices and evidence on which it depends. For high-energy physics, this shifts part of the training challenge from code production toward scientific stewardship: researchers must be able to validate, explain, reproduce, maintain, and justify software and workflows partly generated or modified by AI. We argue that AI-aware software training should therefore combine dedicated instruction on AI systems with the integration of AI into established software and analysis training. Testing, provenance, reproducibility, resource judgment, and scientific validation should be exercised in AI-assisted workflows, with competence judged by the evidence supporting a result rather than by code generation alone. We frame this as a problem of sustainable scientific software: AI-assisted workflows should remain trustworthy and maintainable, use computational resources responsibly, and avoid making core competence unnecessarily dependent on privileged access to particular tools or infrastructure.

title: Pedological classification as a key determinant of arable soil microbial communities and effects of cash-crop management
abstract: Climate and soil-related variables, along with soil management practices, have been identified as key determinants of soil microbial composition and, consequently, soil ecosystem functioning. While numerous biogeographic studies at local to continental scales have identified several variables such as pH, soil carbon quality and quantity and total precipitation as important predictors of microbial composition and diversity, these observations have not been validated by similar biogeographic research within agricultural systems, limiting our ability to compare microbiomes from cultivated sites. This observational study of topsoil microbial composition in Quebec's cash crop fields is one of the rare biogeographical studies conducted in arable land that investigates a wide range of soil, climate, and farming-related variables. In this study, the taxonomic and predictive carbon-related functional composition of microbial communities was investigated in 80 cultivated mineral topsoils across 38,000 km2 in Quebec, Canada. Using multivariate statistics, we examined how two climatic variables (precipitation and growing degree-days), 9 soil-related variables (pedological classification, soil texture and structure, pH, carbon and nutrient concentrations), and 6 agricultural management practices (crop diversity indexes, tillage intensities, organic fertilization type and compaction risk) influenced community variation (represented by the robust Aitchison beta diversity). Pedological classification, based on the Canadian System of Soil Classification, emerged as one of the strongest and most consistent predictors of prokaryotic and fungal community structure and of the structure of inferred prokaryotic carbon-cycling functional potential, whereas farming practices showed little relative influence. All six climate- and soil-related variables that significantly explained microbial variance in the biogeographic analyses were also significantly different between pedological soil classifications. We also hypothesized that the strong predictive power of soil classification indicates that it serves as a proxy for additional key variables. Further taxonomic analyses revealed that stratifying samples by pedological groups provided a more nuanced understanding of the specific effects of organic fertilizer type and soil tillage intensity, with distinct taxonomic families responding within each soil classification and some soils showing distinct sensitivities to specific farming practices. This evidence supports integrating soil classification as a foundational framework for assessing microbial responses to farming practices across soil types and for monitoring the soil microbiome at large geographic scales.

title: Mapping 20-years winter wheat dynamics in global primary planting areas using Gaussian mixture models with adaptive thresholds
abstract: Understanding the spatiotemporal dynamics of winter wheat is essential for ensuring global food security. Currently, limited research has focused on the global dynamics of wheat over the past decades. In this study, we propose a novel framework to map fractional winter wheat dynamics from 2001 to 2020 at 1 km resolution in key global planting areas from MODIS satellite data, utilizing a flexible Gaussian mixture model (GMM). We first created the stratified samples of winter wheat fractions at 1 km resolution from multiple public crop datasets to establish the training base, and then developed a robust random forest regression model using MODIS surface reflectance to map regional fractional distributions of winter wheat. Subsequently, we estimated the actual wheat cover fractions across different regions and years by analyzing crop mixtures within 1 ° × 1 ° grids with GMM. The model parameters were utilized to determine optimal thresholds for winter wheat extraction. The performance of our proposed framework was evaluated spatially and temporally, revealing significant insights into global winter wheat dynamics. Results demonstrated that our mapping approach aligns closely with existing local winter wheat maps and statistical data, achieving annual coefficients of determination ( R 2 ) above 0.81 with FAO statistics in primary planting regions and exceeding 0.72 at subnational scales. We present the first comprehensive effort to map global winter wheat distribution and dynamics from 2001 to 2020 at a near-global scale. The proposed framework is readily adaptable to other major crops and demonstrates strong agreement with existing maps and statistical records. The resulting high-resolution global winter wheat map series provides valuable inputs for global crop modelling and contributes to achieving the “Zero Hunger”. The product is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32149033 (Wen et al., 2026).

title: Fresh and degraded maize shoot and root residues temporarily change hydraulic properties of a loamy soil
abstract: Mulching and incorporation of crop residues (CR) into soils are common strategies to sustain soil carbon stocks, return nutrients, and regulate water losses through bare soil evaporation. To date, implementing the effects of mulching strategies into soil-plant-atmosphere models remains a challenge as there is limited information on how this layer of CR changes with time and how it thereby influences processes such as evaporation, water infiltration or the transport of pollutants. An important, hitherto unknown key property of a mulch layer and the incorporation of plant residues is their influence on soil hydraulic properties (SHP) as well as on the persistence of these effects over time. We hypothesized that increasing amounts of incorporated maize CR increases water retention and reduces unsaturated hydraulic conductivity, and that the quality of the CR would determine the persistence of the effects, i.e., that mulching with relatively fast decaying shoot residues would be less persistent than incorporating root residues. In a laboratory study, we quantified the effect of maize CR in various concentrations (0 wt %, 2 wt %, and 5 wt %) on the SHP of a loam soil and additionally measured the SHP of a mulch layer (100 wt % CR) from saturation to oven dryness. We differentiated between shoot and root CR to quantify the effect of biomass quality and adapted the simplified evaporation method to measure the hydraulic properties of 100 % CR layer. The experiments were run in triplicate in a climate constant room (20 °C, 65 % RH) and repeated after three weeks of incubation under optimal conditions for biological activity (30 °C, 90 % RH) to simulate organic matter degradation after harvest. CR decay was monitored by carbon and nitrogen composition of fresh material, after the first measurement of SHP (pre-incubation) and at the end of the experiment (post-incubation, incubation plus second measurement of SHP). Comparing the SHP with different CR mixtures provided direct information on how CR concentration modifies water retention and conductivity, comparing pre- and post-incubation measurements provided information about the temporal dynamics of CR effects on SHP. Compared to the control, water retention increased systematically by 2 vol % to 5 vol % across the CR-soil mixtures from saturation to field capacity while the unsaturated hydraulic conductivity was slightly reduced. However, biodegradation of CR started immediately after harvest especially for shoot residues, simultaneously altering residue carbon and nitrogen concentrations. During the experimental time of 31 d for CR-soil mixtures and of 48 d for 100 % CR layers, carbon mass exponentially decreased about 46 %–50 % in 100 % CR layers, 7 %–15 % in root-soil mixtures and 21 %–27 % in shoot–soil mixtures. Despite this degradation, a positive effect on the soil water retention curve persisted, with water content increasing on average by 1.5 vol % per gram of carbon in a kilogram of soil at saturation and by 1.3 vol % at field capacity. In contrast, the slight decrease in conductivity at field capacity diminished after three weeks of incubation. Overall, the study demonstrates that the beneficial effects of CR incorporation on the SHP of a loam soil increase with CR amount and persist for at least one month after harvest. In agroecosystems, this post-harvest period and the mulching process are crucial for defining the initial soil conditions for the subsequent crop. Furthermore, the relatively low unsaturated hydraulic conductivity of the 100 % CR layer at field capacity confirms field observations that mulch layers can effectively reduce water losses through bare soil evaporation.

title: A Review of Occupational Safety and Health in Uganda's Agricultural Sector: National Legal Policies, Hierarchy of Controls, Gender and Literacy
abstract: Agriculture is the backbone of Uganda's economy, employing over 70% of the population and contributing about a quarter of the national Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Yet farm workers, employers, visitors, and communities living near agricultural land remain exposed to mechanical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, and psychosocial hazards, while institutional attention in the sector has focused on productivity, food safety, and value addition rather than on the safety and health of the people who do the work. The purpose of this review was to examine agricultural occupational safety and health (OSH) in Uganda with respect to four themes: the national legal and policy framework, the hierarchy of controls, gender, and literacy. A narrative review design was adopted, drawing on national legal instruments, government policy documents, International Labour Organization (ILO) and United Nations publications and peer-reviewed studies, including twenty recent studies published between 2021 and 2026, which were synthesised thematically. The review found that Uganda's OSH legislation, anchored in the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda (1995), the Occupational Safety and Health Act (2006), the Workers' Compensation Act (2000) and the Employment Act (2006), is general rather than sector-specific and does not adequately address agricultural hazards, including child labour, which is concentrated in agriculture. Recent evidence shows that fewer than half of farmers in developing countries handle pesticides safely, that musculoskeletal pain, machinery injuries and heat stress are widespread, and that hazard control on farms relies heavily on personal protective equipment, the least effective level of the hierarchy of controls, which is itself seldom used in full. Women form a large share of the agricultural workforce and experience distinct exposures, and low literacy limits workers' awareness of their OSH rights and of preventive practices. The review concludes that agricultural OSH in Uganda is constrained by mutually reinforcing legal, technical and social gaps. It recommends agriculture-specific OSH regulations aligned with ILO Convention No. 184, systematic application of the hierarchy of controls in farm machinery design and agricultural extension, gender-responsive OSH programmes, and translation of OSH instruments into local languages supported by digital training tools. Keywords: Agricultural occupational safety and health, Hierarchy of controls, Gender, Literacy, Labour legislation, Uganda

title: From naïve to vigilant: how inflammatory and metabolic cues shape human T cells
abstract: CD4⁺ T cells are essential regulators of adaptive immunity and can differentiate into distinct helper T cell subsets depending on signals from their environment. Among these subsets, T helper 17 (Th17) cells play a crucial role in protecting against bacterial and fungal infections but are also implicated in chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. This thesis investigates how environmental and metabolic factors influence human Th17 cell differentiation and function. Using a defined human in vitro model, we demonstrate that Th17 development is shaped by a combination of signals, including TGF-β, extracellular lactate, and hypoxia. These factors modify cellular transcriptional programs and converge on key regulatory pathways, particularly STAT3. We further show that mitochondrial activity is closely linked to Th17 differentiation. Cells with high mitochondrial membrane potential are more likely to develop into Th17 cells, but also display characteristics associated with functional exhaustion. The clinical relevance of these findings was explored in osteoarthritis, where synovial T cells were found to remain activated and responsive despite longstanding disease. Together, the results show that T cell differentiation is highly dynamic and determined by interactions between environmental cues, metabolism, and tissue context. Understanding these interactions may provide new therapeutic opportunities for chronic inflammatory diseases.

title: Faogf: Auditable Evidence Provenance ForAutonomous Financial Ai Agents On Opentelemetry
abstract: Autonomous AI agents now read regulatoryfilings, compute figures and distribute reports inside financial firms, but their telemetry cannot tell an auditor which filing versions a decision rested on, under which authority and policy version an action ran, or whether untrusted content was in the model’s context. We present FAOGF (Financial Agent Observability and Governance Framework), an OpenTelemetry-compatible audit layer. Its core architectural contribution is context-bound evidence provenance recorded on two paths: a gateway binds every modelcall and action to the version-exact, content-hashed evidence actually in the model’s context, and writes that binding synchronously to a hash-chained evidence store before exporting standard spans, so audit completeness no longer depends on what the tracing pipeline keeps. We evaluate nine audit queries. In 15 controlled experiments with a scripted agent (200 workflows × 5 seeds, and a real OpenTelemetry Collector on two machines), all nine queries were evaluated: FAOGF answered the seven answerability queries (Q1–Q7) exactly in every configuration, detected 88–97% of spans lost to export-queue overflow (Q8) and 100% of audit attributes stripped by a Collector processor (Q9). Standard OpenTelemetry tracing recovered only 9–12% of protected actions at 10% head sampling and was silently stripped by a common Collector configuration; full prompt logging could not answer authority or policy questions. In a live study on SEC EDGAR filings with gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4o on public Finance Agent Benchmark questions, wescored the two queries the live workload exercises, supporting filings (Q3) and untrusted-context exposure (Q7). FAOGF was exact on both, standard tracing misattributed 4–18% of supporting filings, and full prompt logging used 7–10× more storage. Neither live model followed any of the 78 injected instructions, so enforcement was evaluated on a simulated susceptible agent. There, escalating only the sends requested with untrusted content in context blocked every injected send with 37% fewer human approvals than requiring approval for every send. FAOGF adds about 0.2 ms median overhead per call.

title: Utilization of WhatsApp Groups for Farmer Peer-Learning and Adoption of Improved Agricultural Practices Among Smallholder Farmers in Bayelsa State
abstract: This study assessed the utilisation of WhatsApp groups for farmer peer-learning and the adoption of improved agricultural practices among smallholder farmers in Bayelsa State, Nigeria. The study adopted a cross-sectional survey design using a mixed-methods approach. The population comprised smallholder farmers belonging to agricultural WhatsApp groups across the agricultural zones of Bayelsa State. A sample of 216 farmers was used for the quantitative analysis, while farmers, cooperative leaders, agricultural extension agents, and WhatsApp group administrators participated in the qualitative interviews. Data were collected using WhatsApp Group Utilisation, Farmer Peer-Learning and Improved Agricultural Practices Questionnaire (WGU-FPL-IAPQ) and a semi-structured interview guide. The questionnaire recorded an acceptable reliability coefficient. Quantitative data were analysed using mean, standard deviation, and Pearson Product-Moment Correlation, while qualitative data were analysed thematically. The findings showed that agricultural information was exchanged at a marginally high extent, particularly information on planting periods, improved planting materials, seasonal changes, weather, flooding, and water management. Farmer participation was low and mainly passive, as farmers read agricultural messages more frequently than they asked questions, responded to other farmers, or shared personal experiences. Farmer peer-learning was also low, although farmers discussed common production problems and encouraged one another to adopt improved practices. The overall adoption of improved agricultural practices was low, despite relatively higher adoption of flood-management, harvesting, storage, and post-harvest practices. Qualitative findings identified flooding, poor connectivity, high data costs, limited digital literacy, inadequate transportation, high input costs, lack of credit, and irregular extension-agent participation as major constraints. The analysis revealed a significant but weak positive relationship between WhatsApp peer-learning and the adoption of improved agricultural practices. The study concludes that while WhatsApp bridges physical extension gaps in difficult terrains, its potential is limited by passive participation. It is recommended that extension agencies and cooperative administrators introduce structured, interactive prompts and subsidized digital tools to transition farmers from passive readers to active peer-learners.

title: Machine Learning Approach Leveraging Crop Datasets for Optimizing Crop Yield Production
abstract: Crop yield prediction based on environmental, soil, water, and weather parameters has become a vital area of research, addressing the growing need for sustainable agricultural practices and food security. This study adopts a machine learning approach to optimize crop yield production within the agricultural landscape of Michika Local Government Area, Adamawa State. Applying extensive crop datasets, machine learning techniques are utilized to analyze, interpret, and uncover critical factors and patterns influencing crop yields. The main objective is to develop a robust predictive model that empowers farmers and stakeholders with actionable insights, to enhance agricultural productivity. The results demonstrate a substantial improvement in yield predicting accuracy through machine learning-based methods compared to traditional approaches. ANN with the lowest RMSE (3136.8), the lowest MAE (2502.2), and higher R² (0.073255), indicates the most accurate predictions. These findings underscore the transformative potential of artificial intelligence in advancing precision agriculture, enabling resource-efficient farming, and bolstering food security. This study also highlights avenues for future research, including optimizing resource allocation strategies, identifying resilient crop varieties, predicting and mitigating crop diseases, and mapping soil suitability for diverse crops. Such efforts would further drive the adoption of smart agricultural systems, enhancing productivity and sustainability while supporting the transition to climate-resilient farming practices.

title: Impact of Agricultural Insurances on Food Security Among Smallholder Farmers in Adamawa State, Nigeria
abstract: This study examined the impact of agricultural insurance on food security among smallholder farmers in Adamawa State, Nigeria. Specifically, the study examined the impact of crop insurance coverage, livestock insurance, index-based weather insurance and input insurance on food security. The study was anchored on Expected Utility Theory and Risk Management Theory. A survey research design was adopted, while the population comprised farmers and agricultural cooperatives in Adamawa State. Due to the difficulty of determining the exact population, Cochran’s (1977) formula was employed to determine a sample size of 384 respondents. Primary data were collected through structured questionnaires, and multiple regression analysis was employed to analyse the data using SPSS version 20.0. Out of the 384 questionnaires distributed, 371 were successfully retrieved, representing a response rate of 96.6%. The regression results revealed that crop insurance coverage (β = 0.294, t = 4.689, p = 0.000) had a positive and statistically significant impact on food security. Similarly, livestock insurance (β = 0.226, t = 3.825, p = 0.000) had a positive and significant impact on food security. The study further established that index-based weather insurance (β = 0.203, t = 3.527, p = 0.000) had a positive and significant effect on food security, while input insurance (β = 0.263, t = 4.254, p = 0.000) also had a positive and statistically significant influence on food security. The model summary indicated an R-squared value of 0.618, suggesting that the four dimensions of agricultural insurance jointly explained 61.8% of the variation in food security. The study concluded that agricultural insurance is an important mechanism for improving food security by reducing agricultural risks, protecting farmers' investments and strengthening their resilience to production-related shocks. The study recommended that government agencies and agricultural insurance providers should expand access to affordable crop and livestock insurance, promote index-based weather insurance and develop accessible input insurance schemes to enhance food security among smallholder farmers in Adamawa State, Nigeria.

title: Fertilizer Subsidy Regulatory Coherence, Institutional Capacity, and Sustainable Agricultural Performance in Indonesia
abstract: Indonesia’s fertilizer subsidy governance reforms introduced through a series of regulations enacted in 2025–2026 have strengthened certainty in procurement, distribution, raw material availability, subsidy payments, and production continuity. However, previous studies have examined economic impacts, distribution, institutional capacity, and sustainability separately, leaving the ability of the latest regulatory architecture to produce sustainable agricultural performance insufficiently understood. This study is essential to prevent subsidy performance from being assessed solely through budget absorption, transactions, and distribution volumes. It aims to analyze regulatory evolution and coherence, contributions to institutional capacity, alignment with economic, social, and environmental dimensions, and a results-based regulatory improvement framework. The study employs an integrative qualitative approach combining content analysis of five principal regulations with a systematic literature review guided by PRISMA 2020. The findings show that the regulations have strengthened legal certainty, regulatory capacity, and supply resilience. Nevertheless, fragmented coordination, unequal regional capacity, unintegrated data, digital exclusion, and inadequate indicators of nutrient-use efficiency and soil health persist. The study recommends regulatory consolidation, a dynamic integrated data system, crop-calendar-based coordination, integration of subsidies with agricultural extension and soil management, and evaluation based on an input–process–output–outcome–impact framework

title: Plant Leaf Disease Classification Using Deep Learning with ResNet-50
abstract: Background/Objective: Plant diseases can reduce crop yield and quality. Identifying visible symptoms at an early stage may help farmers respond before damage becomes widespread. This study evaluates an image-level classifier that assigns leaf photographs to 38 healthy and diseased categories using Res-Net-50. Methods: The New Plant Diseases Dataset (Augmented) contains 70,295 training images and 17,572 validation images. Images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels and normalised. Random horizontal flipping, rotation and colour jitter were applied during training. A ResNet-50 model with a 38-class output layer was trained from random initialisation for three epochs on a CPU, using cross-entropy loss and the AdamW optimiser. Pretrained ImageNet weights could not be downloaded in the experimental environment. Results: The best checkpoint, obtained at epoch 3, achieved 99.80% validation accuracy: 17,536 of 17,572 images were classified correctly, while 36 were misclassified. Among the reported per-class results, the lowest recall was 0.96 for corn Cercospora/Gray leaf spot, and the lowest precision was 0.97 for corn Northern Leaf Blight. Conclusion: The model achieved high accuracy on the dataset’s validation split. However, this split is not an independent test set, and the dataset contains augmented images. The result should therefore be interpreted as a baseline under controlled conditions; evaluation on independent field images is still required.

title: ProtFlap: Structure-based Deep Learning Prediction of Protein Flexibility from Atomic Energy Networks
abstract: Protein flexibility is a key determinant of molecular recognition, catalysis, and regulation, yet remains difficult to characterise at scale. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide detailed descriptions of time-dependent dynamics but are computationally expensive. Although recent AI-based structure prediction methods have substantially improved access to high-quality static protein structures, they inherently lack information regarding the dynamic fluctuations essential for functional understanding. There is therefore a need for scalable, structure-based computational approaches that can infer intrinsic protein flexibility without explicit dynamical sampling. We present ProtFlap, a graph neural network framework for predicting relative residue-level flexibility directly from static protein structures. ProtFlap represents proteins as residue interaction graphs and integrates empirical atomic energy features extracted from a single energy-minimised snapshot with structural and sequence-derived descriptors. Central to our approach is the hypothesis that the local atomic energy network encoded in a frozen protein structure contains sufficient information to estimate structural flexibility. Trained using atomic mobility labels, quantified via normalised root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) derived from short MD simulations, ProtFlap achieves robust and accurate flexibility prediction across diverse protein domains. Feature attribution analysis reveals that van der Waals–related energy terms are the dominant contributors to the prediction. Key Points ProtFlap is a graph neural network that predicts intrinsic residue-level protein flexibility. The framework evaluates single, static structures, bypassing computationally expensive molecular dynamics simulations. Predictions are physically grounded by integrating structural descriptors with empirical atomic energy terms. Feature analysis reveals that local thermodynamic constraints, primarily Van der Waals forces, dominate flexibility prediction.

title: AMPK activation by aldometanib alleviates inflammation and autoimmune disease via suppressing inflammatory T cell generation
abstract: Background: Aberrant T-cell activation and differentiation are central drivers of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. However, current therapies targeting T-cell function to ameliorate these pathological conditions frequently carry risks of immunotoxicity. AMPK activators have been shown to exert therapeutic effects in metabolic disorders and preventive effects against tumour progression; however, it is not clear whether they can modulate T-cell responses to suppress inflammatory and autoimmune pathologies. Methods: We utilized an in vitro OVA-triggered OT-II CD4 + T cell model to examine the functional changes in T cells induced by diverse AMPK agonists. Aldometanib, a selective lysosomal AMPK activator that mimics glucose starvation, was further characterized for its effects on T-cell function. Mechanistic studies were performed via RNA-sequencing, immunoblotting, and rescue experiments using a CRISPR-Cas9 system and mixed bone marrow chimeras. The therapeutic efficacy of aldometanib was assessed in murine models of acute lung injury, allergic inflammation and chronic colitis, as well as in spontaneous lupus-prone mice. We further investigated whether aldometanib suppresses cytokine production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) isolated from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) under ex vivo conditions, providing preliminary proof- of-concept evidence. Finally, we compared the effects on immune homeostasis, safety profile, and tissue toxicity of aldometanib, rapamycin, and MK2206. Results: We analyzed the effects of AMPK activators on T cells and reported that aldometanib significantly inhibited IFN-γ secretion by CD4 + T cells while preserving cell survival. Aldometanib suppressed T-cell activation, proliferation, and differentiation via AMPK activation and PTEN-associated programs. Moreover, compared with that of rapamycin, aldometanib

title: Sustainable Plant Disease Management through Eco-friendly Approaches: A Review
abstract: Plant diseases are major biological constraints to agricultural productivity, food security, farm profitability and the stability of global food systems. Disease management has traditionally depended on synthetic fungicides, bactericides, soil fumigants and other chemical plant-protection products. Although these inputs remain important in many production systems, excessive or poorly targeted use can accelerate selection for resistant pathogen populations, increase pesticide residues and environmental loading, disturb beneficial organisms and increase production costs. Sustainable plant health therefore requires approaches that reduce disease pressure while conserving ecological processes and limiting unnecessary pesticide exposure. Eco-friendly disease management combines exclusion and sanitation, cultural practices, resistant cultivars, biological control, botanicals, natural elicitors, organic amendments, disease-suppressive soils, physical treatments and increasingly precise molecular and digital technologies. Beneficial microorganisms such as Trichoderma, Bacillus and Pseudomonas can suppress pathogens through mycoparasitism, antibiosis, nutrient competition, niche exclusion, lytic enzymes, volatile compounds and induction of systemic resistance. Compost and biochar may enhance suppressiveness by altering soil physicochemical conditions and microbiome structure, while chitosan and other elicitors can prime host defence. Bacteriophages and spray-induced gene silencing offer highly targeted options against bacterial and fungal pathogens, respectively, and nanotechnology may improve delivery, stability and detection. Remote sensing, artificial intelligence, molecular diagnostics and forecasting further support timely, site-specific intervention. Nevertheless, field inconsistency, formulation stability, variable environmental performance, regulatory requirements, cost and ecological risk assessment remain barriers to wider adoption. This review examines the mechanisms, practical applications, advantages, limitations and future prospects of major eco-friendly approaches and argues that their greatest value lies in integration. An adaptive disease-management system built on prevention, host resistance, ecological regulation, early diagnosis and targeted intervention can reduce pesticide dependence while maintaining reliable crop protection.

title: Digital Inclusion in Agribusiness: Access, Capabilities, Market Power and Smallholder Outcomes
abstract: Digital technologies increasingly mediate agricultural advice, input procurement, finance, marketing and coordination across agrifood value chains, yet their availability does not necessarily confer meaningful participation on smallholders or rural enterprises. This critical narrative review examines the mechanisms through which digitalisation may reduce transaction costs and improve decision-making, alongside the socioeconomic, organisational and governance conditions that can reproduce exclusion. The review integrates experimental studies of agricultural information delivery, observational analyses of participation and livelihoods, research on digital financial services, critical accounts of platform-mediated commerce, and recent studies of inclusion-oriented design. Evidence indicates that well-designed digital advisory interventions can improve knowledge and adoption of selected practices, although effects on output, profits and sustained welfare are more variable. Access to a device or network is an inadequate proxy for inclusion because language, literacy, control over devices, household bargaining, service relevance, market infrastructure and financial risk condition the conversion of connectivity into benefits. Digital marketplaces may expand reach while imposing fees, logistical obligations or dependence on powerful intermediaries; digital finance can facilitate transactions and savings while creating new exposure to opaque credit practices. The review develops a staged, relational account of inclusion that distinguishes technical reach, effective use, economic agency, distributive outcomes and rights over data. It identifies the need for long-term, disaggregated causal evaluations; enterprise-level evidence beyond farm adoption; transparent assessment of public–private delivery models; and governance arrangements that make information quality, affordability and accountability enforceable. Bridging technology gaps requires coordinated investment in basic infrastructure, trusted human support, locally adapted services and fair commercial institutions rather than expanding digital interfaces in isolation.
journal: Asian Journal of Agricultural Extension, Economics & Sociology

title: CrystaL Artificial Intelligence Monitoring (CLAIM) Study of the OMERACT Ultrasound CPPD Subtask Working Group: Interim Analysis of Automated Ultrasound Grading of Knee Meniscal CPPD.
abstract: OBJECTIVE We aimed to develop and evaluate artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods for automated grading of calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) in ultrasound (US) images according to the Outcome Measures in Rheumatology (OMERACT) US scoring system. METHODS Within the OMERACT CrystaL Artificial Intelligence Monitoring (CLAIM) project, two deep learning strategies were explored using knee meniscus US images graded from 0 to 3. Image-level classification was evaluated using convolutional neural networks (CNN) trained directly on cropped meniscus images (n = 446). A semantic segmentation approach was developed using a subset of 279 images with manually annotated masks identifying meniscus and deposits. Models were evaluated using an 80/20 training-validation split and stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Segmentation was assessed using Intersection over Union (IoU). For automated grading, an area ratio (AR), representing CPPD pixels relative to meniscus and CPPD pixels, was applied to predicted masks. RESULTS Image-level classification achieved an accuracy of 0.69 in the single-split analysis and a mean accuracy of 0.59 (SD 0.10) in 5-fold cross-validation. End-to-end AR grading achieved accuracies of 0.64 and 0.61 (SD 0.10), with a grade 3 recall of 0.25 in the single split. AR grading on manually annotated reference masks achieved an accuracy of 0.82. The best-performing segmentation model achieved mean IoUs of 0.86 for background, 0.60 for meniscus, and 0.37 for CPPD. CONCLUSIONS These findings provide a methodological basis for automated CPPD US grading, but performance remains far from clinical applicability, highlighting the need for larger datasets and improved segmentation.

title: Bacterial DnaK Promotes CHIP-Mediated GPX4 Degradation: A Bone-Targeted DNAzyme-Nanozyme Strategy for Repair of Infected Bone Defects.
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus infection impairs bone repair, but how bacterial proteins disrupt osteogenic progenitors remains unclear. The bacterial chaperone DnaK promotes glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) degradation in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), accompanied by lipid peroxidation, ferroptotic injury, and impaired osteogenic differentiation. GPX4 protein turnover increases without a change in Gpx4 mRNA abundance. A candidate E3-ligase screen identifies the C terminus of Hsc70-interacting protein (CHIP) as a mediator of this response. Catalytically inactive CHIP attenuates DnaK-associated K48-linked GPX4 ubiquitination, while CHIP knockdown preserves GPX4 and osteogenic proteins in primary BMSCs. To target bacterial DnaK and host oxidative injury, a bone-targeted deoxyribozyme (DNAzyme)-nanozyme platform (DMPA) combines a dnaK-targeting DNAzyme with manganese hexacyanoferrate, polydopamine, and alendronate. In infected cultures, DMPA reduces bacterial dnaK transcript and DnaK protein abundance and improves BMSC redox balance and matrix mineralization. In a mouse model of infected tibial defects, DMPA promotes bone regeneration. These findings link bacterial DnaK to host GPX4 degradation through CHIP and establish a bone-targeted DNAzyme-nanozyme strategy that combines bacterial DnaK suppression with redox regulation to promote repair of infected bone defects.

title: Histone Chaperone ASF1B Promotes Progenitor-Like Cell States in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Through H3.3-Dependent SOX9 Transcriptional Activation.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS Tumor plasticity contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression and therapy resistance, but chromatin mechanisms underlying progenitor-like malignant cell states remain incompletely defined. This study investigates whether ASF1B functions as an oncofetal chromatin regulator of these states in HCC. APPROACH AND RESULTS Integration of a human hepatocyte differentiation model with clinical and single-cell datasets identifies ASF1B as an oncofetal histone chaperone reactivated in HCC and associated with poor differentiation and unfavorable survival. Functional analyses show that ASF1B promotes progenitor- and stemness-associated properties, favors less-differentiated malignant cell states, and enhances tumor growth, metastatic phenotypes, and sorafenib resistance. Mechanistically, ASF1B interacts with histone H3.3, increases H3.3 enrichment and RNA polymerase II engagement at the SOX9 promoter, and enhances nascent SOX9 transcription, with HIRA contributing to replication-independent H3.3 deposition. ASF1B and H3.3 also exhibit dynamic co-condensation in live cells and a reconstituted system. Genetic epistasis establishes SOX9 as a major downstream effector. Liver-directed ASF1B depletion reduces tumor burden and enhances sorafenib responsiveness in an immunocompetent HCC model. CONCLUSIONS ASF1B promotes progenitor-like malignant cell states through an H3.3-SOX9 chromatin regulatory axis and represents a candidate therapeutic vulnerability in HCC. ASF1B and H3.3 additionally exhibit dynamic co-condensation, suggesting a possible biophysical feature.

title: Digital Technologies to Address Transparency and Traceability for Sustainable Supply Chain Management: A Stakeholder Perspective
abstract: The concept of supply chain transparency and traceability as a crucial aspect of sustainability is gaining traction among academics, practitioners, and policymakers. In this perspective, digital technologies are recognized as essential enablers to address transparency and traceability for sustainable supply chain management in organizations. Despite the increasing global shift in digitalization in various industries, the adoption of digital technologies in the agricultural sector in developing economies remains limited. Hence, this exploratory study aims to investigate the use of digital tools enabling stakeholders to address transparency and traceability for sustainable supply chain management in the Sri Lankan tea sector. A qualitative research methodology was used and 24 semistructured interviews were conducted with 13 participants holding different positions in the Sri Lankan tea supply chain. Drawing on the resource‐based view and stakeholder theory, the study findings highlighted various digital tools as valuable resources facilitating upstream, midstream, and downstream stakeholders to address transparency and traceability for achieving economic, environmental, and social sustainability in tea supply chain operations. The study contributes to the existing literature through detailed investigation and empirical mapping of digital technologies used by supply chain actors across upstream, midstream, and downstream activities in the Sri Lankan tea supply chain. Using the perspectives and in‐depth insights of 13 stakeholders across the Sri Lankan tea supply chain, the findings present a grounded picture of how digital technologies are operationalized in a specific agricultural supply chain in a developing economy context.

title: Economic and pest-management tradeoffs of low-tunnel adoption in day-neutral strawberry: pest- and disease-driven quality losses and management costs.
abstract: BACKGROUND Low tunnels are increasingly used for the cultivation of day-neutral strawberries (Fragaria × ananassa Duchesne); however, adoption depends on whether protected cultivation sufficiently increases marketable yields to justify the additional expenditures on infrastructure, labor, and crop protection. This study integrates three years of field trials conducted in Geneva, New York, USA with a representative 1-acre economic model to assess the viability of low tunnels as a component of integrated pest and pollinator management. RESULTS The implementation of low tunnels led to an increase in total yield in two of the three trial years and enhanced fruit marketability across all three years. In the commercial baseline scenario, the use of low tunnels increased modeled marketable output from 14 414 to 23 784 pounds per acre and net operating profit from $13 250 to $35 393 per acre. Over a five-year period, the incremental net present value was approximately $79 121 per acre, with a benefit-to-cost ratio of 3.93 and a payback period of 1.07 years. Profitability was most sensitive to variations in price, marketable-yield response, packout, and additional costs associated with Tetranychus urticae management. CONCLUSION Low tunnels may present an economically advantageous option for Northeastern day-neutral strawberry cultivation when they maintain marketable yield and T. urticae is managed effectively. The study offers pest management and investment thresholds that delineate the conditions under which protected cultivation is likely to enhance grower returns. © 2026 The Author(s). Pest Management Science published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd on behalf of Society of Chemical Industry.

title: Quantum state texture from the average absolutes of density entries
abstract: Quantum state texture is recently recognized as an important quantum resource in quantum information tasks. The only textureless state firstly proposed in $(Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 260801 (2024))$ is $f_1=\ket{f_1}\bra{f_1}$, \textcolor{red}{where $\ket{f_1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\ket{i}$.} We take into account the modulus of the density matrix entries, and reasonably define the textureless states to be ones that all the modulus of the density matrix entries are equal. We present a quantifier of quantum state texture with respect to such non-convexity set of textureless states. As an application, we demonstrate in the transverse field Ising model that the texture of the subsystem of the ground state effectively characterize the quantum phase transitions, providing an alternative texture-based characterization of quantum criticality. We also provide the relationships among the quantum state texture, coherence and purity. Furthermore, we explore the quantum state texture based quantum speed limit in dissipative dynamical processes and derive the lower bound on the time required in texture variation for some dynamical processes.

Can AI-assisted analysis of antidepressant drug online reviewers (ADORE) inform real-world use of antidepressants?
abstract: BACKGROUND Antidepressant selection is constrained by limited comparative-effectiveness data, with randomized trials measuring symptom reduction rather than patient-reported tolerability. We tested whether AI-assisted analysis of patient-written online reviews recovers drug-level tolerability signals that converge with the strongest randomized evidence. METHODS We did a cross-sectional analysis of 8348 reviews of 16 antidepressants for major depressive disorder posted to Drugs.com (February 2008-March 2025; ≥1 month reported use). Two independent large language models (Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro) classified each review across 17 clinical dimensions using identical structured prompts; a stratified 100-review subsample (1700 classifications per reviewer) was independently rated by two experts, with all agreement statistics highly significant. We compared per-drug top-rating prevalence with Cipriani et al.'s 2018 network meta-analysis retention and efficacy odds ratios (Spearman correlation). RESULTS Mean inter-LLM Cohen's κ was 0.81; expert reviewers agreed substantially with the dual-AI consensus (mean κ = 0.75 and 0.80). Top rating correlated strongly with Cipriani et al. retention odds ratios (ρ = +0.79, p < 0.001) but not with efficacy odds ratios (ρ = -0.14, p = 0.64). Within-SNRI heterogeneity was substantial. Emotional blunting was the strongest negative predictor of satisfaction (OR 0.20). LIMITATIONS Reviews are from a single platform and self-selected users; drug-level comparisons rest on few agents; and the design is cross-sectional and ecological. CONCLUSIONS AI-classified patient reviews recover the drug-level tolerability signal of randomized retention data and surface within-class heterogeneity, particularly among SNRIs, as a hypothesis-generating signal. Within the comparable-efficacy range of contemporary antidepressants, tolerability, especially emotional blunting, principally correlates with patient satisfaction.

title: Agentic AI for intelligent battery management systems: From diagnosis to autonomous control
Cyber-Secure Wearable, Ultra-Low-Power Networked Sensors for Soldier Health Monitoring: Insights from the CAPSARII project
abstract: The CAPSARII project advances a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable platform and Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) framework to support real-time monitoring of military personnel and data-driven decision support. The architecture integrates smart-textile sensing, a body/squad area mesh, edge-deployed AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning and comparative studies. Two representative use cases--pilot fatigue and warfighters operating in harsh environments--guide requirements, validation, and interface design (including HUD and haptic feedback). As an initial step toward embedded models, we benchmark stress classification on a public wearable dataset: tree-ensemble baselines achieve state-of-the-art performance for accuracy and F1 (e.g., XGBoost: $\mathrm{Accuracy}=0.901\!\pm\!0.023$, $\mathrm{F1}=0.920\!\pm\!0.019$), while a feature-based Transformer attains the highest AUC ($0.963\!\pm\!0.025$), informing feature-engineering and compression choices for edge deployment. Building on these results, CAPSARII employs HW/SW co-design, model compression (pruning, quantization, distillation), and precision tuning to meet stringent energy and memory budgets; it further investigates Processing-in-Memory accelerators for future efficiency gains. A structured gap analysis highlights the remaining challenges: establishing validation standards for physiological signal quality and textile durability; achieving low-latency, scalable BAN/SAN communications under mobility and interference; and deploying hybrid lightweight/post-quantum cryptography with robust device identity and side-channel resilience on constrained endpoints. By consolidating these elements into a coherent, secure IoBT stack, CAPSARII delineates a practical roadmap from laboratory baselines to mission-ready soldier monitoring in both training and operational scenarios.
