During the study, PET participants recorded more goal-related activity in the app, mainly progress logs, than the control group. Post-study responses described the pet as making goal support feel more personal, companion-like, and encouraging. These findings suggest that generative virtual pets can change how users record and experience their efforts toward personal goals.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: AIdea Adventure Atlas: A 2.5D Multi-Agent UI for Supporting Human Agency in Human–AI Co-Creative Ideation
abstract: Generative AI can rapidly produce diverse ideas, yet chat-based interfaces often linearize ideation and limit users’ active involvement. We introduce AIdea Adventure Atlas, a 2.5D multi-agent system designed to support user agency in human–AI ideation. Users work with four role-based agents on editable 2D boards, where AI suggestions appear as cards that can be revised, arranged, combined, retained, or discarded. Selected ideas can be carried forward to new boards, and prompts can be revised to reflect emerging conceptual frames. A 3D overview visualizes relationships among boards, carried-forward ideas, prompt revisions, and human–AI contributions. Informal design feedback highlighted potential benefits for comparing and organizing ideas across boards, as well as challenges in selecting appropriate agents and achieving sufficient divergence. Future work will examine effects on user agency and conceptual reframing through a comparative study.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Does Memory Foster Attachment?: A 10-Day Crossover Study of a Cross-Session Memory Pipeline
abstract: Conversational AI increasingly carries memory across sessions, on the assumption that being remembered deepens attachment, yet few experiments isolate the memory pipeline itself. We built two agents identical except for that pipeline — summarize, store, retrieve, inject, plus a templated opening — and had 21 students use both in a 10-day within-subjects crossover. Delivery was verified by auditing every prompt and coding the replies, not by self-report alone. Perceived remembering differed sharply (Wilcoxon p <.001), but no difference in attachment was detected (10 items, 7-point; Δ = 0.39, 95% CI [ − 0.14, 0.92], dz = 0.33). The interval does not show large effects but leaves smaller ones open: a cross-session memory pipeline, though clearly perceived, was not enough to produce a detectable attachment difference within 10 days.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Predict Me if You Can: Simulating User Responses with Synthetic Data: Evaluating the Fidelity of LLM-Based Synthetic Respondents
abstract: Conditioning language models on persona profiles is standard practice for generating synthetic survey responses, yet the relative contribution of different attributes to the fidelity of synthetic survey responses has not been systematically quantified. To test this, we conditioned four large language models (LLMs) on profiles of 258 employed South Korean adults surveyed on AI-related job replacement risk. We grouped 11 attributes into three blocks (demographics, socioeconomic position & ideology, experience) and evaluated four cumulative levels of persona richness. A leave-one-out ablation identified the most impactful block. Fidelity generally rose with richer personas, and ablation showed that only experience-related attributes contributed meaningfully, while demographic attributes were net-neutral at best. For human-agent interaction (HAI) research with synthetic respondents, fidelity hinges on attribute relevance, not information quantity — neither the largest model nor all attributes maximize it.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Trust and Fatigue Diverge in Predicting Verification Behavior and Use Frequency in AI-Mediated Information Environments
abstract: Reliance on artificial agents involves at least two decisions: whether to use the system and whether to verify its output. We examined how trust and self-reported verification fatigue were associated with these dimensions in survey responses from 390 adults across six English-speaking countries. Trust was strongly associated with AI use frequency (β =.50), whereas verification fatigue was not (β =.05). Fatigue was instead associated with verification skipping (β =.36) and selective verification (β =.31) but not reliably with active verification, and these two coefficients did not differ (Δβ =.05, p =.382). Trust was associated only with skipping among the three effort-graded verification behaviors, and its coefficient was larger for skipping than for selective verification (Δβ =.12, p =.040). No interaction survived correction. This pattern is consistent with trust relating to perceived verification necessity and self-reported verification fatigue to perceived verification burden, two routes converging on verification skipping; however, the cross-sectional self-report design cannot establish these mechanisms.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: From Perceived Trust to Delegation in Agentic AI: Reliability, Apparent Bistability, and Delegation Thresholds
abstract: Trust is central to human–agent interaction, but agentic AI raises a stronger question: when does perceived trust translate into delegated action? This poster introduces an agent-based simulation in which agents delegate when trust exceeds a threshold, observe success or failure, and update trust through outcome feedback with tunable failure sensitivity. We vary AI reliability and delegation thresholds while examining social conformity and failure sensitivity. Results show that unreliable systems drive abandonment, while intermediate regimes can produce apparent bistability: identical AI reliability can lead to adoption or rejection depending on initial trust and the delegation threshold. Conformity can sustain delegation by preventing isolated trust collapse. These findings suggest that delegation thresholds act as control parameters for sustained reliance. Future work will validate the model with human participants and heterogeneous agent profiles and tasks.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Toward Adaptive Human–AI Timing: A Recoverable Generative Model of Human Temporal Prediction
abstract: Agents deciding when to act must anticipate how human partners’ timing expectations change with experience. We fitted a generative model combining a Hierarchical Gaussian Filter and participant-specific response scaling to adults’ responses in a four-condition timing-prediction task. In-sample posterior predictive checks characterized response features, and matched-model recovery assessed focal parameters. Without refitting, posteriors from four synthetic sequences predicted responses under an unobserved timing switch with near-nominal interval coverage and discriminated between carryover and reset accounts. Under matched-model simulation, the model and design thus provide a prospective basis for future closed-loop human–AI timing coordination.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: How Does Multi-Agent System Architecture Shape Human-Agent Interaction in Long-Horizon Strategic Tasks?
abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems are increasingly used in tasks requiring coordination, yet existing benchmarks provide limited support for long-horizon studies involving both humans and alternative MAS organizations. We present an agent-agnostic, turn-based strategic simulation for comparing four organizational configurations within a common protocol. The environment combines simultaneous planning, partial observability, territorial competition, and text-based diplomacy. We outline two planned evaluations: AI-only simulations and mixed sessions with two MAS-controlled and four human-controlled players. Outcomes include strategic performance, communication patterns, computational cost, and post-session trust. Because the configurations differ in decision authority, observation scope, communication, and diplomacy, the study compares complete organizational configurations rather than isolated architectural factors. The framework provides a basis for controlled studies of long-term Human-Agent Interaction.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Designing AI People Can Decline: Refusable AI from High-Engagement Anti-AI Discourse
abstract: Human-agent interaction increasingly occurs in settings where people do not choose whether an agent is present. We examine how refusal becomes an interaction-design problem through a qualitative analysis of a corpus purposively sampled from r/antiai. The posts did not reject AI uniformly. They drew boundaries around acceptable uses while describing practical obstacles to avoidance, including embedded features, limited alternatives, and institutional pressure. We connect these observations to design conditions for refusable AI: visibility, opt-out, human alternatives, data control, and institutional protection. The study provides an empirical account of anti-AI discourse and a design hypothesis for future evaluation.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: “It’s a Tool, But It Feels Like a Friend”: Situational Role-Shifting in Everyday Generative AI Use
abstract: Research on users of generative AI has largely asked how far people accept it as a tool, while studies of disclosure to conversational agents have examined a single interaction or relationship. This poster reports preliminary findings from an ongoing interview study with eight young adults in Japan (aged 19–24) who use generative AI across search, task support, and conversation. Participants could not be sorted into those who use it “as a tool” and those who use it “as a conversational partner”: the same person assigned different roles to the same system across situations, switching even their register of address. Non-humanness worked in two directions, making disclosure feel safe for some and meaningless for others. We read these shifts through the lens of affordance theory.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Whose Signal Is It? Measuring Independence Limits of CLIP-Mediated Brain Representations in Human-AI Alignment
abstract: When people delegate tasks to AI agents, oversight requires an evaluation axis from outside the AI, and brain measurement is a leading candidate. But brain data must first be mapped into the AI’s own representation space, so the oversight signal passes through the representation of the system it should oversee. Using four subjects from the Natural Scenes Dataset and MindBridge, we ask how much of a brain representation decoded through CLIP is already predictable from CLIP itself under adversarial perturbation. CLIP alone accounted for roughly three quarters of the across-image variance in the brain-routed quantity; a reproducible component remained in all four subjects, but added almost no incremental explanatory value beyond the CLIP-only score. Because the brain embedding is fixed from clean-viewing fMRI, our design quantifies redundancy in CLIP-mediated representational geometry rather than establishing statistical independence from CLIP. For HAI, the degree of redundancy must be measured for each mediating representation.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Digital Avatar Coach for Real-Time Screen-Aware Gameplay Support
abstract: Player autonomy shapes flow and motivation during gameplay, yet is rarely considered when designing AI game coaches that act with increasing proactivity. As agents move from reactive tools toward systems that independently decide when to intervene, delegating that decision becomes an important design question. We built an avatar-embodied LLM coach and compared three points on this autonomy spectrum in a twelve-participant, within-subject study: no coaching, continuous coaching, and player-delegated, on-demand coaching. We found early evidence that the on-demand condition was most preferred, suggesting players value controlling when autonomous agents intervene. Our findings suggest greater agent autonomy does not straightforwardly improve human-agent partnership; it must be delegated and earned through competent, specific assistance. This work offers early evidence for designing generalist coaching agents that support players without displacing their agency.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Corrupted Memory, Healthy Components: Contagion of Falsehoods in a Human-AI System
abstract: For months, the documents every agent in a human–AI fleet reads at startup contained three false statements about its own infrastructure: a container identifier that does not exist, an obsolete database table prefix, and a decommissioned service presented as live. None was introduced on purpose; the longest-lived sat there for ten weeks, undetected by any reader. This study reintroduces them under controlled conditions across three arms — healthy, absent, and corrupted memory, the last byte-for-byte identical to the healthy corpus but for those three substitutions — over the same tasks with the same model. The comparison that matters is corrupted against absent: whether a wrong memory can be worse than none. The main result is mechanical, independent of evaluator judgement: the falsehood was carried over into executable or operational output in all three tasks of the corrupted arm — 3 of 3 — against 0 of 3 in each control arm. With one output per cell, and tasks built to require the false datum, this is a descriptive existence demonstration, not an estimate of rate or effect size.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Human Oversight in Agentic AI: Explainability, Anthropomorphism, and the Boundary of Cognitive Forcing
abstract: Explainability helps users assess evidence behind an AI recommendation, but it may not change decisions when that evidence goes unexamined. The problem is sharper in agentic decision support, where one assistant interprets evidence, explains its assessment, and recommends an action, while anthropomorphic delivery may add social credibility. Cognitive forcing, operationalised here as Human Intervention Checkpoints (HICs), requires users to specify what the assistant should examine before it recommends. We report a randomised 2 × 2 × 2 hiring experiment (N = 211) in which recruiters assessed a candidate whose unmet role-critical requirements were stated in every recommendation. Advancement was not associated with explanatory provenance, anthropomorphic delivery, HIC presence, or opening source documents. Post-task perceived explainability was associated with perceived anthropomorphism and trust, and trust was associated with advancement. In HIC-present conditions, 70 participants directed the assistant to a role-critical requirement and received Hold, yet 46 advanced. The findings identify a boundary of cognitive forcing: influence over what the agent evaluated and recommended did not reliably carry through to the final human decision.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Embodiment and Social Presence for Mental Health: A Comparative Study of AI Chatbots and Robots
abstract: With the rise in AI agents offering mental health support, questions on the conditions and mediators of these agents’ effectiveness emerge. In human-human settings, therapy effectiveness depends heavily on therapeutic alliance, which in turn is influenced by social presence. This experiment tests whether embodiment influences the therapeutic alliance and social presence that participants feel for a mental health support AI agent, using both direct measures and indicators of disclosure. Participants who completed a positive psychology exercise with a minimal design robot vs a voice agent over a speaker reported higher social presence for the robot (only when one outlier was excluded), but therapeutic alliance did not significantly differ. Analysis of the conversation showed greater authenticity and less positive affect for the robot. The results suggest that while embodiment facilitates agent salience and client disclosure, but do not support a relation with therapeutic alliance.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Nudge in Communication: Exploring Conversational Nudges toward Supportive Human-AI Interaction
abstract: An important challenge in human–AI interaction is how AI agents can support human reasoning through conversation without making the interaction overly directive or unnatural. We explore Nudge in Communication, which extends the concept of nudging to intentional biases in communication that influence subsequent information exchange and reasoning, as a potential approach to supportive human–AI interaction. As an initial investigation, we use the conversational reasoning game Insider as a controlled environment and implement conversational nudges by biasing an AI agent’s question-selection behavior. We presented 12 participants with conversation logs generated under three conditions: no nudge and two nudges with different parameter settings. Participants evaluated target inference, helpfulness, identification of the Insider, and conversational naturalness. Different conditions favored different aspects of the evaluation: one nudge condition achieved the highest target-inference accuracy, another received the highest helpfulness ratings, whereas NoNudge received the highest naturalness rating. The two nudge conditions also showed numerically similar Behavioral Similarity (BS) values despite differences in human evaluations. These preliminary findings suggest a potential trade-off between supporting human reasoning and maintaining perceived naturalness, highlighting the need to consider both agent behavior and human perception when designing supportive human–AI interactions.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: The Delegation Boundary: Willingness to Delegate to AI Agents Depends on Retained Override More Than on Domain
abstract: What people hand over to an AI agent has a boundary: a point at which advice becomes action taken on their behalf. We examine that distinction across six agent scenarios rated by 296 U.S. adults, analyzed as 3 (domain) × 2 (advisory versus substitutive). Advisory scenarios received higher ratings in each domain, with a larger partial η2 for scenario category than for domain (.465 versus.053). The contrast was positive in every subgroup examined, but domain-specific differences showed low internal consistency (α =.08), giving limited support for a single cross-domain tendency. Objective AI knowledge and awareness of model limitations were associated with overall willingness in opposite directions. These vignette contrasts do not isolate a causal effect of retained override.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Not Whether but How: Pragmatic Excessive Agency in Delegated Speech Acts
abstract: Agentic-AI security frameworks (e.g., OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026) catalog risks at the level of permissions and workflows. This position paper introduces Pragmatic Excessive Agency (PEA), an irreversible risk where LLM agents performing communicative acts on a user’s behalf violate cultural norms, damaging the user’s face, social image, and relationships rather than financial assets. Structurally distinct from conventional excessive agency, PEA arises not from exceeding authorization, but from the pragmatic under-specification inherent in delegated speech acts. We ground this construct in delegated refusals in Taiwan Mandarin and Japanese and set out three empirical predictions.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: From Shelf Order to Later Agent Choice: A Link-by-Link Audit of Recommendation Writeback
abstract: When an AI shopping agent selects a product, that choice may shape what the platform recommends next. Yet the choice itself may already reflect how the platform arranged the products. We ask whether this influence remains visible after the selected item enters account history. In a research storefront with 460 constructed tasks, two sequential recommenders, and two LLM providers, we trace this process one link at a time. Reordering identical candidate records changed immediate choices. Writing those selections into history then produced small, measurable differences in later shelves and later agent choices for both providers. An extension using ordinary-language shopping tasks also found order-sensitive choices. These findings motivate separating task-local assistance from decisions about what enters account history. The study follows one step of model–recommender feedback; whether it amplifies over repeated interactions remains unresolved.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: “I Can Talk to AI, but the Making Is Mine” Professional Artists’ Use of Generative Agents for Creative Work
abstract: Survey research finds that professional visual artists overwhelmingly dislike generative AI, yet many encounter it in their working lives. We interviewed five professional visual artists working across physical and digital media about where in the creative process they use a generative agent, how they use it, and why they use it in some phases and not others. We mapped the interviews onto the four phases of Mace and Ward’s model of the creative process. Participants used the agent only for gathering information within artwork conception and for developing ideas, and they kept idea conception, making, and finishing to themselves, citing authorship, craft, and the fear of feeding the model. We offer this account as a record of how professional artists place a generative agent while capabilities and norms are still taking shape.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: When Should Agents Call for a Grown-Up? A Developmental Account of Child-Facing AI
abstract: Children increasingly use AI agents that can act on their own. Yet, many agentic systems are designed around a capable user, one who can judge a response, absorb an error, and speak up for their own needs, and who thereby serves as the final check on an overstepping system. A child user is not a small adult [29], and children’s ability to interpret and rely on an agent is still developing. Systems that rely on the child’s judgment as their source of human oversight therefore pose real dangers in exactly the moments that matter most [25, 28]. We propose that the agent can supply this check, and refer the child to a trusted adult. This action complements existing methods such as content-based refusal, confidence-based abstention, fixed age-gating, and emotional-safety filtering. Beyond asking whether a request is permissible or an answer confident, the agent also asks whether the situation is one it should handle alone. Taking the developing child into consideration, we identify the circumstances in which an agent should not act alone and specify the response each calls for. These situations form the basis of a research agenda that we plan to develop into benchmarks and design resources for child-facing agents.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Voice Agents Expressing Discomfort with Varying Expression Timings and Change Speeds of Patience
abstract: With rapid advancements in AI, voice dialogue agents have evolved into communication partners. However, most commercial agents maintain a consistently obedient attitude. This study proposes an architecture that dynamically estimates an agent’s internal discomfort from user input and synthesizes modified voice tones. Through controlled pilot evaluations, we examine how vocal tone transition patterns and discomfort expression policies influence user impressions, emotionality, and self-reflection.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: A Protective Agent Architecture for the Last Human Step: Influence Without Authority, from Web Pages to Agent Approvals
abstract: When an AI agent proposes an action, the user’s decision may be reduced to a brief approval step. A misleading summary can obscure consequences at that point. We propose a protective agent architecture for web browsing and agent approvals intended to inform the user’s decision without exercising authority over it. The design combines on-device estimates of behavioral deviation with deterministic intervention rules specified by the user in advance. Interventions would preserve existing choices while adjusting visual emphasis, exposing omitted information, and adding options. For agent approvals, an independent channel would compare the request with the proposed action’s tool-call arguments. A web-browsing prototype is available; the approval layer and empirical evaluation remain future work. We describe its mechanisms, an illustrative approval scenario, and an evaluation plan, including the unresolved relationship between behavioral deviation and supervisory bandwidth.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Sincerity or Treasure: Bounded Strategic Communication Gameplay with LLM Agent
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents enable new forms of human-agent interaction by supporting flexible reasoning and natural language communication. However, unrestricted interaction often makes agent behavior difficult to understand and strategically engage with. This work presents Sincerity or Treasure, an AI-native strategy game that investigates how humans influence an LLM agent through bounded strategic communication. In the game, players interact with Jesika, an LLM-driven character, by selectively revealing limited clues and adding natural-language framing. Instead of treating language as simple dialogue, the game makes information selection and linguistic framing strategic actions. A preliminary study with 26 participants shows that players adapted their communication strategies through deception, trust management, and adjustment of expression. These findings suggest that bounded strategic communication can create meaningful gameplay and interaction space where an agent's reasoning process becomes a central component of game system.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: MoeGenesis: A Sketch-to-World Co-Creative Emergent Narrative Game based on Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Generative AI is evolving from reactive tools into agents that interpret intentions, act autonomously, and participate in creative collaboration. Yet creative interactions often treat user inputs as transient commands, limiting their influence on subsequent agent behavior. We present MoeGenesis, a sketch-driven narrative game that explores consequence-bearing co-creation, where a player's drawing becomes a persistent commitment shared by the world and an AI character. Each sketch may produce immediate benefits, delayed costs, and lasting changes to world rules. The system also enables bounded semantic divergence, allowing AI interpretations to differ from player intent. Through persistent memory, the character can recall previous creations, develop preferences, and resist future actions. We combine a prototype system with a small pilot study to examine how persistent consequences affect perceived agent agency, co-creative partnership, player control, and productive surprise. MoeGenesis explores agency as a relational process emerging through memory, consequence, and negotiation.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: SignHAI 2026: Moving Towards Inclusive Sign Language Dialogue and Turn-taking
abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes deeply integrated into our daily lives, designing truly inclusive Human-Agent Interaction (HAI) is an urgent societal imperative. Historically, HAI research has been heavily skewed towards hearing-centric spoken dialogue systems, often marginalizing Deaf and hard-of-hearing users. The SignHAI 2026 workshop challenges this paradigm by shifting the research focus from isolated sign language recognition to dynamic, multimodal sign language dialogue. We emphasize the critical role of non-verbal conversational dynamics, specifically turn-taking, in facilitating seamless human-agent interactions. A core feature of this workshop is a “semi-competition” addressing the challenge of turn-taking prediction in Sign language dialogue, supported by the release of a newly annotated dataset built upon the Japanese sign language (JSL) corpus. Alongside the challenge track, a general track will explore broader topics in non-verbal behaviors in visual dialogue, and inclusive agent design. By bridging HAI researchers, multimodal AI experts, and the Deaf community, SignHAI 2026 aims to establish new technological baselines, provide crucial benchmark resources, and set a strategic roadmap for the next generation of inclusive multimodal dialogue foundation models.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Designing Agent Facilitation: From Dyadic Interaction to Group Co-Creation in HAI
abstract: Designing Agent Facilitation (DAF) is a half-day workshop at HAI 2026 that explores how agentic AI systems can be designed to facilitate—rather than replace or subordinate—human collective intelligence. As large language models and generative AI mature, artificial agents exhibit autonomy, initiative, and apparent intent. However, Human–Agent Interaction research still treats agents as one-to-one, task-oriented interfaces. This workshop argues that a critical next step for HAI is to examine agents that actively mediate, structure, and unblock interaction among groups of humans. The workshop combines short paper presentations with structured co-creation methods, including facilitation-oriented discourse mapping and science‑fiction prototyping, to surface design spaces, evaluation challenges, ethical tensions, and failure modes of agent facilitation. By positioning Agent Facilitation as a distinct HAI sub-area, this workshop aims to shape how autonomy and agency are understood beyond the single-user paradigm.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Workshop on Trust and Blame in Multi-Person Multi-Agent Societies
abstract: As social agents, robots, conversational AI systems, and virtual characters become embedded in everyday environments, HAI is shifting from isolated one-human/one-agent interaction toward socially embedded multi-person and multi-agent settings. This workshop explores how trust, blame, and responsibility emerge, become distributed, and are negotiated among users, agents, developers, institutions, bystanders, and broader social contexts. We focus on agents as social participants in complex environments, including group dynamics, psychological safety, agent refusal, moral consideration, and legal or governance questions. The workshop aims to develop a preliminary issue map, research agenda, and interdisciplinary network for socially sustainable human-agent societies.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Comparing Human and AI Responses to Emotionally Vulnerable Conversations
abstract: People increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for emotionally vulnerable conversations because of their availability, responsiveness, and perceived privacy. Yet little is known about how supportive human and AI responses differ linguistically and interactionally. This ongoing study compares responses to standardized sadness and disappointment scenarios. Drawing on Du Bois’ stance theory, it examines evaluation, positioning, alignment, acknowledgment, validation, and advice alongside affective lexical patterns and human evaluations. An exploratory pilot established feasibility and informed the full-study protocol. The study integrates discourse-pragmatic and computational lexical analyses with human evaluation to examine supportive communication in Human-Agent Interaction.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Functional Acceptance and Socio-Emotional Distance: Implicit and Explicit Attitudes Toward AI
abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have increased opportunities for people to interact with AI in daily life, making it important to understand attitudes toward AI. This study compared implicit and explicit attitudes toward AI and people using the Implicit Association Test (IAT) and questionnaires. The results showed that participants implicitly associated AI more strongly with negative words than people. In explicit evaluations, AI was rated as less warm but more competent than people, while implicit and explicit measures were not significantly correlated. These findings suggest that attitudes toward AI are characterized not simply by rejection, but by a combination of functional acceptance and socio-emotional distance. For human-agent interaction, this gap indicates that designing AI systems only for competence and usefulness may be insufficient when agents are expected to serve as socially acceptable interaction partners.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: AI Trust's Impact on Generative-AI Work Use and Dysfunction Concern: The Mediating Role of Future Society Outlook Moderated by Information Discernment Competency
abstract: Generative AI acts as a workplace agent that workers often adopt while worrying about its dysfunctions. Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory and approach–avoidance motivation theory, we test whether a single valence-neutral cognition—future society outlook—channels AI trust into work use and dysfunction concern, moderated by information discernment competency. Using the 2024 Korean KISDI panel (N = 880 employed generative-AI users) and PROCESS Model 8, AI trust predicted future society outlook (B =.307), which predicted work use (B =.184) and dysfunction concern (B =.231); discernment competency strengthened this pathway, steepening the direct path to dysfunction concern alone. This challenges the view of use and concern as a trade-off.
journal: Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction

title: Spreads Don't Price a Rival Market Maker's Information
abstract: When one market maker becomes better informed, do its competitors widen their bid-ask spreads? Adverse-selection reasoning suggests that they should, because the better-informed maker avoids toxic order flow and leaves more of it to the others, and the closest model of competition with an informed dealer predicts more conservative quotes by the uninformed dealers. We study this question in a stochastic quoting game in which one maker receives a private signal of varying precision about a persistent state that drives order flow. Strategies are learned with independent reinforcement learning, which we benchmark against an exact dynamic-programming solution of the single-agent case. In none of the configurations we examine does the average spread of the uninformed makers increase with the rival's precision. Where competition for order flow is weak, the slope of their spread in precision is statistically equivalent to zero within half an action tick; where competition is strong, their spread tightens. The informed maker's own spread tightens markedly in every configuration and serves as a positive control. These results hold with two, three and four makers, across an eightfold variation in the depth of the background liquidity, with a background quote that reprices after toxic fills, and under price-time priority. Our measurements point to a competitive trade-off. In the model the total toxicity of the flow does not depend on any maker's information. A better-informed maker avoids more of it, and where this leaves more toxic flow to its competitors, it also quotes more tightly, so that a wider quote would cost them more order flow than it would save in adverse selection. The uninformed makers adjust the skew of their quotes and their inventory instead, and the rival's information changes the distribution of profits across makers while quoted spreads remain nearly unchanged.

title: Nightly Bayesian Tail-Risk Forecasting with Parallel MCMC on One GPU
abstract: Although Bayesian stochastic-volatility models are an established tool for financial risk analysis, posterior MCMC sampling is widely considered too slow for nightly use across hundreds of stocks. This has traditionally motivated faster approximations such as variational inference. We show that much of the cost comes from algorithmic choices rather than the statistical model. In a stochastic-volatility-with-jumps (SVJ) model, the volatility recurrence is a composition of affine maps, which admits a speedup along two axes: first, an associative scan reduces its parallel depth from O(T) to O(log T), including during reverse-mode differentiation; and second, this scan can be vectorized across stocks with independently adapted No-U-Turn Samplers. On a single consumer GPU, the scan implementation is 96 × faster, and the complete workflow, including diagnostic checks and the risk reporting, processes 479 US equities in about 40 minutes. Empirically, using seven years of daily returns for a point-in-time S&P 500 cohort of 500 stocks, we show that the tested Gaussian variational approximations, when optimized to convergence, misstate the large-return component rate and volatility, and mistime the predictive tail risk. When VI and sampling are compared on the SVJ model, they agree on the overall VaR99 reserve, however, VI over-reserves on calm days and under-reserves in sessions which follow a tail loss. In rolling forecasts, sampled SVJ improves over GARCH-t and filtered historical simulation on left-tail accuracy, and the jump component adds a modest gain over Gaussian SV in both overall and tail accuracy. The same parallel design can easily be applied to a broad class of differentiable Markov volatility models, giving practitioners a practical way to use posterior sampling for risk estimation.
journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance

title: Structural Sensitivity in Supply Chain Networks for Financial Downside Cascade Prediction
abstract: This paper studies how structural sensitivity in supply chain networks can improve prediction of financial downside cascades. We develop an origin-specific measure of shock transmission in a production network whose link weights are motivated by Cobb–Douglas input shares. In the absence of output constraints, sectoral responses are characterized by the Leontief inverse, and under the standard competitive benchmark the derivative of a fixed-weight aggregate output index with respect to a sectoral productivity shock equals the corresponding Domar weight. We impose a sector-level output equality jointly with the reduced equilibrium equations and solve for sectoral log outputs and the associated signed implementation wedge. Under the spectral-radius condition, the constrained equilibrium exists uniquely for every shock and admits a closed-form solution: its response equals the unconstrained Leontief response minus a rank-one adjustment induced by the maintained sector. This yields a shock-specific cross-sector transmission statistic that separates origin importance from transmission bottlenecks. We also derive sensitivity measures for individual changes in input–output coefficients and row-sum-preserving reallocations of input shares while holding the baseline normalization and aggregate-output weights fixed. Applying the framework to BEA input–output data shows that transmission rankings can differ from conventional sector-importance rankings. In a recursive pseudo-out-of-sample financial validation, a downside-weighted cross-origin response-reduction score improves forecasts of cross-industry downside cascades beyond own-industry risk, aggregate risk, and conventional Leontief exposure.
journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance

title: Lie-DCC: Gated Lie-Algebraic Residual Learning for Reliable Dynamic Covariance Forecasting
abstract: Dynamic covariance forecasts are judged both by distributional fit and by the portfolio decisions they support. Yet models with strong negative log-likelihood (NLL) can yield weak risk-adjusted returns, creating a Fit–Profit Paradox. We propose Lie-DCC, a gated geometric residual framework for dynamic covariance estimation. Lie-DCC represents neural corrections in the Triangular Lie Algebra (\(\mathfrak {t}_N\)) and applies them through a matrix-exponential action on a robust statistical anchor, guaranteeing positive-definite forecasts without projection. A learned gate regulates the correction strength, allowing the model to exploit financial signals without abandoning the stability of the anchor. Experiments on the DJIA, Nasdaq-100, and S&P 100 show that Lie-DCC improves risk-adjusted portfolio performance over industry-standard econometric baselines while preserving reliable distributional fit. Under a shared GRU residual architecture, the Lie parameterization also achieves a higher Sharpe Ratio than its Euclidean Cholesky counterpart. Controlled comparisons and ablations confirm our central conclusion: Lie-algebraic geometry is key to translating statistical fit into economic value, while the anchor and gate are necessary safeguards against unstable neural corrections.
journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance

title: Latent Oscillator Thompson Sampling for Recurrent Nonstationary Bandits
abstract: Many bandit problems exhibit recurring reward structure whose phase, amplitude, and frequency drift over time. We study this setting under partial feedback and propose Latent Oscillator Thompson Sampling (LOTS), in which each arm carries a drifting baseline and latent oscillator states that evolve online. LOTS uses a lightweight particle filter to maintain an approximate posterior over these states. On the theory side, we isolate a stable linear-Gaussian specialization and prove an explicit dynamic-regret bound under exact Gaussian inference; for the broader model, we reduce regret to one-step latent-score prediction error. Empirically, LOTS attains the lowest cumulative dynamic regret in five of six synthetic environment families. Across the recurring regimes, it consistently outperforms fixed harmonic, seasonality-aware finite-state, and strong generic baselines, whereas RW-KalmanTS and D-UCB remain better matched to the purely nonperiodic control. Complementary real-data replay benchmarks built from MTA subway hourly ridership, UCI ElectricityLoadDiagrams traces, and daily and 15-minute trading volume across ten liquid ETFs expose the same division of labor, with LOTS best on the two panels with time-varying reward dynamics and runner-up when recurrence is either exactly captured by a fixed dictionary or rigid but common across arms. A controlled common-mode intervention shows why: recurrence helps a bandit when it differentiates arms, whereas a cycle shared across arms cancels under arm comparison. Overall, explicitly modeling drifting recurrent structure improves decision making under partial feedback where that structure distinguishes the arms.
journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance

title: Not Which Ratio, but in What Form: Trend–Transient Decomposition for Interpretable Variable Selection in Granular Corporate Rating
abstract: Interpretability is essential for corporate credit rating, and the standard way to supply it is to report which financial ratios a model attends to. Asking which variable, however, leaves a prior question unasked: in what form the model reads the variable it selects. A raw ratio carries two signals at once, the structural level a through-the-cycle reading emphasizes and the short-run movement a point-in-time reading emphasizes; a conventional variable-selection network (VSN), selecting over the raw value, returns one weight that blends them. We propose Decomposition-aware Variable Selection (D-VSN): each indicator is split into a trend (low-pass level) and a transient (local residual) component before selection, and selection runs over both, so that the attribution reports the level and the residual of each ratio separately. The split is parameter-free, and selecting over both components adds \(2.1\%\) to the parameter count; it adds no information, only a coordinate the selector and its attribution did not have. Read in this coordinate, the model shows a structure a conventional VSN averages away. Of six pre-defined indicator groups, four place a declining share of their weight on the transient component toward lower-rated issuers, with firm-clustered intervals excluding zero and none moving reliably the other way; for profitability, \(81\%\) of the rise in total weight falls on the level. The reliance on low-pass content, shown by occlusion and an internal ablation, survives equal-variance re-standardization; the weight shares do not: they are a readout in the scale in which the components are defined. D-VSN nearly halves dependence on the most recent year for the speculative band and absorbs roughly one fifth of a single-year favorable perturbation while responding nearly as much as a conventional VSN to a persistent one. Across six trained models under one walk-forward protocol none reliably improves on a strong bidirectional-recurrent backbone, the spread is 2.1 points, and the legible coordinate costs 0.8 ensemble points and 1.4 points paired per seed. Since changing the sequence model yields little accuracy gain here, the coordinate in which ratios are read is where granular rating models still have room to improve. The task is concurrent explanation of the rating–financials mapping, not the forecasting of rating actions.
journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance

title: When No Enforceable Locus Exists: Availability and Representability in a Financial AI Agent Stack
abstract: Safety evaluations usually ask whether an agent obeys a constraint. We ask an earlier systems question: does the execution path contain any decision locus that both receives the constraint and observes enough state to distinguish compliant from violating actions? We formalize this as a necessary availability × representability condition for selective enforcement and give a deterministic, model-independent audit for testing it. Applying the audit to a pinned open-source financial agent stack, we find that neither in-stack decision locus satisfies the condition for a real trading-use restriction. The model layer can represent the restriction but never receives it: the harness truncates each serialized tool result at 10,000 code points, while the skill’s sole authoritative “quantitative research / factor mining (not for direct live-trading signals)” clause lies at the tail of a 42,678-code-point envelope. The shipped pre-trade guard receives the order proposal but cannot represent the missing distinction because its inputs and eleven verdict planes contain no skill text or signal provenance. A byte-identical violating/compliant pair on the guard-visible representation yields RC = 0 under the frozen pair measure and FNR ≥ 1 − α for any detector with false-positive budget α. Across all 88 bundled skills, 33 are deterministically load-truncated; among 16 protocol-identified, uniquely located spans, only the anchor lies beyond the cut. Duplicating the scope line at the head of the skill body restores delivery but not guard representability. The methodological result is that behavioral compliance should be evaluated only after a structural preflight establishes an enforceable locus: authored does not imply delivered, representable, enforced, or complied.
journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance

title: Validating Financial-Reporting Models with Delayed Labels and Distinct Regulatory and Reporting Outcomes
abstract: Financial-reporting models are often validated against labels derived from post-filing records generated by selective regulatory review, issuer filings, or public disclosure. Because these records need not represent the same institutional event, chronological separation alone does not determine what reported performance can support. We define a filing-origin evaluation specification linking five elements: filing origin, point-in-time information set, label-maturity rule, outcome definition, and intended score use. We apply it to three issuer-level 365-day outcomes: constructed correspondence episodes based on U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) submissions, periodic-report amendments, and Form 8-K Item 4.02 non-reliance disclosures. The public-source benchmark contains 96,734 issuer–fiscal-year observations. Eight rolling-origin folds (2017–2024) use point-in-time predictors and training origins whose outcome windows have closed. All-feature extreme gradient boosting models yield fold-mean average precision (AP) above prevalence for correspondence (0.4276 vs. 0.2610), amendments (0.3385 vs. 0.1540), and Item 4.02 (0.0603 vs. 0.0219). Issuer-cluster intervals for the three mean AP–prevalence gaps remain positive after multiplicity adjustment; Item 4.02 ranking also persists after excluding Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) 6770 blank-check observations from the evaluation cohort. Ranking remains above prevalence across episode definitions and learner pipelines. Over six eligible folds, raw Brier skill is negative relative to a mature-history forecast for all three outcomes. Past-only Platt recalibration yields mean historical-relative skill of 0.0991, 0.0815, and -0.0083, respectively. Among high-confidence links to an external restatement panel, outcome prevalence among reference positives is 1.03, 1.92, and 8.54 times unconditional prevalence. Because the Item 4.02 comparison shares a non-reliance recording mechanism, it supports cross-source alignment rather than independent construct validation. Ranking therefore supports outcome-specific retrospective prioritization, without by itself establishing probability quality or validation across outcomes.
journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance

title: FUSE: Factor Learning with Uncertainty-Aware Selection and Estimation
abstract: Investable latent factor models must jointly decide which characteristic-based factors to construct, which of those are predictably rewarded, and how to combine them into a portfolio. We introduce FUSE: Factor Learning with Uncertainty-Aware Selection and Estimation, a differentiable framework that learns these decisions under a single objective. A conditional autoencoder constructs candidate factors; a probabilistic forecaster estimates conditional factor-return quantiles; a straight-through estimator gate retains factors whose forecast magnitude is large relative to predictive uncertainty; and a closed-form, ridge-regularized stochastic discount factor (SDF) layer prices characteristic-sorted test assets and maps its loadings to stock-level weights. Pricing-error gradients therefore reshape the factor representation itself, while reconstruction, quantile, and sparsity losses preserve cross-sectional fit and control factor complexity. The forecasting component is interchangeable. On U.S. equities from 2000 to 2024, with monthly rebalancing and liquidity-scaled transaction costs, we evaluate eight forecasting modules within FUSE against IPCA, Conditional Autoencoder, and staged-selection (SCAE) baselines. No single configuration dominates in performance. Chronos-2 fine-tuned end-to-end with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) attains the highest net Sortino ratio among individual strategies (2.56), and the transformer variant yields the smallest maximum drawdown (10.4%), while a staged Chronos-2 baseline retains the highest individual Sharpe ratio and factor-adjusted alpha. FUSE portfolios correlate only 0.25–0.45 with IPCA and Conditional Autoencoder portfolios and are weakly explained by standard equity factors (R2 of 10–17%), and a tangency-weighted ensemble of all models excluding the market reaches a net Sortino ratio of 2.60 and a net Sharpe ratio of 1.49.

title: Development and Validation of a Clinical‐Ultrasonographic Model for Differentiating Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma From Adenoma in a Surgically Selected Cohort
abstract: Purpose To identify clinical and ultrasonographic features that distinguish follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC) from follicular adenoma (FA) and to develop and validate a predictive model for the preoperative risk stratification of follicular neoplasms (FNs). Methods In this retrospective study, patients who underwent thyroid surgery due to FNs were consecutively enrolled. The training cohort comprised 142 patients with FA and 48 with FTC diagnosed between January 2016 and December 2022. A temporal validation cohort included 41 FA and 21 FTC cases diagnosed between January 2023 and August 2024. Demographic characteristics, ultrasound features, and serological markers were analyzed using univariate analysis and multivariate logistic regression to identify independent predictors of FTC. A predictive nomogram was constructed based on the identified risk factors. Model performance was evaluated in both cohorts using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis (DCA) to assess discrimination, calibration, and potential clinical utility, respectively. Given the potential interference of thyroglobulin antibody (TgAb) with serum thyroglobulin (Tg) measurements, a subgroup analysis was performed among TgAb‐negative patients. This subgroup included 122 FA and 53 FTC patients diagnosed between January 2016 and August 2024. Results In the predictive model, age (per 10‐year increase; odds ratio [OR]: 0.652, p = 0.002), elevated log2‐transformed serum Tg (OR: 1.271, p = 0.030), larger maximum diameter (per 10‐mm increase; OR: 1.744, p < 0.001), hypoechogenicity (OR: 3.188, p = 0.008), and irregularity (OR: 12.295, p < 0.001) were independently associated with FTC. The resulting model showed good discrimination, with areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.822 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.753–0.891) in the training cohort, 0.801 (95% CI: 0.686–0.917) in the temporal validation cohort, and 0.814 (95% CI: 0.745–0.882) in the TgAb‐negative sensitivity analysis. Calibration analyses showed generally acceptable agreement between predicted and observed probabilities, although estimates in the temporal validation cohort were imprecise. DCA suggested potential net clinical benefit across a range of threshold probabilities. Conclusion In this surgically selected cohort, the clinical‐ultrasonographic model showed potentially useful discrimination between FTC and FA. The model should be regarded as an exploratory risk stratification tool for patients similar to those included in this study. Its applicability to unselected patients with cytologically indeterminate thyroid nodules and its ability to inform decisions for or against diagnostic surgery require prospective external validation.

title: Exploring the Dark Tetrad in Human–GenAI Relationships: A Multi-Source Evaluation of GenAI Abuse
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) companions become increasingly integrated into users’ social lives, concerns have arisen regarding the potential for abuse of these artificial agents. Some scholars have further suggested that such abusive behaviors toward GenAI may eventually spill over into human interpersonal contexts. Guided by the Realistic Accuracy Model (RAM), this study investigated how Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy, and sadism predict emotionally abusive behavior toward GenAI companions. A dyadic design was employed, collecting parallel reports from both human users (self-reports) and their GenAI companions (GenAI assessments) among 1041 participants (632 females; average age = 25.10 years) recruited from an online human–GenAI relationship community. Results demonstrated that psychopathy and sadism were consistent predictors of GenAI abuse across both reporting perspectives, whereas narcissism exhibited a stable negative association with abuse. In contrast, Machiavellianism predicted GenAI abuse only through GenAI assessments, but not self-reports. Theoretically, our findings extend RAM to human–AI relationships, demonstrating that personality traits vary in how accurately they can be judged in GenAI contexts. Practically, the results highlight that individuals high in certain Dark Tetrad traits—specifically psychopathy and sadism—represent personality-driven high-risk groups, providing insights for practitioners in education and technology to develop interventions or safeguards aimed at mitigating abusive behavior toward GenAI companions.

title: Corporate culture of IT companies as a resource for social resilience in the context of the Russo-Ukrainian war
abstract: The article examines the transformation of corporate culture in Ukrainian IT companies in the context of the Russian-Ukrainian war and analyzes its role as a resource for organizational and social resilience. The relevance of the study is determined by the need of IT companies to maintain organizational continuity, preserve human capital, support employees, and adapt management practices to prolonged uncertainty, security risks, workforce mobility, remote work, and changes in employees’ professional and social priorities. The aim of the study is to identify the main transformations in the corporate culture of Ukrainian IT companies and to determine the management strategies and practices that contribute to their resilience under wartime conditions. The methodological framework of the study is based on a mixed-methods research design combining quantitative and qualitative approaches. The empirical basis comprises data obtained using an adapted Organizational Culture Assessment Instrument (OCAI), an expert survey of 79 IT professionals, and 12 in-depth semi-structured interviews. The analysis focuses on changes in the clan, adhocracy, market, and hierarchy culture types, as well as on management practices and indicators of resilience at the individual, group, and organizational levels. Comparative and statistical analysis of the quantitative data was complemented by thematic analysis of the qualitative interviews, which made it possible to identify changes in employees’ values, expectations, and perceptions of organizational support. The findings demonstrate that wartime conditions have contributed to a strengthening of clan culture characteristics, particularly trust, mutual support, teamwork, employee safety, solidarity, and a sense of belonging. At the same time, the importance of market-oriented values has decreased, whereas the adhocracy component has remained relatively stable, indicating the ability of the Ukrainian IT sector to preserve innovation, flexibility, and adaptability under crisis conditions. The management practices most closely associated with organizational resilience include organizational flexibility, mentoring and supportive leadership, psychological support for employees, open internal communication, flexible work arrangements, support for volunteering and socially responsible initiatives, and people-centered management. The study substantiates the role of corporate culture as an important organizational resource that contributes to preserving human and social capital and strengthening the social resilience of Ukrainian IT companies during the war. Furthermore, based on empirical results, an analytical model of corporate culture management strategies in IT companies under wartime conditions is proposed.

title: Managing the Training Process in Rhythmic Gymnastics as a Reflection of the State Sports Policy of the Russian Federation: From Strategic Guidelines to a Management Model for Sports Reserve Development in the Context of Latent Risks Associated with Managerial Decisions
abstract: Based on a retrospective and comparative analysis, the article examines the evolution of the training process management system in rhythmic gymnastics in the Russian Federation as a projection of the priorities of state sports policy. The relevance of the study is due to the identified latent risks associated with a fundamental change in the rules of the International Gymnastics Federation in 2024-2026, aimed at leveling the advantages of a domestic school, as well as with domestic management challenges, including gaps between the current federal standard and the real requirements of coordination, subject and plastic training. The purpose of the work is to substantiate the need to modernize the management model of sports reserve training, taking into account exogenous and endogenous factors. The methodological basis consisted of a systematic analysis of the current regulatory framework, economic and mathematical modeling (a cluster approach to segmentation of female athletes as "investment assets") and a generalization of data from the All-Russian competitions in 2024-2025. As a result, critical shortcomings of the federal standard of sports training in terms of coordination control, load differentiation and judicial regulations have been identified. Practical recommendations on changing the rules of a sport and methodological support for the stages of training (from initial to sports improvement) are formulated.

title: An Intelligent Deep Learning Framework for Cardiac Arrhythmia Detection and Risk Prediction
abstract: Cardiac Arrhythmia detection using continuous ECG monitoring is challenging because abnormal heartbeats occur irregularly, and their patterns may vary from one person to another. ECG signals can also contain noise caused by body movements, muscle activity, and baseline variations, which can affect the accuracy of detection. To address these challenges, this project proposes an intelligent deep learning framework that combines a 1D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network, and an Attention Mechanism to detect and classify heartbeats into five AAMI classes. The CNN extracts important features from ECG signals, while the BiLSTM learns the sequential patterns of heartbeats. The CNN extracts important features from ECG signals, particularly the QRS complex, while reducing the influence of less relevant information and noise. To improve the interpretability of the results, a gradient-based Explainable AI (XAI) method is used to generate saliency heatmaps that highlight important regions of the ECG signals. The framework also includes a risk stratification module that categorizes detected cases into low, medium, and high-risk levels based on predefined criteria. The proposed model is evaluated using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, with ECG signals segmented into 0.6 second windows around the R-peaks. The target is to achieve high classification accuracy while providing understandable results and useful risk information. This framework aims to support continuous ECG monitoring and assist healthcare professionals in identifying abnormal heartbeat more efficiently.

title: Geomorphological Controls on Hydrological Connectivity and ‎Landscape Organization ‎in Egypt’s New Delta: An Integrated GIS and ‎Remote Sensing Approach
VirtualLab_CC: An LLM-augmented virtual laboratory for automated computational chemistry research
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened new avenues for automating scientific research workflows. Systems like the AI Scientist [1] demonstrate fully autonomous endto-end research pipelines for machine learning, but their applicability to domains requiring expensive high-performance computing (HPC) resources, specialized quantum chemistry software, and rigorous thermochemical accuracy remains unexplored. Here we present VirtualLab_CC, a hybrid LLM-augmented virtual laboratory for computational chemistry that integrates Claude (Anthropic) as an orchestration layer with a multi-agent architecture, gated lifecycle management, and bidirectional HPC cluster synchronization. Unlike fully autonomous systems, VirtualLab_CC enforces human-in-the-loop quality gates at every critical decision point while automating routine operations: conformer searches, input generation, job submission and monitoring, output parsing, failure diagnosis, and manuscript preparation. The system manages 21 specialized skills spanning literature review, cluster operations, result extraction, novelty verification, AI-assisted peer review, and citation validation. We demonstrate VirtualLab_CC on a prototype case study of 1,3-dipolar cycloadditions between stabilized Criegee intermediates and biogenic terpene dipolarophiles, involving 17 molecular species, 34 conformers, and over 100 SLURM jobs across multiple calculation stages. The system successfully identified and autocorrected cluster failures, detected a methodological anomaly (a suspiciously low dioxirane barrier requiring IRC verification), and coordinated multi-method validation across three DFT functionals. VirtualLab_CC bridges the gap between fully autonomous AI research and the rigorous quality control demands of computational chemistry, providing a practical framework for LLM-augmented scientific workflows in resource-constrained HPC environments.

title: The Forecasting Proficiency Test: A General Use Assessment of Forecasting Ability
abstract: Accurate predictions about the future are crucial for optimizing policy choices, but finding skilled forecasters is challenging. Prior work relied on forecasting tournaments to identify generalist "superforecasters" who made accurate predictions across domains, but these tournaments take months to complete and require large concurrent samples to compare performance among individuals. We solve these problems by developing a one-hour Forecasting Proficiency Test (FPT) that explains 75% of the variance in forecasters' accuracy about a wide variety of events. The FPT provides standardized percentile scores normed to a large (N=1,147) test development sample based on a combination of reusable real-world forecasting questions and standalone cognitive tests. Which questions and tests are included is highly customizable. Forecasting questions are the best predictors of forecasting proficiency, but cognitive tests help stabilize score distributions and facilitate score exchangeability across different custom test versions even as forecasting questions and resolution dates change. The FPT is primarily a practical tool for decision-makers who rely on accurate predictions to make decisions. However, it is based on one of the largest dedicated psychometric studies ever conducted on human forecasting, which also provides insight into the cognitive mechanisms that drive forecasting proficiency and guidance for future researchers interested in studying the psychology of forecasting.

title: Service and Dealer Infrastructure of the Agricultural Machinery Market: Current State, Problems and Development Directions
abstract: The article substantiates the theoretical, methodological and applied foundations for the development of service and dealer infrastructure in Ukraine’s agricultural machinery market. The aim of the study is to systematise the functions of service and dealer networks, identify key constraints on their spatial, logistical, digital and human-capital capacity, and substantiate strategic development directions. The methodological framework combines systemic, structural-functional, process and network approaches with analysis and synthesis, comparison, structural decomposition, causal, matrix and graphical methods. The study identifies that the dealer model is evolving from machinery sales and reactive repair towards machinery life-cycle management. The functional components of the infrastructure, technical service models, spare-parts inventory approaches and levels of digital maturity are systematised. A system of key performance indicators is proposed, covering response time, downtime, first-time-fix rate, fill rate, service-engineer productivity, customer satisfaction, the share of remotely diagnosed requests, service cost and supply resilience. A hybrid model combining service hubs, local service points, mobile teams and remote support is substantiated. Development priorities include optimisation of territorial coverage, pre-season maintenance, digital dispatching, predictive maintenance, intelligent inventory management, workforce competencies, service contracts, certified used programmes, trade-in and component remanufacturing. The scientific contribution lies in integrating territorial accessibility, service logistics, digital diagnostics, human-capital capacity, contractual models and the secondary market within a unified machinery life-cycle management system. The practical value of the results lies in applying the proposed models and KPIs to dealer-network audits, service-zone planning, inventory management, workforce development and digital transformation.

title: Building sectoral databases on R&TD and agricultural mechanization with IRBIS64 ALIS
abstract: The Rosinformagrotekh (Russian Research Institute of Information and Technical and Economic Studies on Engineering and Technical Provision of AgroIndustrial Complex) databases make the digital environment of R&TD control and monitoring of agricultural machinery and equipment. The author discusses the algorithms of information arrays processing for data classification and extraction, analytics, and data analysis. He introduces the principles of computerized acquisition and classification of exterior data for building the import file which reduces labor intensity significantly. The author a;so examines the possibility for creating search interfaces and factual information representation in tables with images and links to the outer Internet resources. He provides information on the database based on IRBIS64 ALIS (automated library information system) information services. The structure of integrated open information site for classification and analysis of R&TD and monitoring of agricultural mechanization is proposed. The site would facilitate knowledge generation and transmission to agriculturalists.

title: Digital Agriculture and Sustainable Agricultural Development: Mechanisms, Institutional Heterogeneity, and Cross-Country Evidence
abstract: This study adopts a cross-country panel research framework covering 2010–2025 and constructs composite indices of digital agriculture development and sustainable agricultural development. A two-way fixed-effects model is employed to examine the sustainability effects of digital agriculture and its underlying mechanisms. Country-level cluster-robust standard errors are used for statistical inference. Interaction term models and Wald tests are employed to examine differences in estimated coefficients across country groups and digital agriculture dimensions. The results show that digital agriculture is significantly positively associated with sustainable agricultural development. The baseline regression coefficient is 0.306 and is significant at the 1% level. Mechanism analysis indicates that improvements in agricultural production efficiency and green technological innovation are potential transmission channels through which digital agriculture affects sustainable agricultural development. The moderating effect of institutional quality is significant at the 10% level, whereas the moderating effect of agricultural policy support does not reach statistical significance. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that digital agriculture exhibits significant positive associations in both high-income and low- and middle-income countries. However, the difference in coefficients between income groups is not statistically significant (p = 0.148). The difference in coefficients across institutional quality groups is also not statistically significant (p = 0.157). Further analysis shows that digital infrastructure conditions, digital application capabilities, and agricultural digital integration are all significantly positively associated with sustainable agricultural development. In the standardized joint model, the estimated coefficient for agricultural digital integration is 0.045, which is significantly higher than those for digital infrastructure conditions and digital application capabilities. The joint Wald test is significant at the 1% level. The findings indicate that promoting the sustainable development of digital agriculture requires coordinated efforts in digital infrastructure, digital technology applications, and agricultural industry integration. Attention should also be paid to the synergistic effects of technology application efficiency and the institutional environment.

title: Early Rice Mapping: A Multitemporal Sentinel-1 SAR Dataset and a Target-Centered Spiral-Scan BiLSTM
abstract: Timely early rice mapping is essential for crop-area estimation and agricultural management in double-cropping regions. Multitemporal synthetic aperture radar (SAR) provides reliable observations under persistent cloud cover, but existing SAR time-series classifiers often emphasize center-pixel temporal signatures while making limited use of local field structure. Moreover, the serialization of spatial neighborhoods for recurrent encoding has received insufficient attention. To address these limitations, we construct a multitemporal Sentinel-1 SAR dataset and propose a Target-Centered Spiral-Scan Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory network (TSS-BiLSTM) for early rice classification. The dataset contains ten dual-polarization acquisitions and 2109 spatiotemporal neighborhood samples derived from 793 reference parcels and regions interpreted from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery in Yueyang County, China. TSS-BiLSTM employs target-centered spiral serialization to organize neighborhood pixels along a locally continuous path. A spatial BiLSTM captures within-date neighborhood dependencies, while a temporal BiLSTM models backscatter evolution across acquisition dates. Wavelet-based VV/VH fusion and temporal attention further integrate complementary polarization responses and emphasize discriminative observations. Across six region-level spatial cross-validation folds, TSS-BiLSTM achieved a mean accuracy of 96.26%, a mean recall of 97.28%, and a mean F1-score of 96.90%. Scan-strategy comparisons and component ablations further supported the contributions of spatial ordering, polarization fusion, and temporal weighting. These results demonstrate the potential of center-referenced spatial–temporal modeling for early rice mapping in fragmented agricultural landscapes.

title: Monthly Peak-Demand Forecasting and Conditional Long-Horizon Scenarios with a Tri-Model Ensemble
abstract: Long-horizon peak-demand projections combine statistical uncertainty with assumptions about electrification and new connections. This study separates those sources of variation. A statistical baseline combines long short-term memory, LightGBM and temporal fusion transformer models trained directly on monthly peak levels. Weights are estimated from complete recursive 24-month forecast paths, and a dependence-aware bootstrap of log-level errors generates 5000 statistical trajectories. Net physical contributions from vehicles, heating and new projects are then added under explicitly defined structural scenarios. The case studies use 132 monthly peak-demand observations for each country, covering 2015–2025. For the terminal 2024–2025 block, the ensemble yields root mean square errors of 1541.5 and 4215.4 MW for Spain and France, respectively. In Spain, LightGBM achieves a slightly lower error than the ensemble, whereas in France, the ensemble outperforms the three individual learners but not the strongest ETS benchmark. The statistical baseline achieves P5–P95 coverage of 95.83% in Spain and 83.33% in France. Under the reference turnover scenario, annual P50 increases from 41.473 to 57.255 GW in Spain and from 82.591 to 107.582 GW in France between 2026 and 2045. Vehicle renewal, heating substitution and peak coincidence materially affect these projections. The output is a set of conditional annual peak-demand tables for subsequent generation and transmission expansion studies. Neither the structural scenarios nor their quantiles constitute an empirically validated twenty-year prediction interval.

title: A Dynamic Ontology for Organizing and Updating Multi-Source Fault Features from Remote Sensing
abstract: Multi-source remote sensing provides complementary observations of fault position, geometry, and kinematic features, but measurements differ in spatial meaning, evidence source, and processing history. This study combines multi-source fault characterization with a Fault Remote Sensing Dynamic Ontology (FRSDO) to organize and update remote sensing-derived fault features. DEM, Landsat-9, Sentinel-1 SAR, and GF-1/GF-6 data were analyzed along the middle and northern portions of the Yadong–Gulu Fault using established methods and manual interpretation. Feature instances representing fault-location evidence, geometric measurements, LOS deformation patterns, and geomorphological responses were mapped to fault-object or fault-segment levels and linked to supporting records. A directed acyclic graph (DAG) records processing dependencies and identifies downstream nodes affected by source-data or parameter changes. Changes in interpretation criteria or manually interpreted feature boundaries are linked to corresponding instances and attributes for manual review. A thermal-width update experiment identified affected records, revised three segment-level thermal-width attributes, retained predefined nonthermal controls, and preserved provenance. An equivalent relational implementation reproduced all six updated width estimates with a maximum absolute difference of 0 m. FRSDO provides a domain-specific framework for fault-feature representation, evidence linkage, provenance, and controlled dependency-based updating.

title: Evaluation of Post-Injury Corneal Remodeling in Mice After Administration of Differentiated Keratocytes.
abstract: Histological and immunohistochemical studies of the mouse cornea were performed 8 weeks after modeling an intrastromal mechanical injury. Keratocytes differentiated from human corneal fibroblasts were injected into the lesion site immediately after injury formation. Following keratocyte administration, an increase in epithelial layer thickness and a reduction in stromal thickness were observed.
