title: Agreement Without Information: Spurious Directional Priors in Foundation Models

authors.name: Fernando Moreno-Pino
authors.affiliation: Intelligent Systems Lab, University of Bristol, Bristol, United Kingdom

journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance
abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) can be applied to produce zero-shot forecasts of financial returns. This raises a basic reliability question: when conditional return direction is unpredictable by construction, do these models abstain or produce systematic directional forecasts? We introduce a surrogate-controlled validation protocol based on a sign-randomized null that keeps each return’s magnitude but replaces its sign with an independent fair coin. Under this null the direction carries no information, and we prove that the neutral forecast f = 0, which we call abstention, is the unique squared-loss optimum, so any non-zero forecast incurs a measurable excess risk. Applying the control to six separately released, open-weight TSFMs, we find that none abstains—every model departs significantly from zero. Given the same randomized inputs, different models tend to forecast the same direction. This shared response tracks the random sign path rather than the retained volatility, and the models agree more on the directionless null than on matched real returns. Non-abstention is universal, but the agreement is structured: five of the six share one momentum-like orientation while the sixth is mean-reverting. This orientation pattern recurs across three disjoint calendar periods, and the sign-path dependence also holds on commodity, FX, and cryptocurrency series. The protocol needs only forecasts and a construct-valid directional null, so it applies directly to new model releases. Our findings characterize model output under this control rather than its cause or deployment consequences.

title: When Should Humans Intervene? Capacity-Aware Oversight for Financial AI Agents

authors.name: Brindha Jeyaraman
authors.affiliation: Aethryx, Singapore, Singapore

journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance
abstract: Human oversight is widely prescribed for high-impact artificial intelligence, but “human in the loop” is not an operational policy when review capacity is finite and agent activity varies over time. We formulate oversight for financial AI agents as a capacity-constrained allocation problem: for each proposed action, a controller decides whether to permit automated execution or consume scarce human review. Unlike a preliminary version of this study, risk scores are not drawn conditional on the realized outcome: observable features are generated first, harm is a hidden logistic function of those features, and a logistic-regression risk model is fit on a separate 60-day, 14,264-action calibration stream, then frozen and evaluated out-of-sample on a held-out 120-day, 28,174-action test stream across five financial domains. The frozen model is well calibrated out of sample (test Brier score 0.091; predicted/observed decile harm rates agree within 1–2 points). We compare no review, random review, a calibration-frozen threshold (uncapped and capacity-truncated), daily risk ranking, a convex risk-severity heuristic, and a genuine expected-loss policy selecting marginal-benefit-maximizing cases under the model’s own optimality argument. The uncapped threshold captures 40.9% of harm value but breaches the 33-action daily capacity on 49 of 120 days; truncating it recovers feasibility at a coverage cost (36.9%). Under the hard constraint, risk ranking captures 38.9% of harm value; the expected-loss policy raises this to 45.5% (a 17% relative gain) and achieves the lowest total expected cost among all evaluated policies, 10.2% below risk ranking at the same 14.1% review rate, while random allocation captures only 13.2%. A 27-cell factorial sensitivity analysis over reviewer effectiveness, review cost, and score discrimination, plus a sweep over harm prevalence and severity dispersion, shows this advantage is stable throughout. Results are computed outputs of the stated synthetic simulation; harm prevention is evaluated in expectation via the assumed reviewer-effectiveness parameter, not observed human-review outcomes. These results show that effective human oversight is jointly a prediction, allocation, and workforce-capacity problem: calibrated risk scores alone are insufficient, and unconstrained cost optimization can redistribute review away from low-severity domains.

title: Coverage Beats Chronology: Distilling Tabular Foundation Models for Drifting, Rare-Event Financial Risk

authors.name: Tian Qin
authors.affiliation: Lehigh University, Bethlehem, USA

journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance
abstract: Distilling a tabular foundation model (TFM) into a CPU-deployable tree is established practice on IID benchmarks, where retention of the teacher’s absolute accuracy exceeds 95%, but financial risk breaks that setting twice over: the data are temporally ordered, and a gradient-boosted baseline is strong enough that the teacher’s edge is only an increment, so absolute retention stays high even when nothing useful transfers. We therefore report gain retention, Rgain, the fraction of the teacher’s advantage over a matched labels-only student that survives compression, and we factorially vary the one choice a practitioner must make: how the teacher’s soft targets are built. On frozen test windows of five temporal fraud streams (Bank Account Fraud with two bias variants, IEEE-CIS and Elliptic), a student scoring a row in 0.52 ms on one CPU core (107 × the teacher’s batched throughput) retains 96% of the teacher’s incremental advantage at a 16K-label budget (+ 8.7 pp PR-AUC). The decisive design choice is target coverage, not chronology: on BAF’s development window, labelling every available row is worth + 3.03 pp against + 0.50 pp for the construction protocol, and forward chaining, the temporally cautious scheme most practitioners reach for, is unnecessary and costs up to 3.5 pp; on frozen test windows the coverage advantage holds in all four replication streams (median + 0.97 pp over 12 cells). That advantage is conditional, and we quantify the condition: across 12 frozen-test stream–budget cells it grows with the teacher’s margin over a matched labels-only tree (r = 0.79), and where a tree already matches the foundation model the selector discards the teacher in 10 of 12 runs, making the choice moot by construction. The calibration cost that appears to accompany distillation is an artifact of temperature-scaled targets, not a property of the teacher, and inverts at no cost to ranking.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Financial Foundation Models: A Survey

authors.name: Mingjun Sun
authors.affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, USA

authors.name: Zijie Zhao
authors.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Boston, USA

authors.name: Shenbo Xu
authors.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Boston, USA

journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance
abstract: Financial foundation models increasingly support workflows spanning financial question answering, disclosure analysis, forecasting, and decision-making. In these settings, uncertainty may concern whether evidence is valid and available at the relevant time, whether an interpretation is justified, which outcomes remain plausible, or which action is preferred under costs and risk constraints. Because these objects arise at different points in a workflow, uncertainty cannot be reduced to confidence in a final output. We introduce a source-aware framework that distinguishes six sources of uncertainty across evidence and context, model and inference, and outcome and action, while treating agentic workflows as the execution layer through which uncertainty can propagate, change form, or be reduced. We develop a mechanism-based taxonomy grounded in how methods construct or verify uncertainty and reliability representations, and use it to assess their applicability across financial task domains. We further map finance-specific empirical studies across the taxonomy and task domains to characterize the current research landscape. Our analysis shows that most reviewed studies address uncertainty in individual parts of financial workflows, with limited work connecting evidence and reasoning reliability to downstream prediction and constrained action. By connecting where uncertainty arises, how it is represented, and how it bears on downstream decisions, this survey provides a unified foundation for studying and evaluating uncertainty in financial foundation models.

title: Market Impact Estimation via Causal Foundation Models

authors.name: Dennis Thumm
authors.affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore, Singapore

authors.name: Ying Chen
authors.affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore, Singapore

journal: Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance
abstract: When a trader executes a large order, the relevant question is not \emph{what will the price be?} but \emph{what would the price have been had I not traded?} Market impact is thus a causal quantity, yet classical models (Almgren--Chriss, propagators) regress price on flow, which is biased whenever informed flow moves prices through information as well as trading. We present a proof-of-concept \emph{Causal Market Simulator}: a continuous-time causal prior-data fitted network (PFN) trained on a synthetic market prior in which a hidden informational flow confounds the flow--price relation by construction, with confounding strength an exact per-episode knob. On this prior, the naive estimator's bias follows a closed form we confirm empirically (up to 68\% overestimation), while the PFN tracks the unbiased true-parameter oracle at high confounding. Its \emph{do-ablated twin}, the same model with the intervention inputs removed, collapses onto the pre-window mean. Zero-shot, the model responds at the ground-truth scale to metaorders in an ABIDES limit-order book (+0.38 pre-onset standard deviations against seed-replay counterfactuals), and its intervention response replicates on about 2,300 detected flow bursts in BTC/ETH/SOL perpetuals and 3,800 on Nasdaq equities, evidence consistent with, though not proof of, causal transfer. Off-prior the response degrades gracefully, and split-conformal recalibration repairs interval calibration. Transfer hinges on encoding the metaorder as added flow rather than a clamped price level, not on more training. A recurrent state-space variant closes the remaining shape gap: its impact accrues over execution duration where the transformer's stays flat, raising the correlation with measured metaorder impact from +0.68 to between +0.92 and +0.96, at the cost of weaker on-prior deconfounding that traces to the training recipe rather than to recurrence.

title: Exploring the implications of methodological choice for exposure and vulnerability integration in impact-based warning provision
abstract: Under a changing climate, severe weather events are expected to become increasingly impactful, prompting a shift from hazard-based to impact-based forecasts and warnings (IBFW). While IBFW systems can improve risk perception and response, their effectiveness depends on integrating high-quality exposure and vulnerability data, which remains a global challenge. This study aims to explore how different IBFW methodologies influence warning provision. Three exploratory methodological comparisons have been conducted, comparing warning levels assigned to areas based on (1) hazard intensity using wind gust footprints, (2) exposure thresholds for buildings and population, and (3) building damage states in a risk-based approach. Two case studies from New Zealand (Cyclone Cook) and the UK (Storm Eunice) were used, with automated risk modelling pipelines using RiskScape software. Results show that hazard-only approaches yield the highest proportion of red warnings, while incorporating exposure and vulnerability data reduces the number and severity of warnings, with notable differences between countries and asset types. The urban-rural bias is demonstrated through comparing warning levels assigned to areas with similar hazard severity and varying population levels. The risk-based approach, though more nuanced, is limited by data availability and completeness, particularly for building characteristics and the availability of damage functions. These findings highlight the critical importance of matching risk assessment methodology and data selection to the intended purpose of IBFW systems, as methodological choices influence who receives warnings and at what level. Future work should address data gaps, expand and extend case studies and sensitivity experiments and explore dynamic exposure to improve IBFW system performance and societal outcomes.

title: A deep learning approach for brain tumor classification using hybrid efficient net and inception networks in MRI images.
abstract: BackgroundA brain tumor is a medical pathology, whereas biomedical imaging is a key element used to visualize the condition. Brain tumor classification is an essential imaging task for early pinpointing and treatment. Accurate and timely tumor characterization supports appropriate treatment planning, prognosis assessment and better patient outcomes.ObjectiveThis paper aims to develop an efficient hybrid deep learning model for early detection of brain tumors from MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) images.MethodsTo classify tumors, this work proposes a hybrid EfficientNet B7 and Inception V4 (ENETV4) network. The Inception network interprets spatial features for improving classification accuracy, while the EfficientNet B7 framework increases the computational efficiency to maintain high feature extraction ability. A unified feature is created by concatenating the retrieved features from the two models. To improve classification performance, a Figshare dataset comprising glioma, meningioma and pituitary tumor MRI images was used. Optimized hyperparameters enhanced generalization across the 70:20:10 train-test-validation split of the multi-sequence MRI dataset.ResultsThe proposed hybrid ENETV4 networks achieved 98.53% accuracy using an independent dataset, outperforming existing methods when evaluated on the dataset. These results accurately differentiate various kinds of tumors. This paper compares the hybrid ENETV4 model with the traditional models, reaffirming that the hybrid ENETV4 method enables effective classification of brain tumors from medical images, helping clinicians select suitable treatment strategies.ConclusionThe proposed hybrid methods provide accurate tumor classification in an early stage, supporting timely clinical decisions and treatment planning.
journal: Technology and health care : official journal of the European Society for Engineering and Medicine

title: Implementing HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) among cisgender female sex workers: A worldwide scoping review to guide the future research agenda for HIV prevention
abstract: Female sex workers (FSWs) experience a disproportionately high burden of HIV. To inform future research and policy efforts on HIV prevention, this study synthesizes global evidence on HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) among cisgender FSWs worldwide. This scoping review was conducted using six multidisciplinary databases searched up to December 2024. Titles and abstracts, then full texts, were independently screened. Data extraction comprised i) general study characteristics (UNAIDS region, country, study type, outcomes, type of PrEP, and study years), ii) detailed data of each outcome (including PrEP knowledge, a priori acceptability – interest, and effective acceptability – use, retention and adherence). Drivers and barriers to PrEP acceptability were analyzed using an adapted conceptual framework encompassing six domains: patient characteristics, individual knowledge and perceptions, medication-related factors, social processes, structural and health system factors, and sex work characteristics. After selection, 120 eligible studies were identified, mostly conducted in Eastern and Southern Africa. PrEP knowledge was initially low but increased quickly once programs were introduced. PrEP interest was consistently high across regions, driven by perceived HIV risk and desire for self‑protection. PrEP uptake, retention and adherence varied widely. Main barriers included sex work realities (i.e., unstable housing, alcohol use), social processes (i.e., stigma), individual characteristics (i.e., mobility), treatment-related characteristics (i.e., side effects), and health system challenges (i.e., clinic access constraints). Drivers included social support and reminder tools. While evidence on long‑acting PrEP remained limited, interest was consistently high as reducing daily burden. Overall, the findings support a socio-ecological understanding of PrEP engagement among FSWs, including the sex work context as a distinct intermediary layer. They highlight the need for differentiated and structurally responsive PrEP delivery models tailored to the realities of sex work. Expanding long‑acting PrEP options and improving service accessibility, community engagement, and stigma reduction strategies will be critical to strengthening HIV prevention among FSWs globally.

title: Emerging Soft Computing Technologies for Groundwater Quality Monitoring, Prediction and Management: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Groundwater is a vital resource for domestic, agricultural and industrial activities worldwide. Rapid urbanization, industrialization, intensive agricultural practices and climate change have increased the risks of groundwater pollution and depletion. Conventional monitoring methods based on field sampling and laboratory analysis are often time-consuming, costly and limited in spatial and temporal coverage, restricting timely assessment and effective groundwater management. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), geographic information systems (GIS), remote sensing (RS) and the Internet of Things (IoT) offer new opportunities to develop integrated monitoring networks to sustain long-term water security through efficient groundwater quality assessment, pollution prediction, contaminant tracking and sustainable water resource management. Following a PRISMA-based screening and eligibility assessment process, 103 relevant studies were selected and systematically analyzed to evaluate recent advances in AI, ML, GIS, RS and IoT applications for groundwater quality monitoring and management This review provides an updated overview of various recent studies and developments concerning the use of AI, ML, GIS, RS and IoT in groundwater monitoring, pollution mapping, health-risk evaluation and intelligent decision-making. It primarily emphasizes on applications of various machine learning algorithms namely artificial neural network (ANN), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) and deep learning in prediction of groundwater quality and water quality index (WQI). This review also focuses on aspects of spatial analysis using GIS and RS, vulnerability assessment and detection of pollution hot-spot and on-line groundwater quality monitoring through IoT-based networks. In addition, some main challenges such as data availability, interpretability of models, reliability of sensors, cyber security and technology implementation are discussed critically. Potential future applications such as explainable AI (XAI), Digital Twins, edge computing, federated learning and intelligent decision support system (IDSS) are also presented. The study concludes that inter-disciplinary integration of environmental science, geospatial technologies and artificial intelligence can bring about robust, scalable and intelligent groundwater.

title: Review of Machine Learning Approaches for Leaf Disease Detection in Rice Crop: Trends, Challenges, and Future Opportunities
abstract: Rice leaf disease is of important concern in developing countries, especially when the livelihood of a major population is dependent on agronomy. Rice is considered a staple crop in South Asian countries, foliar pathogens in rice cause substantial yield loss and economical burden. This review systematically examines the evolution of machine learning and state-of-the-art deep learning approaches for the detection of rice leaf disease. Unlike studies concentrated only on model performance, this review focused on the complete pipeline - spanning challenges observed during image acquisition, preprocessing steps, data characterization, features representation, classification methodology used, along with misused evaluation metrics leading to unsuccessful real-world deployment. This literature reveals a clear paradigm shift from handcrafted feature-based machine learning systems to deep learning architectures, because of their consistently high accuracy, learning discriminative representations directly from raw images without any human intervention. This review also highlights the growing demand for lightweight models for smarter IoT deployments. Overall evidence indicates that the future of automatic rice leaf detection depends on creating standardized benchmark datasets, robust cross-domain validation, and collaborating with smart agriculture frameworks combined with cognitive computer vision and domain adaptive learning, which are capable of accurate disease diagnosis under diverse field conditions.
journal: International Journal of Electrical and Electronics Engineering

title: Forecasting High Electricity Demand Using Explainable Machine Learning
abstract: The objective of this study was to predict the onset of high demand, the highest half-hourly average power, and the total duration of high demand over the next two hours using historical electricity consumption data from residential households. Half-hourly measurements from 2013 for 200 standard-tariff residential households selected from the Low Carbon London dataset were used. High demand was defined as exceeding the 90th percentile of each household’s average power values during the January–February period. The models were developed using data from 160 households; transfer performance was evaluated on the 40 households not included in model training. The process was divided into a training period (March–June), model selection in July, calibration of prediction intervals in August, and a testing period (September–December). The selected models were retrained using March–July data. Separate models were built for the three targets; Random Forest, histogram-based gradient boosting (HistGB), XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost were compared against a weekly seasonal reference. Model selection was initially based on average precision (AP) for the target and mean absolute error (MAE) for power and duration. For the residential units used in the training, the HistGB model selected during the testing period produced an AP of 0.4183; the CatBoost models produced an MAE of 0.2704 kW for power and 9.2361 minutes for duration. The contributions of historical consumption and calendar features to the model predictions were examined using the SHAP method. In the early warning evaluation, 78.81% of relevant events in known residential units were detected in advance; 60.93% of early warnings were identified as false alarms. The improvement in duration prediction relative to a reference that yields a duration of zero in every window remained limited. The findings indicate that the approach could contribute to monitoring residential demand; however, the burden of false alarms and the limited success in duration prediction must be taken into account from a practical standpoint.
journal: Balkan Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering

title: Collective Social Behaviours of AI Agents: A Survey of Causes, Effects, and Interventions
abstract: Multiple AI agents, most of them built on large language models (LLMs), are collectively deployed to complete certain tasks. Their interactions produce collective behaviours known from human societies, such as conformity, polarisation, echo chambers, and capture by zealots. These collective behaviours cannot be fully predicted or observed by studying single agents alone. In this tutorial and survey paper, we discuss thirty-three behaviours and classify them as observed, emerging, or anticipated. Nineteen major observed behaviours are reviewed in six families, namely agreement, division, minority influence and manipulation, contagion and diffusion, cooperation and coordination, and structure and hierarchy. We review the causes, effects, and interventions of each. Interventions suppress a behaviour when its effects are harmful and promote it when its effects are beneficial. We also give examples to explain key models. A synthesis section summarises the drivers and interventions shared across families and presents a perspective on the fourteen remaining behaviours, which are either recently observed, emerging, or anticipated. Emerging and anticipated behaviours can affect the stability of societies and financial markets when LLM agents become prevalent. Moreover, we present a case study with a scalar model showing that similarity-based memory retrieval acts as an endogenous confidence bound. This retrieval can produce echo chambers among simulated agents with no network homophily. Also, we evaluate diversity-aware retrieval as an intervention. Finally, we discuss open research directions. The paper is multidisciplinary, bridging the humanities and social sciences, the study of social networks, and AI.

title: Multimodal Foundation Models for Industrial Dataset Generation: Methods, Evidence, and Open Challenges
abstract: Industrial dataset generation (IDG) must preserve task-relevant defects, operating conditions, cross-modal relationships, and provenance. This critical review examines how pretrained multimodal foundation models (MFMs) and their components contribute to reusable manufacturing datasets through direct synthesis, assisted annotation, and tool-mediated construction. We compare visual inspection, numerical time series, engineering geometry, and process-linked observations by model role, conditioning resources, output interface, and validation setting, retaining conventional generators as explicit comparators. Three findings organize the synthesis. First, supervision and inference resources determine the meaning of few-shot, zero-shot, and training-free claims; frozen weights can coexist with inference-time embedding optimization. Second, the generated artifact determines the checks: image labels require boundary verification, numerical outputs require units and acquisition context, and CAD programs require execution and geometry assessment. Third, reported gains are conditional on each study's data access, split, metric, and resource budget. A six-stage lifecycle connects these comparisons to source acquisition, alignment, adaptation, screening, independent validation, and release. The resulting evaluation guidance separates artifact quality from real-task utility and supports traceable reporting of constraints, uncertainty, and cost. The mapped evidence is strongest for visual defect synthesis and CAD construction; calibrated multichannel generation and longitudinal production validation remain less established.

title: Systematic benchmarking of molecular foundation models for natural-product annotation and biosynthetic inference
abstract: Molecular foundation models offer a potential route to improve natural-product annotation and support biosynthetic inference, but their utility across these tasks remains insufficiently characterized. We benchmarked eight foundation-model representations against Morgan fingerprints across five tasks covering natural-product-likeness, natural product chemical class prediction, PMN and KEGG pathway association, and PlantCyc reaction-neighbor prediction. Models were evaluated under random and scaffold-based splits using both full data and sample-efficiency settings. In the full data setting, MolFormer achieved the highest mean AUROC for natural product likeness prediction, while Morgan fingerprints were strongest across other tasks. In the sample efficiency analyses, pretrained foundation model representations showed advantages when labeled data were scarce across several tasks. Even in the PMN pathway task, where foundation models did not outperform Morgan fingerprints individually, their embeddings provided complementary predictive information, as shown by error pattern and ensemble analyses. These results show that molecular foundation models are particularly useful for tasks related to global structural characteristics and when labeled training data are limited. This benchmark extends the evaluation of molecular foundation models beyond conventional drug-property tasks and provides a practical reference for selecting and developing representations for natural-product annotation and biosynthetic inference.

title: District-Level Rice Yield Prediction in Karnataka: Evaluating Machine Learning Models Under Different Validation Strategies
abstract: Rice is an important food crop in Karnataka, and its yield is affected by different factors such as rainfall, temperature and irrigation. Machine learning models can be used to study these factors and predict rice yield, but the accuracy of these models may change depending on how the data is divided for training and testing. This study uses district-level rice yield and climate data from Karnataka for the period 2000–2023, with 636 observations from 27 harmonised districts. Rainfall data were collected from CHIRPS, temperature data from NASA POWER and rice area, production and yield data from the ICAR-IIRR Rice APY Dashboard. Three machine learning models, Ridge Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost, were evaluated using random train-test splitting and chronological walk-forward validation, and compared with two simple baselines. The study also looks at whether irrigation information and a PMFBY policy-era indicator improve prediction results. The models achieved reasonably good scores under random splitting (average $ R ^ 2 $ of 0.693–0.726), but their $ R ^ 2 $ was lower under chronological validation (0.643–0.664), which gave a more realistic picture of how the models perform when predicting later years. A simple previous-year yield baseline also had a lower mean absolute error than every model. The additional irrigation experiment showed mixed improvements, while interestingly, the PMFBY policy-era indicator improved prediction performance across all three models in the separate repeated random-split experiment, with $ R ^ 2 $ improvements of approximately 0.019 to 0.036. A variable importance analysis of XGBoost showed that district identity was the most important input in every experiment that used the full dataset, followed by rainfall and then temperature, while the irrigation group was the most important input in the irrigation experiment. These results need to be interpreted carefully because of data limitationsf and do not establish a direct effect of the policy. The study more so highlights the importance of choosing suitable validation methods and conditions before concluding that a machine learning model is accurate.

title: Inverse Design of Multilayer Thin-Film Coatings with Neural Networks and Differentiable Transfer-Matrix Optics
abstract: A thin-film coating is a stack of nanometre-thick layers whose reflectance spectrum is set by interference. Computing the spectrum from the thicknesses (forward problem) is easy with the transfer-matrix method (TMM); finding thicknesses that give a desired spectrum (inverse problem) is hard because many different stacks give similar spectra. We build a 200 000-sample dataset of 8-layer TiO 2 /SiO 2 stacks on glass (400–800 nm), train a neural network that maps spectrum to thicknesses, show that the straightforward network fails because of non-uniqueness, fix this with a tandem network whose loss is computed through a differentiable TMM, and finally polish each prediction with an L-BFGS-B optimiser using an analytic gradient. On 300 unseen test spectra the mean spectral error falls from 0.114 (naive network) to 0.059 (tandem) to 0.013 (naive + refinement), i.e. about 9 lower than the naive network, at 0.05 s per target and with 92% of targets matched to within 0.05 mean error.

title: Toward Intelligent Net-Positive Farming: Integrating Artificial Intelligence, IoT, Digital Twins, and Measurement-Driven Regenerative Agriculture - A Comprehensive Review
Intelligent Manufacturing Scheduling Optimization Based on Genetic Algorithm and MES
abstract: Against the backdrop of intensified global manufacturing competition and the deep advancement of Industry 4.0, production scheduling, as a core link in efficient operations within intelligent manufacturing, faces challenges that traditional methods can no longer meet, such as delayed data acquisition and insufficient dynamic response. Therefore, a scheduling model for Industry 4.0 intelligent manufacturing based on a Genetic Algorithm (GA) and a Manufacturing Execution System (MES) is proposed. During the process, the particle swarm algorithm was used to optimize the Genetic Algorithm's parameters serially, thereby reducing complexity. At the same time, the ant colony algorithm was integrated to optimize key processes, improving the model's stability and convergence and establishing a scheduling optimization model that integrates data collection, rapid processing, and reasonable allocation. The experimental results show that the inventory turnover rate of the intelligent manufacturing scheduling model constructed in this study has increased by 3.24%, 4.58%, and 6.17%, respectively, compared to the control model’s. Meanwhile, the on-time delivery rate reaches 92.13% and 91.75% across two datasets, both above 91%. The task delay rates are 7.69% and 8.67%, showing significant advantages over the comparison models at 10.45% and 11.75%, respectively. These results indicate that the proposed model can achieve efficient allocation of production resources and dynamic responsiveness, thereby improving production line efficiency and offering a new approach to intelligent manufacturing scheduling.
journal: Journal of Engineering, Project, and Production Management

title: A unified YOLOv11 framework for multi-crop detection of diseases, pests and nutrient deficiencies, with preliminary field validation and mobile decision support
abstract: Diseases, insect pests and nutrient deficiencies account for substantial annual crop losses worldwide, yet field diagnosis remains largely dependent on expert visual inspection. Although deep learning has shown considerable promise, most existing studies focus on a single crop or stress category under controlled conditions, with limited attention to nutrient deficiencies and few progressing to real-world deployment. This study presents a unified crop-stress detection framework covering 53 classes (41 biotic stresses, five nutrient deficiencies and seven healthy classes) across seven economically important crops of the Oriental region of Morocco. A dual-device dataset of 159,000 images was assembled, 90.4% acquired in the field with a DSLR camera and a smartphone and 9.6% from open-access sources used for training only. A lightweight YOLOv11n detector was trained at 832 × 832 resolution, with all settings selected on a separate field-acquired validation partition. On an independent test partition not used for model selection, it achieved Precision = 0.977, Recall = 0.972, F1-score = 0.974, mAP@50 = 0.975 (95% CI 0.973–0.977) and mAP@50–95 = 0.953, outperforming YOLOv8n trained under the same protocol on every metric (mAP@50–95 = 0.934) whilst being lighter. In the complete 53-class confusion matrix, all residual misclassifications (3.2%) occurred between visually similar classes of the same stress category, a pattern requiring confirmation on externally acquired data. Performance did not depend on crop recognition alone, as multi-host classes reached a mean mAP@50 comparable to that of single-crop classes (0.968 vs 0.976). Preliminary independent validation on 150 farmer-captured field images covering five stress classes yielded an overall accuracy of 98.7% (148/150; 95% CI 95.3–99.6%). The exported ONNX model reproduced all class predictions of the original PyTorch model on these 150 images. The model was integrated into a multilingual, offline-capable mobile application developed with Flutter and ONNX Runtime Mobile. A preliminary usability assessment with the System Usability Scale, completed by the same 50 farmers, gave a mean score of 93.7 (SD 3.2), a very high value that probably also reflects social desirability and a ceiling effect. This work represents a step towards translating AI-based crop-stress detection from experimental research to practical decision support for farmers.

title: Smart agriculture: deep transfer learning frameworks for high-accuracy cotton crop disease classification
abstract: In recent years, the agricultural industry has seen significant progress in precision and accuracy, due to the remarkable improvement and development of new artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning algorithms especially for monitoring the crop health in cotton industry. However, previous research has some limitations in terms of generalizability and computational cost. These challenges have been addressed by considering the top ten deep learning frameworks such as VGG16, VGG19, InceptionV3, Xception, ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ResNet101, ResNet152, ShuffleNetV2 and EfficientNetB0 leveraging transfer learning for high-accuracy classification of cotton leaf health conditions. Utilizing the field-based SAR-CLD-2024 dataset comprising 9,137 standardized images across seven distinct leaf condition categories. In this research, we systematically examines the tradeoffs between static architectural complexity, dynamic training convergence, and generalization performance. Experimental results demonstrate that structural design and optimization strategies significantly affect diagnostic effectiveness, even within a highly imbalanced real-world test environment. Among the models tested, EfficientNetB0 achieved the highest mean accuracy of 91.29%, while ResNet50 and ResNet101 achieved strong mean accuracies of 90.48% and 89.55%, respectively. Conversely, VGG19 yielded the lowest overall accuracy of 57.63%, indicating a clear tradeoff between architectural simplicity and representation capacity for multi-class agricultural tasks. Furthermore, confusion matrix and qualitative analyses highlight that early stopping was essential for mitigating overfitting in deeper networks. While features such as herbicide damage and leaf variegation were readily captured, complicated color and textural overlays correlated with higher misclassification vulnerability in shallower models compared to deeper residual architectures. Overall, this work provides valuable insights for developing edge-oriented smart agriculture diagnostic systems withlow resource consumption.

title: Internet use and livelihood resilience: micro-level evidence from 364 household surveys in China
abstract: As agricultural digitalization advances, Internet Use is becoming an important tool that shapes how farmers access information, make production and management decisions, and respond to risks. However, evidence on the relationship between Internet Use and the Livelihood Resilience of crop-farming households remains limited and inconclusive. Using survey data from 364 crop-farming households across 18 prefecture-level cities in Sichuan Province, China, collected in 2025, this study constructs a comprehensive Livelihood Resilience index based on three dimensions—Buffer Capacity, Adaptive Capacity, and Livelihood Reconfiguration Capacity—with indicator weights determined using the Entropy Weight Method. An Endogenous Switching Regression (ESR) Model is employed to examine the relationship between Internet Use and Livelihood Resilience, together with its underlying mechanisms related to land productivity and risk perception. After accounting for self-selection bias, the Livelihood Resilience of Internet users is estimated to be 4.98% higher than under the counterfactual scenario of non-use, while for current non-users, Internet Use would increase Livelihood Resilience by 2.45% (conditional on the ESR identification assumptions). The estimated effects vary across the three resilience dimensions, with the largest effect observed for Adaptive Capacity (5.32%), followed by Buffer Capacity (3.89%) and Livelihood Reconfiguration Capacity (2.91%). The effects also differ across Internet application scenarios: Marketing-oriented Internet Use shows the largest estimated effect (5.85%), compared with Production-oriented (3.92%) and Management-oriented use (3.23%). The mechanism analysis provides evidence consistent with two potential channels: higher land productivity and stronger risk perception. Overall, this study extends the literature on the economic effects of Internet Use from a Livelihood Resilience perspective and provides empirical evidence relevant to strengthening farmers’ capacity to respond to risks in the context of digital rural development.

title: Sustainable agricultural production under climate change shocks: an analysis of impacts and adaptation strategies
abstract: Climate change is no longer an external shock to agricultural production. It has become a structural constraint, and this makes it central to any discussion of sustainable agricultural development. Drawing on recent empirical and review studies indexed in the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) and Scopus, this review organizes the evidence along four lines. (1) The theoretical pathways through which climate factors affect agricultural production run through crop physiological stress, nonlinear meteorological-statistical relationships, and economic factor allocation. In each case, the response function is threshold-dependent and state-dependent. (2) Quantitative evidence on yield and welfare losses points in a consistent direction, but magnitudes remain highly dispersed across regions, crops, and scenarios. Accounting that uses calories as the sole metric systematically underestimates costs related to nutritional quality and household welfare. (3) Climate-adaptive agricultural practices are generally effective, yet their effects have clear failure zones and sign reversals. Engineered adaptation and mitigation also trade off against each other in observable ways. (4) Future strategies should replace single-policy approaches with instrument mixes. The estimated moderating association of agricultural insurance is state-dependent: it varies with shock type and intensity and with credit and policy conditions, rather than weakening monotonically as risk intensity rises. The efficiency gains of digital technologies have not yet been conclusively shown to translate into climate resilience, and green finance and policy coordination face development-threshold constraints. This reviewed evidence points to three consistent judgments. Conventional accounting underestimates the true costs of climate change. The effectiveness of adaptation measures is conditional. And the marginal effects of single policy instruments are state-dependent: they may weaken or strengthen with shock type and intensity, and in some high-risk contexts they fail outright. Research gaps center on three areas: regional imbalances in global evidence, weak causal identification of adaptation effects, and the lack of a unified analytical framework for adaptation-mitigation trade-offs.

title: Governance and Compliance Mechanisms as Drivers of Farmer Behavior Under the New Common Agricultural Policy: A Literature Review
abstract: The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) 2023–2027 replaces compliance-based oversight with a performance-based implementation model, supported by the Performance Monitoring and Evaluation Framework (PMEF), the Integrated Administration and Control System (IACS), and remote sensing-based monitoring. This shift primarily concerns the relationship between the European Commission and the Member States; conditionality and administrative controls at the farm level remain in place. This narrative synthesis, guided by PRISMA principles, examines how these governance and compliance mechanisms relate to farmers’ attitudes, trust, and behavior. It is based on a search of the Web of Science Core Collection and includes 81 studies. The studies point to a major institutional shift, the benefits of which are contingent upon an incomplete coherence across governance levels, while control and audit mechanisms are frequently described as sources of administrative costs and complexity. Institutional trust and perceived fairness emerge as explanations for farmers’ reactions; however, the evidence is largely attitudinal, pertains to earlier periods of the CAP, and does not test trust as a mediator. Findings regarding the erosion of intrinsic motivation are mixed. Digitalization may reduce administrative burdens, but its effect on the perceived opacity of compliance verification has not yet been examined among farmers. We propose longitudinal, farm-level research and comparisons between Member States in Central and Eastern Europe and other Member States.

title: Technological Quality and Regional Variation in Common Wheat in Romania During the 2024 Drought Year
abstract: The 2024 wheat crop in Romania developed under extreme heat and severe drought affecting Southeastern Europe. This study evaluated the technological quality of 82 common wheat samples nonrandomly collected from 41 counties across seven Romanian agricultural regions. Hectoliter mass, Hagberg–Perten falling number, protein content, wet gluten content, wet gluten deformation index, and gluten index were assessed together with agrometeorological conditions, regional soil context, contamination indicators, and colorimetric traits. Mean values were 77.3 kg/hL for HM, 383 s for HFN, 14.14% for P (dry matter), 23.73% for WG, 3.31 mm for WGDI, and 81 for GI. Exploratory Pearson correlations indicated regional associations among technological-quality, environmental, contamination, and colorimetric variables. Technological quality varied regionally across different agrometeorological, contamination, and broad pedological contexts. Given the single-year design and nonrandom sampling, these associations should be interpreted as exploratory rather than causal. Higher protein or wet gluten content did not consistently correspond to better technological functionality, supporting integrated multi-parameter assessment. This approach may support wheat classification, processing, traceability, and market decisions under increasing drought risk in Romania and Southeastern Europe.

title: Estimation of Rice Leaf Area Index Coupling Feature Selection from Multi-Temporal UAV Imagery with Machine Learning
abstract: Leaf Area Index (LAI) is a key biophysical parameter characterizing crop canopy structure and growth status. Large-scale, dynamic, and high-precision estimation of LAI using remote sensing is critical for crop growth assessment and yield forecasting. This study investigates rice LAI estimation across multiple growth stages by integrating optimally selected features from multi-temporal unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery into modeling algorithms. Based on controlled experiments with varying nitrogen fertilizer gradients, rice field LAI data were synchronously collected alongside high-resolution red–green–blue (RGB) and multispectral UAV images. Vegetation spectral indices were then extracted, and principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on these indices to obtain the first principal component (PC1). Subsequently, gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) calculations were conducted on the PC1 image to extract texture features. Feature selection was performed separately using recursive feature elimination (RFE) guided by Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) for random forest (RF), variable importance in projection (VIP) for partial least squares regression (PLSR), and backward elimination for stepwise regression (SR). Each model was developed using its corresponding selected predictors for individual growth stages and the combined dataset. The results demonstrated that the RF model for the entire growth cycle performed the best, with a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.9197, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.4309, and a relative root mean square error (rRMSE) of 16.85%. The estimated LAI maps clearly revealed the spatial distribution patterns and gradient variations in LAI under different growth stages and nitrogen treatments. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that integrating multi-source, multi-temporal UAV remote sensing features with modeling algorithms enables the high-precision retrieval of rice LAI, effectively capturing within-field growth heterogeneity. This study provides reliable technical insights for dynamic crop monitoring, variable-rate fertilization decision-making, and smart agricultural management.

title: Partial Cost Information and Empirical Contingency in Building Retrofit Cost Prediction
abstract: This study retrospectively evaluated partial cost information and empirical contingency in an archived extract of public-building retrofits. The primary reporting sample comprised 246 records, with all 250 retained for sensitivity analysis. Adding four recorded component costs reduced total-cost mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 23.35% to 17.30% for genetic-algorithm-weighted case-based reasoning and from 23.05% to 14.68% for Extra Trees. The primary comparison did not establish a larger improvement for Extra Trees. Predicting the remaining cost and adding the observed subtotal produced 12.72% total-cost MAPE, but remaining-cost-weighted absolute percentage error was 19.28% and remaining-cost MAPE was 29.42%. The paired target-route difference also remained uncertain. Additional nested selection across 14 family-target routes yielded 12.64% total-cost MAPE within the same archive. The historical project-level 90th-percentile (P90) allowance was 35.47%; separate training/calibration/evaluation splits achieved 76–98% coverage with empirical P90 allowances calibrated on disjoint records. For the largest-area holdout, remaining-cost weighted error reached 46.74%, and the 35.47% historical allowance covered only 62% of cases. The selected extract differed from the other records in our 419-record research archive. Field timing and project dates were unavailable. The results support an evaluation framework, not demonstrated early-stage forecasting accuracy or a transferable contingency rate.

title: Intelligent Crop Recognition and Cultivation Structure Monitoring in an Agricultural Area of the Eastern Tibetan Plateau Based on UAV Remote Sensing
abstract: The crop planting structure is a key indicator for assessing agricultural sustainability. However, crop identification in complex plateau environments remains challenging due to limited spectral separability among crop types, low classification accuracy, and poor model transferability. In this study, a representative agricultural region in the eastern Qinghai–Tibet Plateau was chosen as the study area. High-resolution UAV imagery was utilized, and an improved ResNet18 deep learning model was developed by incorporating the CBAM (Convolutional Block Attention Module) and the AdamW optimizer (Adaptive Moment Estimation with Weight Decay). The proposed model enhances the extraction of discriminative features, enabling intelligent crop identification and planting structure monitoring of typical plateau crops. The results show that, across 687 independent test parcels, the improved ResNet18 model achieved the highest OA, precision, and F1 score—85.88%, 87.31%, and 83.62%, respectively—among all models, while its recall of 82.28% was not the highest. In the experimental area, the average planting area proportions for beans, tubers, wheat, and rapeseed were 22.30%, 10.73%, 27.44%, and 39.53%, with deviations from the actual planting proportions of +1.14, −6.70, −2.32, and +7.88 percentage points, respectively. The mapped area for tubers was underestimated by 38.44% compared to the reference area, indicating that there are notable differences in area estimation among different crop categories. It should be noted that this study only classified parcels where the cultivation of the four target crops was confirmed through field surveys. The resulting crop distribution maps rely on existing field survey information and do not represent fully automated crop mapping for all farmland parcels independent of field investigation. These findings can provide a valuable reference for monitoring agricultural planting structures and conducting crop surveys in plateau regions.

title: Workload Scheduling and Battery Dispatch in Geographically Distributed Data Centers: A Feasibility and Techno-Economic Assessment
abstract: Workload flexibility and battery storage can support data-center energy management, but evaluating their operating value requires explicit checks of execution feasibility, numerical solution quality, and economic accounting. This study assesses these dimensions in a six-region benchmark with 50,000 tasks and 2407 hourly intervals. Event-time checks reveal resource violations hidden by hourly accounting; regional reassignment restores modeled feasibility but can worsen service and cost outcomes. Same-objective dispatch comparisons and numerical sensitivity analyses improve export revenue and grid-exchange smoothness relative to the historical low-carbon result, without further reducing already-zero purchased-grid emissions. Matched controls and conditional cycle-wear tests show that balanced-policy cash savings can reverse, whereas tested cost-priority adaptations retain positive improvements. Six restricted joint mixed-integer linear programs yield no additional incumbent gain. A seven-point ε-constraint analysis of cost–grid-variation tradeoffs, followed by post hoc checks, identifies one numerically non-dominated candidate and tolerance-dominating alternatives for the other six under the stated tolerances. Auxiliary forecasting remains separate and does not establish a statistically significant advantage of the tested nonlinear predictor. The findings concern deterministic, full-information operating comparisons and do not establish full-scale joint optimality, physical charging provenance, or lifecycle investment profitability.

title: Genome-Wide Identification and Comparative Analysis of the TGA Gene Family in Theaceae Reveals Evolutionary Conservation and Lineage-Specific Expression Divergence
abstract: TGA (TGACG motif-binding factor) proteins are plant-specific group D basic leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factors that bind as-1/TGACG elements. TGA proteins regulate salicylic acid (SA)-dependent transcription and have context-dependent roles in jasmonic acid (JA)-related defense, growth, development and stress responses. Tea (Camellia sinensis) and oil tea (Camellia oleifera) are Theaceae crops grown for beverages and edible oil, and anthracnose, drought and chilling reduce their yield and quality. Although tea bZIP genes, including group D TGA members, have been cataloged, a comparative, family-wide analysis of TGA genes across representative Theaceae genomes and their cultivar-dependent responses to anthracnose has not been reported. We therefore identified TGA genes genome-wide in six representative Theaceae species: Camellia chekiangoleosa, C. oleifera, C. sinensis, Camellia crapnelliana, Camellia japonica and Stewartia sinensis. Arabidopsis thaliana was included as a reference species. We then examined their phylogeny, gene structure and conserved motifs, codon usage, duplication and collinearity, and promoter cis-elements. Public expression data for 32 TGA genes from C. sinensis, C. oleifera and C. chekiangoleosa were analyzed across tissues and under salt, drought and cold treatments, and a pericarp transcriptome dataset from the resistant ‘MY53’ and susceptible ‘MY01’ C. oleifera genotypes was reanalyzed after inoculation with Colletotrichum fructicola. The survey identified 68 non-redundant TGA genes (10–13 per species), each with intact bZIP and DOG1 domains and predicted nuclear localization. Phylogenetic analysis resolved five groups, and Theaceae members clustered mainly in Groups II and IV, where motif composition and exon–intron structure were conserved. Codon usage bias was weak (effective number of codons: 52–54; codon adaptation index: 0.77–0.80). For 27 within-species paralogous TGA pairs, Ka/Ks distributions remained below 1 (range of 0.046–0.429), and no pair exceeded the Ks > 2 saturation criterion, indicating purifying selection. In the current duplication classification, 6–11 of the 10–13 TGA genes per species were assigned to WGD- or segmental-duplication classes, but family sizes remained similar to A. thaliana (10 genes); the data therefore do not indicate substantial net family expansion. Promoters were enriched in cis-elements responsive to light, JA, SA and abscisic acid (ABA). Expression varied between tissues, and several genes were enriched in fruit and leaves. Salt, drought and cold each induced a subset of TGA genes. The 12 ColeTGA genes resolved into four cultivar-dependent expression patterns; ColeTGA3 and ColeTGA2 showed stronger increases in the resistant ‘MY53’ genotype, whereas ColeTGA7 increased in both genotypes. Together, these comparisons clarify how TGA genes have been conserved and how they diverged among the six sampled Theaceae species.

title: EBSFFormer: An Expert-Behavior-Guided Spatial–Frequency Collaborative Transformer for Remote Sensing Image Super-Resolution
abstract: Remote sensing image super-resolution requires local detail and wider structural context. The mixture-of-experts (MoE) designs compared here select or combine expert outputs without explicitly passing behavior statistics to subsequent spatial–frequency restoration. We propose EBSFFormer, which aggregates routing preferences and response-weighted proportions within restoration groups and converts them into channel gains for later spatial and frequency branches. Heterogeneous experts and a content–cumulative-change router supply these statistics. We train on AID and evaluate on AID, DIOR, DOTA, and NWPU-RESISC45 under bicubic ×4 degradation. Across three AID training seeds, EBSFFormer obtains 31.2639 ± 0.0009 dB peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), with mean improvements of 0.0121 dB over MambaIRv2 and 0.1037 dB over SwinIR. Single-checkpoint evaluation on NWPU without fine-tuning gives the highest Y-channel PSNR and structural similarity index (SSIM) among the compared methods and the third-lowest learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). Component ablations, red–green–blue (RGB) metrics, and ground-truth-referenced visual comparisons characterize the reconstruction gains. EBSFFormer has fewer parameters and lower mean latency than MambaIRv2, but the highest peak allocated memory in the runtime comparison.

title: Remote Sensing-Enhanced Geologically Constrained Reinforcement Learning with Dynamic Spatial Search for Mineral Prospectivity Mapping
abstract: Mineral prospectivity mapping typically relies on static evaluations of individual research units. Although existing spatial modeling methods capture spatial patterns and relationships, they rarely represent spatial relationships as a sequential process of decision making that depends on the current state. This limits their ability to represent spatial changes and cumulative effects. This study proposes a geologically constrained reinforcement learning framework with dynamic spatial search for mineral prospectivity mapping. The method uses a graph neural network to identify geochemical anomalies. It also integrates favorable geological conditions with surface spectral information to construct a geological environment score. Remote sensing responses further refine the spatial representation and differentiation of favorable geological environments. These scores define an integrated prospectivity field and a local geological constraint that guide an agent to move among neighboring units or stop searching. During inference, each research unit serves as an independent starting state, and its prospectivity is evaluated using both the stop-action value and path-averaged prospectivity generated by the learned policy. The chromite case study in Balikun, Xinjiang, indicates that the proposed method identifies high prospectivity areas showing some spatial correspondence with known deposits and exhibits relatively good predictive performance compared with the selected baseline methods. A comparison with a model that excludes remote sensing information provides case-specific evidence of the contribution of these enhanced geological constraints to prospectivity prioritization when the exploration area is fixed. Ablation analysis and other experiments further support the effectiveness and validity of the proposed method.

title: An Object-Level Active Semantic-Driven Posterior Probability Change Detection Method for Remote Sensing Images with Limited Annotations
abstract: Change detection in high-resolution remote sensing imagery is susceptible to the adverse effects of within-class spectral heterogeneity, shadows, and complex spatial structures. Meanwhile, change detection methods based on land-cover posterior probabilities generally rely on reliable semantic training information, making complete manual interpretation costly. To address these issues, this study develops a change detection framework that integrates SEEDS-guided SAM object construction and active learning-based interpretation with FCM-CSBN-CVAPS posterior probability inference. First, representative points of SEEDS superpixels are used as prompts for SAM to generate candidate objects and construct a mutually exclusive object partition. Second, based on the spectral statistical features of the superpixels and an XGBoost classifier, active learning is employed to select highly uncertain samples for limited manual annotation, thereby obtaining object-level semantic information. Finally, FCM is used to characterize pixel-level spectral uncertainty, while CSBN incorporates spatial context to estimate posterior probabilities of land-cover classes. Bi-temporal change measurement and changed-area extraction are then performed in the posterior probability space. Experimental results show that the proposed framework achieves stable change detection performance by manually annotating only approximately 10% of the superpixels in the target scenes. On DS1, DS2, and DS3, the Kappa coefficients reach 83.87%, 86.05%, and 90.21%, respectively, while the corresponding F1 scores are 87.62%, 91.78%, and 91.31%, achieving the highest Kappa and F1 scores among the evaluated methods under the specified experimental settings. These results indicate an effective balance between false-alarm suppression and missed-detection control for change detection using limited target-scene semantic annotations. In adaptive evaluation experiments, the mean Kappa and F1 scores reach 84.58% and 87.84%, respectively, further confirming the effectiveness and stability of the proposed framework across diverse remote sensing scenarios.
